The Stoned Ape at the Edge of History

“The mushroom spoke, and our symbiotic relationship with it is what has give…”historyethnobotany
“The mushroom spoke, and our symbiotic relationship with it is what has given us souls.”

Terence McKenna's most famous hypothesis — that psilocybin mushrooms catalyzed the evolution of human consciousness, that they sit at the origin of language and culture and the doubled brain — is almost certainly wrong in its mechanism and possibly right in its direction.

The specific claim is this: as hominids migrated out of the forest into the grasslands of Africa roughly two million years ago, they began following herds of cattle. The cattle grazed. The cattle produced dung. In the dung, particularly in the tropical lowland conditions that pertained along migration routes, grew Psilocybe cubensis mushrooms. Hominids who ate the dung — as many primates will opportunistically eat the dung of other animals for nutritional and microbiological reasons — encountered the mushrooms. At low doses, the psilocybin improved visual acuity, potentially providing an advantage in hunting. At higher doses, it produced the states of visual, auditory, and conceptual richness that McKenna associates with the origins of religious experience, language, and art.

McKenna supported this argument with data on human brain expansion: the hominin brain doubled in size over approximately two million years, from around 530 cubic centimeters in Homo habilis to around 1450 in anatomically modern humans. This expansion is real. It is one of the most dramatic brain size increases in evolutionary history. McKenna argued that psilocybin, by stimulating synaptic density and the growth of new neural connections, could plausibly have contributed to this expansion.

The problem is that this argument has two levels, and only one of them can be evaluated with current science.

The evolutionary claim — that mushroom consumption drove the doubling of the hominin brain — lacks fossil evidence and genetic confirmation. We have no mushroom residue in early hominin coprolites. We have no genetic signature of psilocybin exposure in ancient DNA. We do not have the kind of evidence that would allow us to distinguish McKenna's hypothesis from dozens of competing explanations for human brain expansion, including increased caloric density from cooking, social complexity and its cognitive demands, the selective advantages of symbolic thinking, or simple sexual selection for intelligence.

The neuroscientific claim — that psilocybin increases synaptic density and promotes the growth of new neural connections — is supported. David Nichols's 2016 Pharmacological Reviews comprehensive survey of psychedelic science documents the mechanism: psilocybin acts as an agonist at 5-HT2A receptors, with secondary effects on glutamate signaling, and produces measurable changes in cortical connectivity. More recently, research from Washington University (Shao et al., 2021) and other groups has shown that psilocybin promotes dendritic spine growth in mouse frontal cortex — the structural substrate of new synaptic connections — and that this effect persists for weeks after a single exposure. The neuroplasticity claim, in other words, is real. The evolutionary timeline it implies is speculative.

What McKenna was most right about was something more diffuse than the specific mechanism. He was right that the relationship between human beings and psychoactive plants is ancient, ubiquitous, and poorly understood. He was right that the standard scientific framework for thinking about drug use — as pathology, as addiction, as a behavior to be explained in terms of reward circuits hijacked by foreign molecules — does not begin to account for the role these substances have played in human cultural history. The ethnobotanist Richard Evans Schultes, whose 1967 NIMH symposium paper documented the extraordinary depth and sophistication of indigenous psychopharmacological knowledge, estimated that the relationship between humans and psychoactive plants predates recorded history by orders of magnitude. Seventy plant species used for intoxication globally, each with its own cultural context, ceremonial tradition, and accumulated empirical knowledge — this is not the behavior of a species stumbling accidentally into drugs. It is the behavior of a species that has organized major portions of its cultural life around these substances.

McKenna was right about that pattern. His error was in the specificity of the causal claim. He wanted to identify the exact molecule that made us human — as if there were such a thing — rather than describing the broader truth that our relationship with plant medicines is woven into what we are. The stoned ape hypothesis fails as a specific scientific claim and succeeds as a rhetorical provocation: it forces you to take seriously the possibility that something important happened at the intersection of human evolution and psychoactive plants, even if what exactly happened cannot yet be specified.

The mushroom spoke. McKenna was confident about that. What it said, and when, and what exactly it did to the brains of the creatures who ate it — those questions remain open, waiting for the kind of evidence that the fossil record may never provide.

Sources

  • McKenna, T. Food of the Gods (1992)
  • Nichols, D.E. Psychedelics. Pharmacological Reviews, 68(2) (2016)
  • Medical History of Psychedelic Drugs. Cambridge HPS dissertation (2007)

DMT in the Brain

“Something in nature knows more chemistry than we do.”neurosciencepharmacology
“Something in nature knows more chemistry than we do.”

N,N-dimethyltryptamine — DMT — is present in your body right now. It has been found in human blood, urine, cerebrospinal fluid, and brain tissue. It is structurally related to serotonin and melatonin. It is produced by the same biochemical pathway that produces serotonin. It is, in the technical sense, an endogenous compound: your body makes it.

What your body makes it for remains almost entirely unknown.

This is one of the most interesting unsolved questions in psychopharmacology, and it sits at the intersection of neuroscience, pharmacology, and the phenomenology of altered states in a way that makes it genuinely consequential rather than merely strange. The three-tier framework for evaluating claims in this area is essential: what is confirmed, what is plausible but unproven, and what is speculative.

Confirmed: DMT is present in human tissue. This was established definitively in the 1970s and has been replicated repeatedly. David Nichols's 2016 Pharmacological Reviews comprehensive review confirms the presence of endogenous DMT and documents its structural relationship to serotonin and the shared biosynthetic pathway. When administered exogenously — injected intravenously in Rick Strassman's FDA-approved studies at the University of New Mexico in the 1990s, or smoked, or consumed as part of ayahuasca — DMT produces dramatic alterations in consciousness that typically last between five and fifteen minutes (when smoked) or several hours (in ayahuasca, where MAO inhibitors from Banisteriopsis caapi prevent its rapid metabolism).

Plausible but unproven: the pineal gland as primary DMT production site. Serena Roney-Dougal, writing in the 2011 issue of Paranthropology dedicated to psi and psychedelic experience, presents the most detailed version of this hypothesis. The pineal gland — a small endocrine structure in the center of the brain — has been proposed by Strassman and others as the likely site of endogenous DMT synthesis, based on several converging lines of evidence: the pineal contains the enzyme machinery required for DMT synthesis, it is anatomically positioned in ways that might allow DMT to reach the brain's receptor systems without being metabolized before arrival, and the timing of certain peak pineal activity (near birth, near death, during REM sleep) correlates with the conditions under which people most commonly report spontaneous experiences resembling DMT states — near-death experiences, birth recall, and vivid dreams.

The hypothesis is physiologically plausible. It has not been confirmed. The specific claim that the pineal produces DMT in sufficient quantities to produce psychedelic effects in the brain requires measurement data that does not yet exist. It is not impossible. It is simply undemonstrated.

Speculative: the broader McKenna-Strassman framework in which endogenous DMT mediates naturally occurring mystical states, death experiences, and potentially psi phenomena. Terence McKenna and his brother Dennis, in True Hallucinations and its companion scientific paper, proposed that the La Chorrera experiment produced a catalysis of the brain's own DMT system — that what happened in the Amazon in 1971 was not simply the effect of externally administered tryptamines but an unlocking of an endogenous capacity. The psi and psychedelic experience literature, as documented by David Luke in Paranthropology's special issue, notes that psychedelics and psi phenomena show consistent co-occurrence across multiple cultural and experimental contexts, and proposes the shared neurochemical mechanism as a possible explanation.

This is genuinely interesting. It is not, by current evidence, more than that.

What the ayahuasca literature — the two Labate and Cavnar volumes published by Springer — adds to this picture is the therapeutic dimension. The beta-carbolines in Banisteriopsis caapi are MAO-A inhibitors, which is why orally administered DMT in ayahuasca produces a much longer experience than smoked DMT: the MAO enzymes that would otherwise metabolize DMT in the gut are blocked, allowing it to reach the brain. But harmine, one of those beta-carbolines, has an additional effect that has nothing to do with the DMT pathway: it inhibits DYRK1A, an enzyme involved in neurogenesis, and this inhibition promotes the growth of new neurons and new synaptic connections. The therapeutic effects of ayahuasca for depression, addiction, and trauma may therefore involve two parallel mechanisms: the DMT-mediated experiential component and the harmine-mediated neuroplasticity component, operating through different pathways simultaneously.

The Changa literature documents the practical consequence of this pharmacology: the addition of MAOI-containing herbs to smoked DMT extends the experience from five to fifteen minutes to thirty to forty-five minutes, and participants report qualitative differences in the character of the experience — more sustained, more integrated, with greater narrative coherence. Changa exists precisely because the DMT experience alone is too brief for the kind of processing that therapeutic benefit requires.

DMT is in your body. What it is doing there, and what it might be doing during your dreams and your deepest experiences and possibly your approach to death, remains genuinely unknown. The questions are specific enough to be scientific. The answers are not yet in. In the meantime, the most precise thing that can be said is what Terence McKenna said about the Amazon itself: something in nature knows more chemistry than we do.

Sources

  • Nichols, D.E. Psychedelics. Pharmacological Reviews, 68(2) (2016)
  • Roney-Dougal, S. in Hunter, J. (ed.) Psi and the Psychedelic Experience. Paranthropology, Vol. 2 No. 2 (2011)
  • McKenna, T. True Hallucinations (1993)
  • Labate, B. & Cavnar, C. (eds.) Ayahuasca Healing and Science. Springer (2021)

The Man Who Spent Twelve Years in the Amazon

“Stay away from Schultes, a Harvard colleague warned a graduate student in t…”ethnobotanyindigenous
“Stay away from Schultes, a Harvard colleague warned a graduate student in the 1970s. He spent a decade alone in the Amazon. He's a dinosaur. The student ignored the advice. His name was Wade Davis.”

In December 1941, a twenty-six-year-old Harvard botanist received orders that would transform his life and, eventually, the history of pharmacology. Richard Evans Schultes had come to the Amazon on a one-year grant to study indigenous arrow poisons. The Japanese had just attacked Pearl Harbor. His government needed rubber — the Japanese had taken Southeast Asia and with it the world's supply. Schultes was told to stay, help revive Amazonian rubber production, and then come back when it was done.

He stayed for twelve years.

When Schultes finally returned to Harvard in 1953, he carried something more valuable than rubber statistics: a comprehensive record of the psychoactive plant practices of dozens of Amazonian indigenous groups, the largest single collection of such documentation ever assembled by a Western scientist. He brought herbarium specimens — over 24,000 plant species, 300 previously unknown to science. He brought photographs, field notes, and chemical samples. And he brought a question that would occupy the rest of his life: how do indigenous peoples know what they know?

The question was not rhetorical. Schultes had documented practices of staggering pharmacological sophistication. The Amazonian preparation of ayahuasca combined two plants — Banisteriopsis caapi and Psychotria viridis — whose interaction was not obvious from their separate properties. The vine contained MAO inhibitors; the leaf contained DMT. Without the combination, DMT is metabolically inactive when taken orally. In an Amazon of 80,000 plant species, indigenous people had identified these two specific plants and discovered their pharmacological synergy. Schultes watched this knowledge in practice and could not account for its origin through any model Western science offered.

His answer was not mystical. Schultes was constitutionally incapable of mysticism. He wore a suit in the jungle. He called his indigenous hosts 'native peoples' with unfashionable precision when the anthropological literature oscillated between condescension and romanticism. His answer was empirical and uncomfortable: he didn't know. The knowledge was real — he could verify its pharmacological accuracy — and its origin was unexplained. He catalogued it and moved on.

At Harvard, Schultes ran the Botanical Museum for decades and became the most influential ethnobotanist of the twentieth century without ever becoming famous. His students became famous: Wade Davis, whose One River is partly a portrait of Schultes; Mark Plotkin, who founded the Amazon Conservation Team; Tim Plowman, who led the definitive botanical study of coca. They became famous partly because Schultes taught them that the story was in the field, not the institution, and partly because he never bothered to become famous himself.

Plants of the Gods, co-authored with Albert Hofmann and published in 1979, was Schultes's only popular book. It was not written for popular audiences — it was written for the record. Ninety-one psychoactive plant species, organized by chemistry and culture, with descriptions of ritual use, botanical classification, and chemical analysis. A catalogue of what was being lost.

Because that was what Schultes knew, with increasing urgency as the decades passed: it was being lost. The aspirin pill. The mission school. The road. These were destroying in years what had taken millennia to accumulate. In 1967, at a government symposium, he said: 'In the search for new hallucinogens, we have much to do and little time in which to do it.' That was fifty years ago. The time has continued to run.

What Schultes documented — the pharmacological intelligence embedded in Amazonian plant practice — was not primitive knowledge that happened to work. It was a research tradition more ancient and in some respects more sophisticated than anything Western science could produce from the same materials in the same time. The ayahuasca preparation is the example that makes this plain: no laboratory starting from scratch in an Amazon rainforest could have identified that specific combination from among 80,000 candidate species in any foreseeable timeframe.

Schultes never speculated about how it was discovered. He documented that it existed. That may have been the more important contribution — the refusal to explain away what he could not explain, and the insistence on keeping the record straight.

Sources

  • Schultes & Hofmann, Plants of the Gods (1979)
  • Davis, Wade. One River: Explorations and Discoveries in the Amazon Rain Forest (1996)
  • Plotkin, Mark. Tales of a Shaman's Apprentice (1993)
  • Harvard Magazine, Richard Evans Schultes obituary (2001)
  • Wikipedia, Richard Evans Schultes
  • Academy of Achievement, Richard Evans Schultes interview

The Curious Molecule and the Country It Broke

“For Aldous Huxley it was the next step in human evolution. For the CIA it w…”historypolicy
“For Aldous Huxley it was the next step in human evolution. For the CIA it was a potential tool for mind control. For Timothy Leary it was the liberator of humankind. The molecule was the same. The theories were not.”

On April 19, 1943, Albert Hofmann rode his bicycle home from a Sandoz laboratory in Basel, Switzerland, and arrived at a different world than the one he'd left. He had deliberately ingested 250 micrograms of a compound he'd synthesized five years earlier and then filed away when the animal tests showed nothing interesting. Now it showed something. The neighbor who brought him milk looked like a malevolent witch. The furniture attacked him. He thought he was dying.

By the following morning he was fine, and the world had a new problem.

Jay Stevens's Storming Heaven (1987) is the history of what happened to that problem over the next twenty-five years, from Hofmann's bicycle to the US government's Schedule I classification in 1968. It is one of the essential books of American cultural history, written with novelistic precision and documented with the kind of archival rigor that makes its most improbable claims verifiable. The story it tells is simultaneously a tragedy of institutional failure, a portrait of an era, and a cautionary tale whose moral has never stopped being relevant.

The structure of the story is a collision. On one side: a clinical and philosophical tradition — Osmond, Huxley, Hoffer, and eventually Grof — that understood LSD as a tool for consciousness research, with applications in treating alcoholism, depression, and end-of-life anxiety. On the other: two forces that couldn't have been more different in ideology but were identical in their interest in scale. The CIA wanted to weaponize it; the counterculture wanted to democratize it. Both succeeded in transforming a controlled clinical substance into a cultural symbol, and the clinical tradition was destroyed in the crossfire.

The CIA chapter is the one that reads most like fiction. Operation Midnight Climax was the program in which CIA operative George White dosed unwitting subjects in San Francisco safe houses while watching through one-way mirrors. White's retrospective assessment of his career, preserved in his private diary and quoted by Stevens: 'Where else could a red-blooded American boy lie, kill, cheat, steal, rape and pillage with the sanction and blessing of the All-Highest?' The program produced nothing useful in intelligence terms. What it produced, in at least one case, was a death — Frank Olson, the Army researcher who was secretly dosed by Sidney Gottlieb and fell from a New York hotel window in November 1953.

The counterculture chapter is the one that reads like elegy. Leary and Kesey were not villains. Stevens is fair enough to show that Leary's Harvard psilocybin project produced genuine results and that his early framing of the experience — careful, concerned with set and setting, grounded in serious psychological theory — was not wrong. What was wrong, or at least what was fatal, was the decision to go public with a mass advocacy campaign at exactly the moment when the clinical evidence was most promising. 'Tune in, turn on, drop out' was not a research protocol. It was a declaration of war on the social order, and the social order won.

The 1968 Schedule I designation was not a scientific conclusion. No evidence of harm was presented that exceeded what was already known, and the clinical trial record — over a thousand scientific papers, forty thousand patients, fifteen years of accumulated practice — was simply set aside. The scheduling was political: a response to the counterculture, to race panic (the drug war's racial targeting would be confirmed by Ehrlichman's 2016 admission), and to the institutional desire to control what could not be controlled.

Fifty years elapsed before the clinical research program resumed. That gap — from 1968 to approximately 2018 when the Johns Hopkins and NYU trials began producing publishable results — is what Storming Heaven mourns. The research wasn't destroyed because it failed. It was destroyed because it succeeded in reaching people the establishment didn't want illuminated.

Stevens ended his book in 1968. He could not have known that the story would resume. As of 2025, psilocybin is in Phase 3 clinical trials in the US and Europe, LSD-assisted therapy is in Phase 2 in Switzerland and Canada, and MDMA-assisted therapy for PTSD has completed Phase 3. The interruption lasted fifty-five years. The curious molecule waited.

Sources

  • Stevens, Jay. Storming Heaven: LSD and the American Dream (1987)
  • Marks, John. The Search for the Manchurian Candidate (1979)
  • Church Committee Hearings, US Senate (1975)
  • Ehrlichman, John, quoted in Dan Baum, Harper's Magazine (April 2016)
  • Hofmann, Albert. LSD: My Problem Child (1979)
  • ACLU, A Tale of Two Countries (2020)

The Anthropologist and the Snake

“The first time an Ashaninca man told me that he had learned the medicinal p…”indigenousphilosophy
“The first time an Ashaninca man told me that he had learned the medicinal properties of plants by drinking a hallucinogenic brew, I thought he was joking. But he was not smiling.”

The combinatorial problem is this: in an Amazon containing approximately 80,000 plant species, indigenous peoples identified two specific plants whose combination creates oral DMT activity. The vine, Banisteriopsis caapi, contributes beta-carboline compounds that inhibit monoamine oxidase. The leaf, Psychotria viridis, contributes dimethyltryptamine. Neither plant alone produces the sustained visionary state that the combination produces, because DMT is ordinarily metabolized before it can cross the blood-brain barrier. The combination defeats this metabolism. This requires knowing both plants and knowing their interaction.

How was this discovered? Richard Evans Schultes spent twelve years in the Amazon and never answered the question satisfactorily. When Jeremy Narby asked his Ashaninca hosts in the Peruvian Amazon in 1984, they answered without hesitation: the plants told us.

The Cosmic Serpent (1998) is Narby's decade-long investigation of what that answer might mean. It is not a credulous book, despite what its critics suggest. Narby is a Stanford-trained anthropologist who spent years trying to dismiss the answer and eventually found he couldn't. The evidence he assembled — from molecular biology, from cross-cultural mythology, from the pharmacology of DMT, from the history of scientific discovery — doesn't prove the shamanic claim. But it makes the Western dismissal of that claim look increasingly like willful blindness.

Narby's central argument operates on two tracks. The first is epistemological: Western science has two built-in assumptions that prevent engagement with the shamanic knowledge claim. First, that hallucinations are internal productions of the mind — projections, not perceptions. Second, that plants cannot communicate with humans through imagery or language. Both assumptions are cultural, not empirical. Both foreclose exactly the investigation that would be needed to evaluate the shamanic claim.

The second track is structural: the serpent. In shamanic traditions across all inhabited continents — including Siberia, where there are no serpents — the primary visionary entity is a snake or pair of snakes. Mircea Eliade documented this pattern across his life's work; Narby extended it. The double helix of DNA — visualized by Francis Crick in a structural model that resembles, in striking ways, the twin-serpent image that appears in shamanic iconography, in the caduceus of Western medicine, in creation myths from Sumer to the Pacific — is Narby's proposed referent. The shamans are seeing DNA, he suggests. Not metaphorically. Literally, at some level he cannot specify but cannot dismiss.

The critics are not wrong that this is a difficult hypothesis to test. Jacques Dubochet, a biophysicist who later won a Nobel Prize, criticized Narby for not designing an experimental test. Publishers Weekly accused him of mistaking enthusiasm for evidence. The accusation has merit: Narby's argument frequently proceeds by analogy and parallel rather than demonstration. A hexagonal pattern in an indigenous artwork does not prove knowledge of benzene rings.

But the dismissal also has a problem: the knowledge is real. Indigenous Amazonian pharmacology has produced compounds now used in Western medicine — tubocurarine from curare, which Schultes studied, is a standard surgical muscle relaxant. The pharmacological accuracy of hundreds of plant preparations has been verified by laboratory analysis. Whatever the mechanism of the knowledge, the knowledge itself is not in question. Narby is asking a question that the dismissal doesn't answer: how did they know?

Ten years after publication, Narby organized an expedition of three molecular biologists to the Peruvian Amazon to undergo ayahuasca sessions under shamanic guidance. The biologists, skeptical and methodologically rigorous, found themselves inside experiences they could not explain by their existing frameworks. The documentary Night of the Liana captures what happened. It doesn't resolve Narby's hypothesis. It demonstrates why the hypothesis is harder to dismiss than its critics suggest.

The combinatorial problem remains. The knowledge is there. The mechanism is not explained. Narby's contribution is to have held that space open — insisting that the unexplained does not become explained by being ignored — while documenting the pressures of biopiracy, deforestation, and cultural erosion that are eliminating the knowledge faster than any research program can document it. The snake is real. What it represents is the question.

Sources

  • Narby, Jeremy. The Cosmic Serpent: DNA and the Origins of Knowledge (1998)
  • Schultes, R.E. & Hofmann, A. Plants of the Gods (1979)
  • Wikipedia, Jeremy Narby
  • Publishers Weekly review, The Cosmic Serpent (1998)
  • Newswise, The Cosmic Serpent press release (1998)

The Experiment at the End of the World

“Because I am either an unsung Newton or completely nuts, there is very litt…”consciousnesshistory
“Because I am either an unsung Newton or completely nuts, there is very little room to maneuver between these two positions.”

In February 1971, five young Americans flew to Colombia, took a series of boats up the Putumayo River, and walked into a fog-bound jungle mission station called La Chorrera in search of a rare indigenous hallucinogen. They were looking for oo-koo-he, a DMT preparation used by the Witoto to communicate with 'little men.' They had brought their academic credentials (Terence McKenna was reading Chinese at Berkeley, his brother Dennis was studying botany), their sleeping bags, and an ambitious theory about the relationship between tryptamine chemistry and human consciousness.

What they found instead was a cow pasture full of psilocybin mushrooms.

True Hallucinations (1993) is Terence McKenna's account of what happened next — written twenty years after the fact, in a voice that holds together self-deprecating irony and genuine cosmic astonishment without letting either one win. It is the most honest book McKenna ever wrote, partly because he could not quite decide whether the events at La Chorrera represented a breakthrough or a breakdown, and he left that ambiguity in.

The experiment itself was Dennis's idea. He proposed that it was possible, through a specific vocalization technique during a mushroom session, to bond the DMT in the psilocybin into the body's endogenous harmala compounds — effectively creating a permanent psychedelic state in which the boundary between self and the collective unconscious would dissolve. Whether this theory was pharmacologically coherent is a question Terence left studiously open. He noted that it was either genius or madness and that the margin between the two was not visible from inside the experience.

Dennis underwent the more dramatic episode — a weeks-long altered state that his brother watched with a mixture of terror and fascination, attempting to determine whether what was happening was dissolution or evolution. Dennis was calm, voluble, and apparently in contact with something Terence couldn't access. He spoke in complex patterns. He made predictions. He was eventually fine. He went on to become one of the most rigorous neuropharmacologists working on tryptamines, and he has spent decades being carefully honest about what he does and does not believe happened at La Chorrera.

Terence's experience was different. During a late-night mushroom session in the forest, he began receiving what he described as a sustained monologue — the mushroom speaking, in his internal voice, on the nature of time, consciousness, and the relationship between human beings and the rest of the universe. He wrote it down. He called it 'the mushroom's claims.' He published them.

From this experience came the Timewave Zero theory — an attempt to map the I Ching's sixty-four hexagrams onto a mathematical model of time's qualitative structure, predicting that novelty would reach a maximum singularity on December 21, 2012. The prediction was falsified. McKenna had acknowledged it was falsifiable, which was one of his more intellectually honest positions. The broader intuition — that time has qualitative structure, that some moments are more 'novel' than others — is a philosophical claim independent of the specific mapping and remains interesting on its own terms.

What persists from La Chorrera beyond the failed prediction is the description. McKenna's account of the machine elves — 'merry elfin, self-transforming, machine creatures, looking like self-dribbling Fabergé eggs on the rebound' — has become the most reproduced phenomenological report in the DMT literature. In a 2020 Johns Hopkins survey (Davis et al., J. Psychopharmacol. 34(9):1008-1020) of 2,561 people who had already had a DMT entity encounter, McKenna's basic description was corroborated across thousands of independent accounts. It documents the phenomenology in detail but sets no prevalence rate, because every respondent was recruited for having had an encounter; the 97% figure often attached to it appears in no published paper. What he saw at Berkeley in 1965 and at La Chorrera in 1971 has since been seen by tens of thousands of people who had never read his description. The consistency of the report is a genuine scientific puzzle, regardless of what it means.

True Hallucinations does not answer the question of what happened at La Chorrera. It documents the question precisely. The book's most valuable quality is its epistemological honesty: Terence McKenna, who spent thirty years speaking with enormous confidence about the nature of reality, spent twenty years uncertain about whether the most important experience of his life was revelation or psychosis. He chose to publish the uncertainty. That is the book.

Sources

  • McKenna, Terence. True Hallucinations: Being an Account of the Author's Extraordinary Adventures in the Devil's Paradise (1993)
  • McKenna, Dennis. The Brotherhood of the Screaming Abyss (2012)
  • Wikipedia, Terence McKenna

  • Sexton et al., J. Psychopharmacol. 33(9) (2019)
  • Davis et al., J. Psychopharmacol. 34(9):1008-1020 (2020)

Soma vs. Moksha: Huxley's Two Drugs

“Thirty years separated them. In Brave New World, the drug was the problem. …”culturephilosophy
“Thirty years separated them. In Brave New World, the drug was the problem. In Island, the drug was the solution. Huxley was the same man. The difference was May 4, 1953.”

Aldous Huxley invented two fictional drugs. The first was soma — Brave New World's instrument of social control, a substance that produced pleasant numbness and kept the population docile and productive. The second was moksha — Island's instrument of liberation, a yellow mushroom that brought Palanese citizens into direct contact with the structure of existence.

Thirty years separated them. In 1931, when Brave New World was published, Huxley had never taken a psychedelic drug. He had no direct experience of what consciousness-alteration could be. Soma was an extrapolation from what he'd observed — the way alcohol, propaganda, and entertainment kept people comfortable inside systems that served their rulers' interests rather than their own.

In 1953, Humphry Osmond gave him four-tenths of a gram of mescaline in a glass of water. The world he'd been describing from the outside became, briefly, accessible from within. The Doors of Perception was the immediate result. Island, which took nine years to complete, was the deeper consequence.

The difference between the two drugs tracks exactly the difference between the two books. Soma operates on the pleasure centers — it produces happiness without content, satiety without fulfillment, peace without truth. It is a sophisticated conditioning technology. Moksha operates on the perception centers — it removes the filters that make ordinary experience tolerable and bearable and safe, and leaves the user confronting reality at a density they cannot manage through their usual cognitive shortcuts.

The political implications diverge accordingly. Soma maintains the social order by ensuring that citizens don't notice what's wrong with it. Moksha threatens the social order by ensuring that citizens cannot unsee what's wrong with it — which is why Island ends with Pala's military invasion. A society organized around genuine perception is not compatible with the interests of the oil companies that want Pala's mineral resources.

Huxley knew this. He'd spent three decades documenting how power uses consciousness-alteration as a tool of social control. What he discovered in 1953 was that the same technology — substances that alter perception — could point in the opposite direction. The question was never whether consciousness could be altered. The question was in whose interest the alteration was designed.

Sources

  • Huxley, The Doors of Perception (1954)
  • Huxley, Island (1962)
  • MIT Press Reader, When Aldous Huxley Opened the Doors of Perception (2021)
  • Wikipedia, Island (Huxley novel)

Bergson and the Brain: The Philosophical Engine

“Huxley borrowed the reducing valve from Bergson, borrowed the C.D. Broad ci…”philosophyneuroscience
“Huxley borrowed the reducing valve from Bergson, borrowed the C.D. Broad citation to give it academic credibility, and built the central neuroscientific argument of his era without any neuroscience.”

Henri Bergson proposed in 1896 that the brain's primary function was not to produce consciousness but to filter it. Most of what the mind could perceive is suppressed in the interests of practical action — what makes it through is the small portion relevant to survival and social functioning. The rest is excluded.

Aldous Huxley read this proposition and recognized it as the theoretical foundation for something he'd experienced in a Los Angeles living room in May 1953. He quoted C.D. Broad's sympathetic commentary on Bergson's argument, gave the mechanism a name — the reducing valve — and built The Doors of Perception's central claim: that mescaline works by impairing the brain's filtering function, allowing more of Mind at Large into awareness.

Huxley had no neuroscience to support this. The tools didn't exist. Brain imaging was decades away. What he had was philosophical precision and the quality of the experience itself — which felt exactly like what the reducing valve model predicted it should feel like.

Sixty-five years later, neuroscientist Robin Carhart-Harris and mathematician Karl Friston published the REBUS model: Relaxed Beliefs Under Psychedelics. Their proposal, derived from predictive coding theory and supported by fMRI data, describes psychedelics as reducing the 'precision weighting' of top-down priors — the brain's predictions about what it's about to perceive. When those predictions are weighted less heavily, bottom-up sensory information enters awareness in greater abundance and with less pre-processing.

This is Bergson's reducing valve, translated into the vocabulary of computational neuroscience. The mechanism Huxley described intuitively in 1954 — impairment of the brain's filtering function, resulting in richer but less practically organized perceptual experience — maps precisely onto what contemporary neuroscience has verified experimentally.

Huxley borrowed the reducing valve from Bergson, borrowed the C.D. Broad citation to give it academic credibility, and built the central neuroscientific argument of the psychedelic literature without any neuroscience. The argument was correct. That's either very good philosophy or very good luck.

Sources

  • Huxley, The Doors of Perception (1954)
  • Carhart-Harris & Friston, Nature Reviews Neuroscience (2019)
  • Bergson, Matter and Memory (1896)

Seven Blocks to the World's Biggest Drugstore

“The Owl Drug Company was known as the World's Biggest Drugstore. Huxley exa…”historyconsciousness
“The Owl Drug Company was known as the World's Biggest Drugstore. Huxley examined its art books while under mescaline and concluded that Botticelli had stood where he was standing.”

At some point during the eight hours, after the flowers and the folds of grey flannel trousers and the Vermeer thought, Aldous Huxley and Humphry Osmond and Maria Huxley made a seven-block walk through West Hollywood to a pharmacy called the Owl Drug Company, known locally as the World's Biggest Drugstore.

This is the strangest passage in The Doors of Perception — stranger, even, than the flowers. Huxley, under mescaline, in a pharmacy. He browsed art books in the magazine section. He turned pages. He looked at Botticelli's Judith and observed, in the purple silk of her pleated bodice, the same 'is-ness' he had been finding all morning in his living room. He concluded that Botticelli had looked at drapery with the same eyes he was currently using. He looked at Van Gogh and found him insufficient — Van Gogh's flowers were symbols of flowers, not flowers. He returned the Van Gogh to its rack.

The episode is routinely skipped over by commentators who focus on the flowers and the philosophy. But it contains Huxley's most specific claim about art: that certain painters had access, constitutionally or momentarily, to the same perceptual register that mescaline temporarily opened. The claim is not that art is inferior to the direct experience — though he says that too — but that the best art is the record of this register, and that it can be identified from within the experience.

Standing in the World's Biggest Drugstore, surrounded by aspirin and cosmetics and pop magazines, Aldous Huxley was conducting what amounted to a quality-assurance review of Western art history. Botticelli passed. Van Gogh did not. Vermeer, consulted earlier from memory, was the standard. The setting — fluorescent lights, commercial pharmacy, the mundane hum of Los Angeles in 1953 — only sharpens the absurdity and the precision of the observation.

He turned the pages. He made his assessments. He walked the seven blocks back.

Sources

  • Huxley, The Doors of Perception (1954)
  • Wikipedia, The Doors of Perception
  • MAPS edition, The Doors of Perception PDF

Cary Grant in the Psychiatrist's Chair

“Cary Grant said he had been born again. He said this publicly, in 1959, to …”historytherapy
“Cary Grant said he had been born again. He said this publicly, in 1959, to journalist Joe Hyams. The LSD sessions, he said, had cured him of everything he had been.”

In the late 1950s, before the counterculture existed, before Timothy Leary had been fired from Harvard, before the word 'psychedelic' was widely known, there was a brief period in Los Angeles when LSD-assisted therapy was simply a promising psychiatric tool used by respectable clinicians on willing patients.

Cary Grant was one of those patients. He underwent LSD sessions with psychiatrist Mortimer Hartman — not experimentally, not recreationally, but in formal clinical psychotherapy, using the drug the way Osmond and Huxley had proposed it should be used: with preparation, with a qualified guide, with intention, in a proper setting. He went repeatedly. He found it transformative.

In 1959, he told journalist Joe Hyams exactly what had happened. The resulting article — published in This Week magazine under the headline 'Cary Grant's Bizarre Experiments' — was one of the first mainstream accounts of LSD therapy. Grant described being reborn. He described crying for the first time in years. He described understanding, finally, why his four marriages had failed. He said the sessions had done for him what years of conventional therapy had not.

Huxley's Doors of Perception had created the conceptual framework for taking this kind of experience seriously — the argument that direct perceptual transformation was not hallucination but revelation, not pathology but insight. Grant's testimony was the famous-person evidence that the framework wasn't just intellectual fancy. Here was one of the most guarded men in Hollywood, describing a softening, an opening, a change that he was willing to put his name on in a national magazine.

The article was received with bewilderment more than scandal. The scandal would come later, when the counterculture made LSD a symbol of social disruption. In 1959, it was strange but not threatening — a movie star trying something odd in a psychiatrist's office and finding it useful. The small window when that was possible opened in 1953 with Huxley's book and closed around 1967 when Leary's public advocacy made any clinical framing politically untenable. Grant's sessions happened in the middle of that window, and his testimony is one of the documents that shows how different psychedelic history could have been.

Sources

  • Stevens, Jay. Storming Heaven (1987)
  • Hyams, Joe. 'Cary Grant's Bizarre Experiments,' This Week magazine (1959)
  • Huxley, The Doors of Perception (1954)

What We Teach Children Not to See

“Huxley's education argument is the passage most people never reach, buried …”culturephilosophy
“Huxley's education argument is the passage most people never reach, buried in the final pages. It is also the passage that has aged best.”

The Doors of Perception is remembered as a book about mescaline. It was written as a book about education.

The final pages — past the flowers, past Botticelli, past the philosophy of the reducing valve — contain Huxley's sharpest argument, and his most practical one. We teach children to reason verbally. We give them no training in direct perception. We have no techniques for transcending the merely conceptual. What mescaline showed him was that the verbal-conceptual mode of experience was not a baseline but a choice — and a costly one. The part of experience that language couldn't carry, that words couldn't reach, that the educational system had spent twelve years teaching him not to notice, turned out to contain a great deal.

The argument has several layers. First, that verbal education confirms the reduced awareness as the only awareness — students graduate believing that what language can describe is what exists, and that what language can't describe probably doesn't. Second, that this belief actively impedes perception: it trains people to look through experience at the concept, rather than at the experience itself. Third, that the cost is not merely aesthetic but practical: a civilization that can't perceive directly is a civilization operating on an impoverished data set.

Huxley's proposed remedy was not that everyone should take mescaline — he was careful about this, repeating that it was 'a gratuitous grace' not 'a necessity.' He argued for what we would now call contemplative education: training in direct perception alongside training in verbal reasoning, with neither privileged over the other.

Sixty years later, 'contemplative education' has entered the curriculum at hundreds of institutions. Mindfulness practices derived from Buddhist meditation traditions are taught in US public schools under secular names. Johns Hopkins now trains clinical researchers through guided psychedelic sessions, on the explicit logic that the experience is part of the professional formation. Huxley's education argument — the most ignored part of his most-read book — has quietly been implemented, piecemeal, in exactly the institutional settings he would have chosen.

Sources

  • Huxley, The Doors of Perception (1954)
  • MIT Press Reader, When Aldous Huxley Opened the Doors of Perception (2021)
  • Davis et al., J. Psychopharmacol. (2021)

The Perennial Philosopher on Drugs

“Huxley had spent two decades arguing that all genuine mystical traditions c…”mysticismphilosophy
“Huxley had spent two decades arguing that all genuine mystical traditions converge on the same truth. Mescaline gave him the experiential evidence for a thesis he had previously argued only from texts.”

In 1945, Aldous Huxley published The Perennial Philosophy — a 300-page anthology of mystical writings from across traditions, organized by his argument that all genuine mystical experience converges on the same recognition: that an impersonal divine ground underlies all particular things, and that the purpose of spiritual practice is to bring this recognition into ordinary awareness.

He had argued this entirely from texts. He had read Eckhart, the Upanishads, the Tao Te Ching, the Desert Fathers, Sufi poetry. He had not, at the time of writing, had a mystical experience himself.

In 1953, the experience arrived chemically. The flowers were not flowers in the ordinary sense. The Suchness Meister Eckhart wrote about was not a philosophical concept but a perceptual quality that the flowers had and he was witnessing. The 'direct, total awareness from the inside of Love as the primary and fundamental cosmic fact' that he described in a letter to Osmond after a later LSD session was not Vedanta as a doctrine but Vedanta as a report.

The Doors of Perception is, among other things, the story of a perennial philosopher getting evidence for his own thesis. This shapes the book's confident tone, which critics found frustrating — Huxley seemed to know what the experience meant before he had it, because he had spent twenty years studying what others who had it had said about it. He came to mescaline pre-theorized.

This is both the book's strength and its weakness. The strength: Huxley could articulate what he experienced in philosophical terms that placed it in a tradition, making it legible to readers who might otherwise dismiss it as individual hallucination. The weakness: the pre-existing framework may have shaped the experience itself — what you expect to find in altered states partially determines what you find, and Huxley arrived expecting Suchness.

The current clinical literature navigates this problem by using standardized measures — the Mystical Experience Questionnaire, the Challenging Experience Questionnaire — that assess experience before the subject has been told what to expect. The evidence they generate is, in a sense, more controlled than Huxley's. It is also, inevitably, less eloquent.

Sources

  • Huxley, The Perennial Philosophy (1945)
  • Huxley, The Doors of Perception (1954)
  • Yaden & Griffiths, Perspect. Psychol. Sci. (2021)

The Word That Changed Everything

“Osmond's winning couplet beat Huxley's losing one. The word 'psychedelic' w…”historyphilosophy
“Osmond's winning couplet beat Huxley's losing one. The word 'psychedelic' won over 'phanerothyme' because it was easier to say. The history of a field turned on a rhyming competition.”

In the spring of 1956, Aldous Huxley and Humphry Osmond were corresponding about a problem neither had solved: what to call these substances. The existing vocabulary was bad. 'Hallucinogen' was pejorative and inaccurate — the experiences were not primarily hallucinatory, and framing them as such imported the clinical assumption that what was seen wasn't there. 'Psychotomimetic' was more accurate but clinically catastrophic — it described the substances as schizophrenia simulators, which guaranteed that the only people who'd investigate them would be looking for applications in interrogation or combat psychiatry.

They needed a new word. Both submitted a proposal, each in the form of a couplet — a gentleman's bet on which would prove more durable.

Huxley's entry: 'To make this trivial world sublime, / take half a gram of phanerothyme.' Phanerothyme, from the Greek for 'making the spirit visible.' Precise, philosophical, and completely unpronounceable.

Osmond's entry: 'To fathom Hell or soar angelic, / just take a pinch of psychedelic.' Psychedelic, from psyche (soul, mind) and delos (to manifest, to reveal). Less philosophically precise but catchier, and containing a recognition that the territory was bipolar — hell was possible alongside the angelic.

Osmond's won. He introduced it formally in a 1957 paper in the Annals of the New York Academy of Sciences, and the word entered the scientific literature. It entered the cultural vocabulary via Leary and the counterculture, acquiring associations that Osmond hadn't intended and eventually becoming so culturally contaminated that researchers now regularly use 'classical serotonergic psychedelics' to avoid it.

But the word survives because the definition was good. Mind-manifesting: not adding something foreign to the mind but revealing what was already there. The dispute about whether psychedelics reveal or distort — whether Huxley's 'Mind at Large' is real or hallucinatory — is still the central dispute in the field. The word that described one side of that debate was coined in a rhyming competition in 1956.

Sources

  • Osmond, Ann. N.Y. Acad. Sci. (1957)
  • Huxley & Osmond, in Moksha (1977)
  • Nichols, Pharmacol. Rev. (2016)

Schizophrenia from the Inside

“Osmond thought the most important thing a psychiatrist could do was take me…”therapyneuroscience
“Osmond thought the most important thing a psychiatrist could do was take mescaline. Not to get high — to understand what their patients were experiencing.”

Humphry Osmond's first insight about psychedelics was clinical and it was simple: they gave him access to what his schizophrenic patients were experiencing.

At Weyburn Mental Hospital in Saskatchewan in the early 1950s, Osmond was working with patients whose subjective experience was, by definition, inaccessible to him. They reported visions, heard voices, experienced the texture of reality differently from how he experienced it. He could observe the behavioral consequences; he could adjust the medications; he could not know what it was actually like to be where they were. The gap between clinician and patient was experiential. No amount of training or empathy could bridge it without some access to the territory.

Mescaline provided that access. Not perfectly, not identically — the comparison between mescaline intoxication and schizophrenia is inexact in ways that subsequent research has documented at length. But sufficiently: what Osmond experienced under mescaline was enough to make him understand what his patients meant when they said the world had become strange and terrible and significant in ways that ordinary language couldn't carry.

He began having his clinical staff take mescaline and LSD for the same reason. This was standard practice at Weyburn before it became controversial everywhere else. The idea was not that clinicians needed the experience to function, but that they needed it to understand — to reduce the experiential gap between the person who administered the treatment and the person who needed it.

Huxley formalized this insight in Doors, writing that the mescaline experience provided a 'gratuitous grace' of understanding that was 'of inestimable value to everyone and especially to the intellectual.' But the origin of the insight was clinical, not philosophical. It came from Osmond watching his patients and realizing that the thing they most needed — to be understood rather than merely managed — required him to go somewhere he'd never been.

The contemporary movement to have clinical researchers undergo psychedelic sessions as part of their training is this same insight, sixty years later. Johns Hopkins and NYU now include guided psilocybin sessions in their clinical psychedelic research programs. The rationale: knowing the territory is part of professional formation. Osmond understood this in 1951.

Sources

  • Osmond, H. A Review of the Clinical Effects of Psychotomimetic Agents, Ann. NY Acad. Sci. (1957)
  • Huxley, The Doors of Perception (1954)
  • Vollenweider & Preller, Dialogues Clin. Neurosci. (2020)

Al Hubbard and the Mystery Captain

“Al Hubbard gave LSD to Aldous Huxley, Gerald Heard, and a remarkable number…”historyculture
“Al Hubbard gave LSD to Aldous Huxley, Gerald Heard, and a remarkable number of Hollywood figures. His methods were Osmond's; his ambition was larger. He called himself the Johnny Appleseed of LSD.”

Alfred Matthew Hubbard defies clean description. He was, depending on who was reporting and when: a bootlegger, a rumrunner, a government informant, an inventor who held early patents on radio navigation, a uranium entrepreneur, and — most relevantly for this story — the man who gave LSD to Aldous Huxley.

Hubbard encountered LSD in 1951 through a connection with Sandoz and became convinced, with the evangelical certainty he brought to everything, that it was the most important substance in human history. He bought large quantities from Sandoz, obtained credentials from a Uruguayan diplomatic service that allowed him to travel with controlled substances, and began administering sessions to everyone he thought could handle and benefit from the experience.

His contact with Osmond was through the clinical network; his contact with Huxley was through the Los Angeles intellectual circle. He turned Huxley on to LSD in 1955 — two years after Osmond's mescaline session, in a setting that reflected Hubbard's characteristic approach: music, art on the walls, careful attention to atmosphere, an implicit faith that the substance itself would do what it needed to do if the environment supported it.

Huxley found the LSD session profoundly different from mescaline — less visually intense, more emotionally transparent. He wrote to Osmond about it, comparing the experiences in the careful phenomenological language they'd developed together.

The correspondence that runs through Moksha includes references to Hubbard, always slightly at arm's length. He was useful — his distribution of LSD to cultural and intellectual figures created the milieu in which Doors of Perception was received — but he wasn't Huxley and Osmond's kind of careful. He self-titled himself the 'Johnny Appleseed of LSD,' which suggested an enthusiasm for scale that made Huxley nervous. Huxley was always worried about scale. He was right to be.

Sources

  • Stevens, Jay. Storming Heaven (1987)
  • Lattin, Don. The Harvard Psychedelic Club (2010)
  • Huxley & Osmond, in Moksha (1977)

How a Psychiatric Hospital Should Look

“Osmond coined the words 'sociofugal' and 'sociopetal' to describe spaces th…”therapyhistory
“Osmond coined the words 'sociofugal' and 'sociopetal' to describe spaces that push people apart or pull them together. The vocabulary came from his experience with psychedelics revealing how environment shapes experience.”

Humphry Osmond's contribution to the psychedelic literature is well-known — the word 'psychedelic,' the Weyburn clinical trials, the partnership with Huxley. Less known is his contribution to architecture.

At Weyburn Mental Hospital, Osmond became preoccupied with a question that his LSD sessions had made urgent: how does physical space shape psychological experience? The standard psychiatric ward of the 1950s — long corridors, institutional furniture arranged in rows, minimal natural light — seemed designed to reinforce the worst features of the conditions it was supposed to treat. Schizophrenia already made the world feel hostile and isolating; an institutional ward made it more so.

Osmond began studying how furniture arrangement and spatial design affected the behavior and reported experience of patients. He collaborated with architect Kiyoshi Izumi, who also underwent LSD sessions at Osmond's invitation, specifically to understand the spatial experience of altered states. The resulting hospital design — built in Saskatchewan in the 1960s — was the first psychiatric facility explicitly designed using experiential evidence from psychedelic research.

From this work came two words Osmond coined that entered standard design vocabulary: 'sociofugal' and 'sociopetal.' Sociofugal spaces push people apart — the standard airport lounge, rows of chairs facing the same direction, maximum individual isolation. Sociopetal spaces pull people together — the kitchen table, the campfire, circular seating. Osmond argued that most institutional spaces, including hospitals, were sociofugal by design and that this made treatment harder.

The correspondence in Moksha contains threads of this thinking, woven through the letters on consciousness and mescaline. Osmond was not a man who separated his ideas. The substance that revealed how environment shaped experience was the same substance whose clinical use was shaped by environment. The letters carry both.

Sources

  • Wikipedia, Humphry Osmond
  • Sommer, Robert. In Memoriam: Humphry Osmond. J. Environmental Psychology (2004)
  • Huxley & Osmond, in Moksha (1977)

The Parting of Ways: Huxley, Leary, and the Decision

“Huxley believed Leary's mass advocacy would destroy the clinical program. H…”historypolicy
“Huxley believed Leary's mass advocacy would destroy the clinical program. He said so in his letters to Osmond. He was right, and he couldn't stop it.”

By 1960, Aldous Huxley was concerned. He had spent seven years building, through Doors of Perception and through the letters and the lectures and the careful philosophical framing, a case that mescaline and LSD were tools for genuine psychological and spiritual development — tools that required preparation, proper setting, experienced guidance, and the kind of sustained intellectual engagement he and Osmond had brought to their own sessions.

Then Timothy Leary had his psilocybin experience in Cuernavaca in 1960, and the trajectory changed.

Huxley and Leary had met. Huxley respected Leary's intelligence and found his energy useful. But in the letters to Osmond, the concern deepens. Leary's approach — mass advocacy, public spectacle, the insistence on democratizing the experience regardless of preparation or context — was the wrong strategy for a substance that required the right conditions to work safely and well. The counterculture's enthusiasm for LSD was not the problem; the problem was that the enthusiasm was disconnecting the experience from everything Huxley thought made it meaningful.

Huxley wrote to Osmond that he was afraid Leary would provoke a crackdown. He worried that the clinical program — the careful work of Hoffer and Osmond and the hundred researchers following their methods — would be destroyed by the association with mass recreational use. He was right about the mechanism. He was right about the timeline. The crackdown came in 1968, three years after his death.

The letters in Moksha are not a record of this in detail — the most direct evidence is in Stevens's Storming Heaven, which draws on the full correspondence. But the texture is there in the published letters: Huxley in his last years, watching the wave he had helped start break in the wrong direction, unable to redirect it, still writing carefully, still arguing for the gratuitous grace rather than the political program.

Sources

  • Stevens, Jay. Storming Heaven (1987)
  • Lattin, Don. The Harvard Psychedelic Club (2010)
  • Huxley & Osmond, in Moksha (1977)

Ergot and the Pharmacist's Daughter

“Ergot had been trying to get Hofmann's attention for years. It was the fung…”historypharmacology
“Ergot had been trying to get Hofmann's attention for years. It was the fungus that stopped postpartum hemorrhage, caused the Dancing Plague of 1374, and eventually, through his hands, became LSD.”

Albert Hofmann joined Sandoz Laboratories in Basel in 1929 and was assigned to study ergot — the fungus Claviceps purpurea, which grows on rye and other grains and had been known since antiquity for two completely opposite properties.

The first: it caused uterine contractions, making it useful for stopping postpartum hemorrhage. Midwives in medieval Europe had used ergot-contaminated rye for this purpose, passing the knowledge through generations without understanding the mechanism.

The second: it caused what medieval observers called St. Anthony's Fire — a syndrome combining hallucinations, convulsions, burning sensations in the extremities, and sometimes gangrene. The Paris epidemic of 1418 killed fifty thousand people. The Dancing Plague of 1374, in which hundreds of people danced uncontrollably for days, is now attributed to ergot in the grain supply. The Salem witch trials may have been ergot poisoning.

Hofmann's task at Sandoz was to isolate the medically useful alkaloids from ergot and develop pharmaceutical derivatives. He succeeded with ergotamine and ergobasine, both of which became important drugs. In 1938, pursuing the pharmaceutical potential further, he synthesized a derivative of lysergic acid — the backbone structure common to all ergot alkaloids — and called it LSD-25. It was the twenty-fifth compound in the lysergic acid series. The animal tests showed nothing interesting. He filed it and moved on.

Five years later — for reasons he described as a 'peculiar presentiment' — he returned to LSD-25. In the final stages of the synthesis, he absorbed a small amount through his skin. The rest is what we know.

What connects ergot's two properties — the obstetrical and the hallucinogenic — is the chemistry of the ergot alkaloids and their action on serotonin receptors. The same receptor family that controls uterine muscle contraction is implicated in the perceptual effects of LSD. Hofmann, working at the boundary between these two pharmacological territories, accidentally synthesized the most potent psychoactive compound known. The fungus had been hiding it in plain sight for millennia.

Sources

  • Hofmann, LSD: My Problem Child (1979)
  • The Lancet, Albert Hofmann obituary (2008)
  • Wacker et al., Cell (2017)

The Day Sandoz Lost Control

“In 1953, the CIA purchased the entire world supply of LSD from Sandoz — app…”historypolicy
“In 1953, the CIA purchased the entire world supply of LSD from Sandoz — approximately 10 kilograms, enough for 100 million doses. Sandoz was relieved to sell it. They had no idea what to do with it.”

Albert Hofmann's problem child became the world's problem almost immediately after it left the laboratory.

Sandoz Laboratories had been distributing LSD-25 since 1947 under the trade name Delysid, primarily to psychiatric researchers studying schizophrenia and alcoholism. By 1953, word had spread beyond the academic psychiatric community. The CIA's Technical Services Division, which was running MK-Ultra under Sidney Gottlieb, learned about LSD's extreme potency and psychological effects and decided it needed to control the supply.

They bought it all. Approximately 10 kilograms — the entire global stock — for an amount Sandoz considered reasonable. This was enough for roughly 100 million doses of 100 micrograms each. Gottlieb's goal was to determine whether LSD could be used as a truth serum, an interrogation tool, a method for temporarily incapacitating enemies, or a vector for inducing psychiatric disorders in targets.

The answers, after a decade of human experimentation including MK-Ultra's various subprojects, were: no, no, no, and unreliably. The CIA's LSD program produced no usable intelligence techniques. It produced a death (Frank Olson in 1953), extensive psychological damage to unwitting subjects, and eventually a political scandal when the Church Committee exposed the program in 1975.

Hofmann, describing this period in My Problem Child, is characteristically measured. He understood that Sandoz had no means to control what happened to LSD once it left the laboratory — the chemistry was publishable, the synthesis was reproducible, and the demand created by the drug's effects was not something a pharmaceutical company could manage. The CIA's purchase was one symptom. Leary's mass distribution was another. The street market that emerged in the 1960s was a third.

What Sandoz could control — and eventually did — was its own production. In 1965, as the counterculture's use of LSD became impossible to ignore, Sandoz stopped making it. By then, illicit synthesis labs had been running for years. The problem child had left home.

Sources

  • Stevens, Jay. Storming Heaven (1987)
  • Marks, John. The Search for the Manchurian Candidate (1979)
  • Hofmann, LSD: My Problem Child (1979)

The Chemist and the Sacred Mushrooms

“Hofmann trekked to Huautla de Jiménez and met Maria Sabina. He gave her tab…”historyindigenous
“Hofmann trekked to Huautla de Jiménez and met Maria Sabina. He gave her tablets of psilocybin — the compound he'd isolated from her mushrooms. She took them. She said they were the same.”

The connection between Hofmann's LSD research and the psilocybin mushrooms of Mexico was not accidental. It was the same man.

In 1957, Gordon Wasson published his account of participating in a Mazatec mushroom ceremony with the curandera Maria Sabina in Huautla de Jiménez in the mountains of Oaxaca. The article, published in Life magazine under the headline 'Seeking the Magic Mushroom,' was the first mainstream Western account of teonanácatl — the flesh of the gods — and it reached exactly the people who were already thinking about consciousness, plants, and the relationship between them.

Wasson sent Hofmann a sample of the mushrooms. Hofmann analyzed them. In 1958 he isolated two new indole alkaloids — psilocybin and psilocin — and determined their chemical structures. The relationship to LSD was immediately visible: both compounds acted on the serotonin system, though through different mechanisms and with different duration profiles.

Two years later, Hofmann traveled to Mexico with his wife and colleagues to see the ceremony in its context. In Huautla, he met Maria Sabina and provided her with pills containing synthetic psilocybin that he had brought from the laboratory. She took them in a ceremony, without knowing exactly what was in them, and afterward reported that their power was the same as that of the mushrooms — she could work with the spirits equally well.

This exchange — the chemist with his tablets, the curandera with her centuries-old tradition, the confirmation that the molecule captured the spirit — is one of the most quietly significant moments in Hofmann's story. It grounded his lifelong argument: that what he had synthesized was not a foreign substance imposed on human chemistry but a compound that human cultures had been working with, in one form or another, for as long as there had been human cultures. The problem child had ancestors.

One Hundred and Two Years

“Hofmann lived to 102. He took LSD on his hundredth birthday. He said the ex…”historymysticism
“Hofmann lived to 102. He took LSD on his hundredth birthday. He said the experience restored something he had felt as a child in the Swiss countryside — a quality of luminous presence in ordinary things.”

Albert Hofmann was born in 1906 and died in 2008. Between these dates, he synthesized LSD, isolated psilocybin and psilocin, studied the chemistry of morning glory seeds, wrote My Problem Child, attended the 2006 Basel symposium on LSD's medical potential, and gave his last major interview at 101.

He took LSD at 100. He was not performing nostalgia or staging a statement. He took it the way he'd always taken it — carefully, in appropriate surroundings, with people he trusted — because the experience still did for him what he had discovered it could do in 1943: restore the quality of perception he had first known as a child.

Hofmann returned throughout his life to a specific memory: a morning walk in the Swiss countryside as a young boy, when the world had appeared luminous and saturated with presence, each thing exactly itself and impossibly significant. This quality had gradually faded with education and maturity, replaced by the ordinary adult perception of objects in terms of their usefulness and category. LSD had not introduced something foreign — it had recovered something that had been there before and been trained away.

This is the deepest claim in My Problem Child, and it is not pharmacological but autobiographical: that the state LSD produces is not aberrant but prior. The drug does not add content to consciousness; it removes the learned suppressions that make ordinary adult perception feel normal. What is revealed is not the drug's creation but consciousness's original condition.

Hofmann died on April 29, 2008 — a Tuesday, four months after his hundred-and-second birthday. He had lived long enough to see the research program he'd hoped for begin again: MAPS-sponsored clinical trials of LSD for anxiety, the first in decades. He did not live to see the clinical results published, but he knew the direction.

The Crystal Structure of the Trip

“In 2017, scientists solved the crystal structure of LSD bound to its recept…”pharmacologyneuroscience
“In 2017, scientists solved the crystal structure of LSD bound to its receptor. The lid that traps the drug in place — explaining its 12-hour duration — was a protein loop nobody had anticipated.”

For most of the century since Hofmann's bicycle ride, the mechanism of LSD's action was understood in general terms — it bound to serotonin receptors, particularly 5-HT2A — but the precise structural explanation for two of its most distinctive features remained unknown: its extreme potency and its unusual duration.

A standard psychedelic dose of LSD is 100 micrograms. A dose of mescaline producing comparable effects requires 200-400 milligrams — roughly 2,000 to 4,000 times more by weight. And where most drugs' effects follow their pharmacological half-life and clear when the drug clears, LSD's effects persist for 8-12 hours even though the drug itself metabolizes faster.

In 2017, a team led by Bryan Roth at UNC Chapel Hill published the crystal structure of LSD bound to the 5-HT2A receptor in Cell. The structure explained both mysteries at once.

On potency: LSD's molecular shape allows near-perfect complementarity with the receptor's binding pocket. The fit is so precise that even tiny amounts occupy the receptor almost completely.

On duration: a protein loop — an 'extracellular lid' formed by the receptor's second extracellular loop — closes over the LSD molecule after binding and traps it inside. The drug cannot leave until the lid opens. This explains why blocking the receptor with ketanserin before the LSD stops the effects but administering ketanserin afterward does not — the drug is locked in, and even the blocker can't reach it.

Hofmann described the intensity and duration of Bicycle Day's experience as a source of bewilderment. He'd expected the compound to metabolize more normally. The lid is why it didn't. The molecular explanation for the most famous accidental dose in pharmacological history was solved in a University of North Carolina laboratory seventy-four years after it happened.

Sources

  • Wacker et al., Cell (2017)
  • Hofmann, LSD: My Problem Child (1979)
  • Preller & Vollenweider, Brain Stimul. (2019)

Paonia to Berkeley: McKenna's Education

“McKenna studied history at Berkeley, not pharmacology. The intellectual for…”historyculture
“McKenna studied history at Berkeley, not pharmacology. The intellectual formation behind Food of the Gods was humanistic — he came to the plants through the library, then through the forest.”

Terence Kemp McKenna was born on November 16, 1946, in Paonia, Colorado — a small coal-mining town in the western part of the state — and grew up reading science fiction and collecting butterflies. He was not a child prodigy in any institutional sense. He was a reader.

At Berkeley in the mid-1960s, he studied history and ecology. The intellectual formation behind Food of the Gods was humanistic before it was pharmacological: he encountered the ideas of Marshall McLuhan, Buckminster Fuller, Carl Jung, and Alfred North Whitehead in the library before he encountered psilocybin in a Californian apartment. He came to the plants through the books, and then let the plants revise the books.

His first serious psychedelic experience was in Berkeley in 1965, with psilocybin mushrooms obtained through the network that preceded the counterculture's full public emergence. He described it, in various interviews, as the most significant intellectual event of his life — not because of what he saw but because of what he understood: that the categories he had been accumulating through five years of serious reading were provisional, that ordinary consciousness was a constrained subset of what was available, and that this had implications for everything.

He left Berkeley without completing his degree and spent several years traveling — across Asia, through India, Nepal, and Southeast Asia, studying shamanism, the I Ching, and the ethnobotanical literature that Schultes had been building at Harvard. He returned to the United States in 1971 having read almost everything available on psychoactive plants in the academic literature and having developed the hypothesis that would become Food of the Gods: that the relationship between human consciousness and psychoactive plants was not peripheral but foundational to what humans were.

The book took twenty years to write, in the sense that La Chorrera in 1971 was the experiential foundation and the 1992 publication was the intellectual elaboration. In between, McKenna became a lecturer, a radio presence, and eventually, in the 1990s, an internet figure whose audio recordings circulated among the early communities of what would become the psychedelic renaissance. Food of the Gods was the argument. The lectures were the argument in performance.

Botanical Dimensions: The Garden McKenna Built

“In 1985, McKenna and his then-wife Kathleen Harrison founded Botanical Dime…”cultureethnobotany
“In 1985, McKenna and his then-wife Kathleen Harrison founded Botanical Dimensions on the Big Island of Hawaii — a living archive of ethnobotanically significant plants, many of them psychoactive.”

Food of the Gods argues that the relationship between humans and psychoactive plants is fundamental — not a curiosity but a constitutive feature of what humans are and have been for most of their evolutionary history. Botanical Dimensions was McKenna's attempt to act on this argument materially.

In 1985, McKenna and his then-wife Kathleen Harrison founded Botanical Dimensions on the Big Island of Hawaii. It was a nonprofit ethnobotanical preserve with a specific mandate: to collect, protect, propagate, and study plants of ethnomedical significance — with an emphasis on the plants that appeared in the psychoactive plant literature Schultes and Hofmann had assembled.

The preserve grew plants that were, in some cases, rarely cultivated outside their native regions. It maintained living specimens of species that were being lost to deforestation and agricultural displacement in their original habitats. It served as a research resource, a conservation site, and a demonstration that the ethnobotanical relationship McKenna described in his writing could be maintained physically as well as conceptually.

Harrison, who remained involved with Botanical Dimensions after the couple's separation, is herself a botanist and ethnobotanist whose work has focused on the cultural contexts of plant medicine use. Her approach — more patient and more careful about cultural appropriation than McKenna's — represents a complementary strand of the same project: the argument that the plants deserve serious attention, sustained relationship, and proper context.

McKenna lived on the Big Island intermittently through the 1990s. He was diagnosed with a brain tumor in 1999 and died on April 3, 2000, in San Rafael, California. Botanical Dimensions continues to operate. The garden he built outlasted the lectures, which is probably what he intended.

Before Food of the Gods: The Invisible Landscape

“Published in 1975, The Invisible Landscape was the theoretical foundation f…”historyphilosophy
“Published in 1975, The Invisible Landscape was the theoretical foundation for everything McKenna would argue for the next twenty-five years. Almost nobody read it.”

Food of the Gods (1992) was Terence McKenna's third book and his first to reach a wide audience. It was also the most accessible articulation of ideas he had been developing since 1975, when he and his brother Dennis published The Invisible Landscape: Mind, Hallucinogens, and the I Ching.

The Invisible Landscape is a stranger, harder book than Food of the Gods — closer to the raw experience of La Chorrera and less processed through the narrative skills McKenna would develop over the following fifteen years. It attempts to construct a mathematical model of time's qualitative structure, based on the I Ching's sixty-four hexagrams, in which novelty is not uniformly distributed but has specific topological features that can be mapped. This became Timewave Zero.

It also contains the first formal presentation of the tryptamine hypothesis: that psilocybin and related compounds are not simply consciousness-altering drugs but represent a class of molecules with special relationships to human cognitive evolution, to the structure of the nervous system, and to what McKenna called 'the Other' — the alien intelligence that consistently presented itself in high-dose tryptamine experience.

The book sold modestly and was largely ignored by academic reviewers. Dennis McKenna went on to complete a doctorate in neuropharmacology and to pursue the underlying questions through conventional scientific channels. Terence went on the lecture circuit.

Food of the Gods distills and translates the Invisible Landscape argument for a general audience: the evolutionary hypothesis becomes the stoned ape; the mathematical model of time becomes the Archaic Revival; the tryptamine entities become the Transcendent Other. The underlying claims are the same. What changed was McKenna's ability to present them in language that reached people who had no reason to work through the I Ching mathematics.

The Invisible Landscape is, in retrospect, the intellectual foundation and Food of the Gods is the cultural intervention. Understanding both is the only way to assess either.
