What the Clinical Record Actually Showed: LSD Therapy 1947-1968

“Over a thousand published papers. Forty thousand patients. Roughly fifty pe…”therapyhistory
“Over a thousand published papers. Forty thousand patients. Roughly fifty percent of treated alcoholics achieving lasting sobriety. The program was not stopped because it failed.”

When the Schedule I designation for LSD took effect with the 1970 Controlled Substances Act, it ended a clinical research program that had been running for twenty-three years and had produced results that no subsequent psychiatric intervention has matched in several key areas.

The program began in 1947 when Sandoz first distributed LSD to psychiatric researchers under the trade name Delysid. The accompanying package insert described two potential research applications: as a model of psychosis (for training clinicians in the phenomenology of schizophrenia), and as a treatment for various neurotic conditions by facilitating the surfacing and processing of psychological material.

By 1965, when Sandoz withdrew Delysid in response to the counterculture controversy, the clinical literature encompassed over one thousand published papers and reports from dozens of research centers. The patient population was heterogeneous: alcoholics, end-of-life anxiety patients, treatment-resistant depressives, and patients with neurotic disorders of various kinds.

The most robust results came from the alcoholism trials. Hoffer and Osmond's work at Weyburn Mental Hospital in Saskatchewan, running from 1952 to approximately 1961, treated over a thousand alcoholic patients with LSD-assisted therapy and documented response rates of approximately 40-50 percent achieving lasting sobriety — rates that were superior to any available alternative treatment. Their methodology was not by modern standards rigorous — the trials were not randomized and controlled by current criteria — but the consistency of the result across variations in method was sufficient for serious clinical attention.

A 2012 meta-analysis by Krebs and Johansen (Journal of Psychopharmacology) examined all available randomized controlled trials of LSD for alcoholism conducted between 1966 and 1970 and found a statistically significant positive effect on drinking behavior, with effects persisting at six to twelve months follow-up. The meta-analysis was limited by the quality of the original trials, but its conclusion — that the effect was real and clinically meaningful — was consistent with the broader clinical record.

The end-of-life anxiety results were comparable. Early trials by Walter Pahnke, Sidney Cohen, and others found that LSD-assisted therapy significantly reduced death anxiety in terminal cancer patients and was associated with reported acceptance of death rather than dread. The mechanism, in Pahnke's account, was the mystical experience: patients who had complete mystical experiences during sessions showed the greatest reduction in anxiety.

This finding — that mystical experience quality predicts therapeutic outcome — has been confirmed in the current psilocybin research (Barrett & Griffiths, 2018; Yaden & Griffiths, 2021) and is one of the most consistent findings across the fifty-year interruption. What was established in the LSD trials of the 1950s and 1960s, lost in the prohibition, and reestablished in the psilocybin trials of the 2010s and 2020s, is: the mechanism of psychedelic-assisted therapy is the quality of the consciousness it occasions, not only the pharmacology.

What was stopped in 1968-1970 was not a research program that had reached its natural conclusion. It was a research program in full development, accumulating positive results, refining its methodology, and approaching the stage at which it might have produced regulatory submissions for specific indications.

The COMPASS Pathways Phase 3 trials of COMP360 psilocybin, reporting in 2025 and 2026, are the research program that the 1970 Controlled Substances Act would have produced forty years earlier if it had not been halted. The clinical evidence for psychedelic-assisted therapy for depression and end-of-life anxiety is now, as of 2026, at Phase 3 quality. This evidence would have existed by approximately 1985 if the program had continued uninterrupted.

Hofmann knew what was being lost in 1968. He had watched the clinical program from Sandoz, contributed to it through his pharmacological analysis, and understood its potential. My Problem Child is partly a document of grief: grief for a research program that was working, for patients who needed it, for a medical opportunity that political decisions eliminated.

Sources

  • Hoffer & Osmond, J. Mental Sci. (1961)
  • Stevens, Storming Heaven (1987)

The Connection Model: Evidence, Limits, and What It Gets Right

“The connection model is not a refutation of pharmacology. It is a correctio…”therapypharmacology
“The connection model is not a refutation of pharmacology. It is a correction of the pharmacological-only model. Both things are true: addiction has chemical dimensions and social dimensions, and the policy implication is that you have to address both.”

The central claim of Chasing the Scream — 'the opposite of addiction is connection' — is a formulation that clarifies and overstates simultaneously. It clarifies because it redirects attention from the drug to the person and the person's environment. It overstates because pharmacological dependence is real, withdrawal is a physiological process, and social connection, however necessary, is not sufficient to reverse all forms of addiction.

Bruce Alexander's Rat Park experiments showed that social enrichment dramatically reduced drug consumption in rats who had been isolated and dependent. The finding was significant and has held up in a general sense across subsequent animal research: social context modulates drug-seeking behavior reliably. The specific Rat Park results have not been directly replicated, and some studies have found the effect less dramatic than Alexander's original data suggested. But the conceptual point — that environment shapes pharmacological behavior in important ways — is now well-established.

The Vietnam natural experiment provides the strongest human data. Lee Robins's 1993 analysis of Vietnam veterans who had been addicted to heroin in the field found that approximately 95 percent stopped using after returning home, without formal treatment. The most important variable was not pharmacological — it was the radical change in environment. The drug was the same; the context was different; the behavior changed.

This finding, combined with the Rat Park data, supports the general claim that social disconnection is a major driver of addiction. But the phrase 'the opposite of addiction is connection' obscures an important nuance: the Vietnam veterans were not simply getting more connection at home. They were getting a different set of environmental affordances — work, family, housing, purpose — that made drug use both less necessary and less available. 'Connection' is a partial description of a richer social ecology.

The pharmacological critique of Hari's strong formulation is that opioid withdrawal is a genuine physiological process that does not reverse simply because a person feels more connected. George Koob and Nora Volkow's framework — which emphasizes the neuroadaptive changes that chronic drug use produces in reward, stress, and executive function circuits — shows that the brain changes measurably with sustained use, and that these changes persist after environmental improvement. The social context model and the neurobiological model are not contradictory; they are complementary accounts of different aspects of the same phenomenon.

The policy implication of this more nuanced picture is: both. Treatment for opioid use disorder needs both medication-assisted treatment (buprenorphine, methadone) and social support (housing, employment, community). Portugal's model, which Hari cites as the strongest evidence for the connection approach, actually implements both: decriminalization removes the legal barrier to treatment-seeking, and the social investment provides the environmental conditions that support recovery.

Where Portugal's results have been weaker — particularly through the 2015-2023 period, when austerity cut social service budgets — the model has underperformed. Not because decriminalization failed but because the social investment was insufficient. The lesson is not that connection is the opposite of addiction; it is that connection is necessary but not sufficient, and that the pharmacological and the social interventions work best in combination.

Hari's formulation, for all its incompleteness, accomplished something the more nuanced version would not have: it made the argument accessible and memorable, it redirected public attention from moral failure to social conditions, and it built the political case for harm reduction and decriminalization that the evidence supports even if the slogan overstates. The compression of a complex finding into a memorable formulation is not always wrong. Sometimes it is the thing that moves policy when the nuanced version would not.

Sources

  • Alexander, The Globalization of Addiction (2008)
  • Gage & Sumnall, Addiction (2020)
  • Koob & Volkow, Neuropsychopharmacology (2016)
  • Robins, Vietnam Veterans Three Years After Vietnam (1993)

The Hypothesis in 2026: What the Evidence Has Become

“Forty-eight years after publication, the Road to Eleusis hypothesis has mov…”historypharmacology
“Forty-eight years after publication, the Road to Eleusis hypothesis has moved from speculative to experimentally feasible and archaeologically evidenced. The direct confirmation — ergot at Eleusis — has not yet arrived. The search is active.”

The Road to Eleusis was published in 1978 as a proposition: that the most revered religious institution of classical antiquity derived its transformative power from a psychedelic sacrament. Wasson provided the mycological and ethnomycological argument, Hofmann provided the pharmacological analysis, and Ruck provided the classical scholarship. Together they proposed that the kykeon — the ritual drink prepared from barley, water, and mint according to the Homeric Hymn to Demeter — contained ergot alkaloids that produced the visions initiates described.

For the first four decades after publication, the hypothesis remained in the category of interesting speculation: suggestive, internally consistent, supported by the ancient testimonies and by Hofmann's pharmacological experiments with water-soluble ergot alkaloids, but without direct archaeological confirmation. Classical scholars were largely hostile; the Eleusis site itself had not produced chemical residue evidence.

In 2019-2020, that changed.

The excavation at Mas Castellar de Pontós — an ancient settlement in Catalonia associated with the Demeter cult — produced two significant findings. In dental calculus from a woman buried at the site (third to second century BCE), bioarchaeologist Jordi Juan-Tresserras found apparent traces of ergot alkaloids alongside phytoplankton associated with the cultivation of cereal grains. In a sealed ritual vessel from the same site, further analysis found ergot spores and residues in direct association with beer-making equipment.

The Catalonia site is not Eleusis. It is an Eleusinian-affiliated sanctuary in the western Mediterranean — evidence that the cult of Demeter, wherever it established itself, used grain-based preparations contaminated with or incorporating ergot. The finding cannot prove that the Eleusinian sanctuary in Greece used the same preparation, but it demonstrates that the preparation was used in cultic contexts associated with the Eleusinian tradition.

The February 2026 Scientific Reports paper by Antonopoulos and Dadiotis at the National Kapodistrian University of Athens provided the chemical mechanism that Hofmann had proposed but not fully demonstrated. They showed experimentally that lye — readily available in antiquity as wood ash solution — converts the toxic ergotamine and ergotoxine alkaloids in ergot into water-soluble lysergic acid amide (LSA) derivatives at doses that would be achievable through ancient preparation methods. This is the specific transformation that would have made ergot psychoactive in the kykeon without producing the dangerous ergotism that ergot had caused in European grain crops.

The Antonopoulos-Dadiotis paper also called explicitly for chemical residue analysis of vessels excavated at the Eleusis site itself — the analysis that would be the most direct test of the hypothesis. As of June 2026, this analysis has not been completed. The Hellenic Ministry of Culture's ongoing excavation program, combined with the attention brought by Eleusis's designation as a European Capital of Culture in 2023, has raised both the research interest and the political complexity of pursuing invasive analysis on one of Greece's most important archaeological sites.

The hypothesis stands in 2026 in a condition its authors in 1978 would have found encouraging: experimentally demonstrated as feasible (the Antonopoulos-Dadiotis chemistry), archaeologically supported in an affiliated site (the Catalonia findings), and directly testable at Eleusis if the political and institutional conditions allow the analysis.

The scholarly resistance has softened. Burkert's generation of classicists who dismissed the hypothesis has retired or died. Brian Muraresku's popular treatment in The Immortality Key reached an audience far larger than the original scholarly edition, and the 2019-2020 archaeological findings gave his argument a stronger evidentiary base than he had when the book went to press.

The question Wasson, Hofmann, and Ruck posed — whether Western civilization's most important religious institution was founded on a psychedelic sacrament — remains open. The evidence that would answer it definitively is in the soil at Eleusis, waiting for the right analysis to reach it.

Sources

  • Wasson, Hofmann & Ruck, The Road to Eleusis (1978)
  • Antonopoulos & Dadiotis, Scientific Reports (February 2026)
  • Mas Castellar de Pontós excavation reports (2019-2020)
  • Muraresku, The Immortality Key (2020)
  • Eleusis 2023 European Capital of Culture documentation

Set and Setting: How Huxley and Osmond Built the Clinical Framework

“The phrase 'set and setting' is attributed to Timothy Leary, but the concep…”therapyhistory
“The phrase 'set and setting' is attributed to Timothy Leary, but the concept was built by Osmond and Huxley, letter by letter, between 1953 and 1963. Leary named it. They invented it.”

The concept of set and setting is now so fundamental to psychedelic research that it appears in the safety guidelines of every clinical trial, in the training materials of every facilitator program, and in the published recommendations of every professional organization working in the field. Set — the mindset, expectations, and psychological state of the person taking the substance. Setting — the physical environment, social context, and relational conditions in which the experience occurs. The two variables together, clinicians now understand, predict a substantial proportion of the variance in psychedelic experience quality and therapeutic outcome.

The phrase is attributed to Timothy Leary, who used it in lectures during the Harvard psilocybin project in the early 1960s. But the concept was developed by Humphry Osmond and Aldous Huxley through a decade of correspondence, beginning with Osmond's May 1953 mescaline session with Huxley in Los Angeles and elaborated across hundreds of letters.

Osmond's clinical contribution was the observation that the same dose of the same substance produced dramatically different experiences in different people and in different contexts. He had seen this at Weyburn: patients who received LSD in the same protocol reported experiences ranging from peaceful insight to terror. The variable was not the drug. The variable was the person and the situation.

Huxley's contribution was the philosophical framework: the drug did not add content to consciousness but removed filters. What was revealed when the filters were removed depended enormously on what was already there — the person's beliefs, anxieties, hopes, and emotional state — and on what the environment provided — whether it was frightening or safe, chaotic or structured, cold or warm. The drug was an amplifier, not a specific producer. What it amplified was everything.

The correspondence worked out the practical implications of this framework over years of reflection. Huxley described his own sessions — the first mescaline session with Osmond, subsequent LSD sessions, his wife's use of psychedelics — with systematic attention to what conditions had contributed to positive outcomes: familiar surroundings, trusted companions, beautiful art, carefully chosen music, freedom from interruption, absence of time pressure. He was building, empirically, a list of set and setting variables based on direct experience.

Osmond was doing the same thing clinically. The Weyburn LSD protocol that produced 40-50 percent sobriety rates in alcoholic patients was not simply 'give LSD.' It was preparation (discussing the experience in advance, establishing trust), dosing (in a carefully prepared room with meaningful objects and music), and integration (follow-up sessions to process what had happened). These three phases — preparation, session, integration — are now the standard clinical model for psychedelic-assisted therapy, formalized in Johnson et al.'s 2008 safety guidelines and mandated by the protocols of every current clinical trial.

A 2024 systematic review published in Expert Review of Clinical Pharmacology (Borkel et al.) confirmed what Huxley and Osmond had established empirically seventy years earlier: set and setting variables predict psychopathology, wellbeing, and meaningfulness of psychedelic experiences across independent samples. A 2024 review of integration session frameworks (Thal & Lommen, Clinical Psychology & Psychotherapy) synthesized 75 clinical trials and found that the therapeutic alliance and the quality of preparation and integration sessions were significant predictors of outcome across conditions.

The letters in Moksha are not simply historical documents. They are the first systematic working-out of what is now the foundational clinical infrastructure of the psychedelic renaissance. When a clinical trial at Johns Hopkins or Imperial College specifies preparation requirements, therapist training, session environment, and integration follow-up, it is implementing the framework that Huxley and Osmond developed letter by letter between 1953 and 1963.

Leary named it. He condensed a decade of careful clinical and philosophical development into a slogan — 'set and setting' — that was both accurate and easily misunderstood. The slogan suggested that you could control the experience by controlling the variables, which was true in a general sense and false in a specific sense: set and setting shape the experience, they do not determine it. The difference between shaping and determining is the difference between a clinical framework and a guarantee, and Leary's promotional style often presented it as the latter.

Huxley and Osmond's letters are the guarantee-free version: two careful people working out, from direct experience and clinical observation, what conditions most reliably support positive outcomes while acknowledging that the experience remains fundamentally unpredictable. This is the epistemic posture that current clinical research is recovering — the posture that Leary's showmanship temporarily obscured.

Sources

  • Huxley & Osmond, in Moksha (1977)
  • Hartogsohn, Constructing drug effects: a history of set and setting, Drug Sci Policy Law (2017)
  • Borkel et al., Set and setting predict psychopathology, wellbeing and meaningfulness, Expert Rev Clin Pharmacol (2024)
  • Thal & Lommen, Therapeutic frameworks in integration sessions, Clin Psychol Psychother (2024)
  • Johnson et al., Human hallucinogen research guidelines for safety, J Psychopharmacol (2008)

LSD at the End of Life: From Island to the Clinic

“Huxley died with LSD. The clinical program he helped create is now treating…”therapymysticism
“Huxley died with LSD. The clinical program he helped create is now treating the same anxiety — cancer, dying, the dissolution of the self — that he faced in November 1963.”

On November 22, 1963 — the day John F. Kennedy was assassinated, though neither Aldous Huxley nor his wife Laura knew this — Huxley was dying of laryngeal cancer. He had lost the ability to speak. He wrote a note asking Laura to administer LSD. She gave him 100 micrograms at 11:20 AM and another 100 micrograms at 1:00 PM, speaking to him softly as he died: 'You are doing this willingly and consciously, and you are doing this beautifully.'

The nurses who were present said they had never seen such a peaceful death.

This event — which Laura Huxley described in a letter to Osmond written shortly after, published in This Timeless Moment — was not an improvisation. It was the culmination of a decade of thinking about what psychedelics could do at the end of life, a decade that began with the Huxley-Osmond correspondence and found its fullest fictional expression in Island (1962), where the moksha-medicine was explicitly integrated into the community's approach to dying.

Huxley had written about death as one of the three or four things that psychedelics could transform. Not prevent, not deny — transform. The moksha experience, in his account, was particularly relevant to dying because what dying required — a release of the ego's grip on its own continuity, an opening to whatever lay on the other side of the known — was precisely what the psychedelic experience trained. The person who had genuinely dissolved the ego's boundaries in a guided session had, in some sense, rehearsed dying.

Osmond, as a psychiatrist who worked regularly with seriously ill patients, had thought about this from the clinical side. He had observed that the LSD sessions with terminal patients produced responses unlike those in other populations: a quality of peace, acceptance, and even gratitude that was not explicable by any pharmacological action on disease symptoms. Whatever was happening was happening to the relationship between the person and their situation, not to the situation itself.

The clinical program that tested this systematically did not begin until after Huxley's death. Walter Pahnke's work at the Maryland Psychiatric Research Center in the 1960s and 1970s established that LSD-assisted therapy significantly reduced anxiety and depression in terminal cancer patients. The research was stopped by prohibition in 1970.

The program resumed, with psilocybin rather than LSD, in 2016, with two landmark studies published simultaneously. Griffiths et al. at Johns Hopkins and Ross et al. at NYU found, in separate double-blind trials, that a single session of psilocybin-assisted therapy produced rapid and sustained reductions in end-of-life anxiety and depression in cancer patients, with effects persisting at six-month follow-up. The mechanism, consistent across both studies, was mystical experience quality: patients who had complete mystical experiences showed the greatest therapeutic benefit.

Australia's Therapeutic Goods Administration approved psilocybin for treatment-resistant depression and MDMA for PTSD in February 2023 — the first regulatory approvals for psychedelic-assisted therapy in any country outside of a trial setting. The approval includes provisions for palliative care contexts.

Huxley wrote Laura's words at the end of life into Island: 'Willingly and consciously and beautifully — you're doing it willingly and consciously and beautifully.' He wrote them into his novel two years before he died; Laura used them at his bedside because they were the right words, because he had worked out what the right words were in decades of thinking about how the mind met its own dissolution.

The clinical program that now provides this to dying patients in clinical trials is the institutionalized version of what Huxley worked out in his letters to Osmond. The language has changed — outcomes, endpoints, MADRS scores — but the underlying event, and the reason it helps, is what the correspondence described.

Sources

  • Huxley & Osmond, in Moksha (1977)
  • Griffiths et al., Psilocybin produces substantial and sustained decreases in depression and anxiety in patients with life-threatening cancer, J Psychopharmacol (2016)
  • Ross et al., Rapid and sustained symptom reduction following psilocybin treatment for anxiety and depression in patients with life-threatening cancer, J Psychopharmacol (2016)
  • TGA Australia, Psilocybin clinical approval (February 2023)

The Second Wave: Why History Is Repeating and How It Might Not

“The people building the current psychedelic renaissance have read Storming …”historypolicy
“The people building the current psychedelic renaissance have read Storming Heaven. They are explicitly trying not to repeat 1968. Whether they will succeed is the open question.”

Jay Stevens ended Storming Heaven in 1968. Fifty-five years later, the research program he mourned has resumed. The question Storming Heaven's history now poses is not historical but prospective: will the current psychedelic renaissance avoid the collapse that ended the first one?

The people building the current renaissance have read Stevens's book — or something equivalent. The explicit institutional memory of what went wrong in the 1960s is present in every major clinical psychedelic research organization. Matthew Johnson's 2008 safety guidelines for human psychedelic research, which have become the baseline protocol for clinical trials, were written with the specific goal of preventing the kind of adverse events and public credibility damage that enabled the 1968 prohibition. The guidelines specify: screening for contraindicated conditions, therapeutic alliance established before dosing, trained monitors present during sessions, post-session integration, careful management of public communication.

This is the clinical tradition Osmond and Huxley built, formalized into something that can survive its most charismatic exponents. The problem in the 1960s was that the clinical tradition depended on individual practitioners — Osmond, Hoffer, Grof, Pahnke — and the moment it was disrupted by public controversy, the institutional infrastructure that might have sustained it did not exist. The current infrastructure — the Society for Psychedelic Outreach, Reform and Education, the Multidisciplinary Association for Psychedelic Studies, the academic centers at Hopkins, NYU, Imperial, and elsewhere — is designed to be more durable.

The specific risks that Stevens documented are also more visible now. The Leary risk — mass public advocacy that overtaxes the regulatory goodwill needed for clinical approval — has materialized in the ayahuasca retreat industry, in the ketamine wellness clinic proliferation, and in the general 'psychedelic renaissance' media coverage that sometimes outruns the evidence. The FDA's August 2024 rejection of Lykos Therapeutics' MDMA-assisted therapy application for PTSD was partly a response to this problem: not a rejection of the underlying science, but a finding that the trial design had insufficient safeguards against expectation effects and therapeutic boundary violations. The FDA's concern was not that MDMA doesn't work — it was that the trial design couldn't prove it works in a way that would survive commercialization at scale.

This is the 1968 problem in new form: the substance is promising, the evidence is promising, and the enthusiasm of advocates is threatening to outrun the methodological rigor needed to make the evidence stick.

The COMPASS Pathways Phase 3 trials for psilocybin in treatment-resistant depression — reporting in June 2025 and February 2026 — represent the methodologically rigorous approach: double-blind design, active placebo comparison, pre-registered primary endpoints, independent data monitoring, and a trial population (treatment-resistant patients) where the effect size is most meaningful. The results met primary endpoints with high statistical significance. The NDA submission is targeted for Q4 2026.

If approved — and the current trajectory suggests approval in late 2026 or early 2027 — COMP360 will be the first psychedelic-assisted therapy with full FDA approval. This is not what the 1960s research was close to producing; the 1960s research would have taken another decade of refinement to reach this point. The fifty-five-year interruption is ending, and it is ending with better methodology than what was interrupted.

But Stevens's other warning — about the co-optation of the clinical tradition by commercial and cultural forces that transform it into something it wasn't designed to be — is still live. The economic incentives in the legal psychedelic market are substantial. The distance between a rigorous clinical protocol and a commercial psychedelic retreat is the distance between Osmond's Weyburn and Kesey's Trips Festival. That distance exists regardless of whether COMP360 gets approved.

What Storming Heaven shows, and what the current renaissance has to reckon with, is that the clinical and the cultural cannot be cleanly separated. They were not separable in the 1960s, and they are not separable now. The question is not whether to manage the relationship but how.

Sources

  • Stevens, Storming Heaven (1987)
  • Johnson et al., Human hallucinogen research guidelines for safety, J Psychopharmacol (2008)
  • Lykos Therapeutics, FDA rejection of MDMA for PTSD (August 2024)
  • COMPASS Pathways Phase 3 Results (2025-2026)
  • Davis et al., Effects of Psilocybin-Assisted Therapy on Major Depressive Disorder, JAMA Psychiatry (2021)

The Epistemology of the Unverifiable: What McKenna's Uncertainty Teaches

“McKenna's central intellectual virtue was the willingness to hold unresolve…”philosophyconsciousness
“McKenna's central intellectual virtue was the willingness to hold unresolved the question of what the entities were. He neither proved they were real nor dismissed them as hallucination. He reported them.”

The entity contact problem is, as of 2026, the most philosophically interesting open question in psychedelic science. It has been reported consistently since the first accounts of DMT use in the 1950s, documented in Strassman's clinical study, documented in detail in a 2020 Johns Hopkins survey of 2,561 people who had had such an encounter (Davis et al., J. Psychopharmacol. 34(9)). Imaging has not yet isolated it: the 2023 Imperial College EEG-fMRI study (Timmermann et al., PNAS 120(13)) mapped DMT's global brain effects, not entity contact specifically. The consistency of the report is established. The explanation is not.

Terence McKenna encountered the entities in Berkeley in 1965. He described them — merry, elfin, self-transforming, fractal, offering visible objects made of language — with a specificity that subsequent independent reporters have consistently corroborated without having read his description. He spent the next thirty-five years neither claiming that they were objectively real in the naive sense nor dismissing them as mere hallucination. He held the question open.

This epistemological position — call it principled uncertainty — is what distinguishes True Hallucinations from both the credulous and the dismissive traditions in psychedelic literature. McKenna was not a simple believer. He acknowledged, consistently, that the entities might be products of his own mind: unconscious material given dramatic form by DMT's action on the brain. He acknowledged that the Timewave was either revolutionary or delusional and that he could not determine which from the inside. He acknowledged that what happened at La Chorrera might have been a psychosis rather than a revelation.

He continued to report what he had experienced. Not as proven fact. As experience.

The philosophical distinction matters enormously. The scientific establishment's refusal to engage seriously with entity contact reports has not been based on evidence that they are mere hallucinations — it has been based on an a priori assumption that if something is produced under the influence of a drug, it cannot be genuinely informative about external reality. This assumption is itself a philosophical position, not an empirical finding, and it is one that the consistency of entity contact reports makes harder to sustain.

The standard materialist account — entities are projections of the unconscious, elaborate productions of a brain temporarily released from its filtering function — is a coherent explanation that fits the available evidence. It is not, however, the only coherent explanation that fits the available evidence. The question of whether DMT entities have any reality beyond the brain that produces them is not currently answerable by available methods.

Researcher Andrew Gallimore has proposed a more rigorous version of McKenna's basic position: that DMT may allow access to a genuine alternative reality — not by taking the brain outside itself, but by reconfiguring the brain's perceptual apparatus to receive signals from a state space that ordinary consciousness excludes. This is Huxley's reducing valve argument, applied to entities rather than flowers: what is usually filtered out is allowed through.

Gallimore's position is speculative but scientifically articulated. It makes predictions: that the entity environment should show internal consistency across users that exceeds what could be explained by shared cultural expectations (the survey data suggests this is true); that entity-contact neural signatures should differ from those of ordinary hallucination (the 2023 Timmermann fMRI data suggests this is true); and that specific features of the entity environment should be reproducible across independent subjects in conditions that control for cultural priming (not yet tested).

Dennis McKenna — the most rigorous neuropharmacologist in the family — has said, in various interviews, that he believes something real happened at La Chorrera, while being careful about what 'real' means. His scientific training makes him unwilling to assert objective external entities. His direct experience makes him unwilling to dismiss what happened as simply drug-induced brain noise.

This is the position True Hallucinations occupies. Not the position of the believer. Not the position of the skeptic. The position of the careful reporter who has experienced something that current frameworks cannot accommodate and refuses either to force it into a framework or to deny that it happened.

The entity contact problem will be resolved, if it is resolved, by better science than currently exists. McKenna's contribution was to keep the question open — to insist on the rigor of accurate phenomenological reporting even when the phenomenon reported was epistemologically inconvenient. That is the book's lasting value: not the answer but the quality of the question.

Sources

  • McKenna, True Hallucinations (1993)
  • Strassman, DMT: The Spirit Molecule (2001)
  • Sexton et al., J. Psychopharmacol. 33(9) (2019)
  • Timmermann et al., PNAS 120(13) (2023)
  • D. McKenna, The Brotherhood of the Screaming Abyss (2012)
  • Davis et al., J. Psychopharmacol. 34(9):1008-1020 (2020)

From Mescaline to Schedule I: The Legal Journey of Huxley's Plant

“Mescaline has been Schedule I since 1970. Huxley's mescaline session was le…”policyhistory
“Mescaline has been Schedule I since 1970. Huxley's mescaline session was legal. The book describing it is legal. The experience it describes is a federal crime.”

When Humphry Osmond administered four-tenths of a gram of mescaline to Aldous Huxley in May 1953, the act was entirely legal. Mescaline had been a pharmaceutical curiosity and occasional clinical tool since the 1890s. The Controlled Substances Act of 1970 placed mescaline in Schedule I — alongside heroin and LSD — not driven by evidence of harm but by the political context of the Nixon drug war, which was, as Ehrlichman later confirmed, explicitly targeted at political enemies and minority communities.

Mescaline's Schedule I status has remained unchanged for fifty-five years despite the absence of documented harm from clinical or ceremonial use. The Native American Church's peyote ceremonies — which involve mescaline as the active compound — received a specific religious exemption in the 1994 American Indian Religious Freedom Act Amendments, making NAC members the only legal mescaline users in the United States.

Colorado's Proposition 122 (November 2022) decriminalized personal possession of mescaline (excluding peyote) alongside psilocybin, ibogaine, and DMT. No other state has followed. The federal Schedule I status remains.

Huxley's book is taught in universities. The experience it describes is illegal. The plant providing the experience has grown in the Chihuahuan Desert for millions of years. The law making it illegal is fifty-five years old and has produced no documented reduction in mescaline use.

Sources

  • Huxley, The Doors of Perception (1954)
  • Controlled Substances Act (1970)
  • Wikipedia, Mescaline

Huxley's Vision, Oregon's Program: Regulated Access in Practice

“Oregon's Measure 109 created the first regulated psilocybin services progra…”policytherapy
“Oregon's Measure 109 created the first regulated psilocybin services program in the US. Over 100 service centers were licensed by 2026. The model is imperfect, instructive, and being revised in real time.”

Huxley's vision in The Doors of Perception was not unlimited access to mescaline but legitimate pathways for people who had the preparation, intention, and support to use psychedelics well. Oregon's Measure 109 is the closest existing policy implementation: adults 21+ can access psilocybin at licensed service centers under licensed facilitators — without prescription, but within a regulated framework.

As of 2026, over 100 service centers are licensed in Oregon. The program has already required significant revision: HB 2387 (signed May 2025) corrected an absurd provision preventing licensed medical professionals from using their professional skills while facilitating sessions. Further modifications were signed in March 2026.

Colorado's Proposition 122 went further: it combined licensed healing center access with broader decriminalization of personal possession and social sharing of psilocybin, ibogaine, DMT, and mescaline (excluding peyote). Colorado's first healing center opened in July 2025. Governor Polis pardoned people convicted of state possession charges.

Both models produce data that will inform the next generation of state and eventually federal policy. What the programs demonstrate is that Huxley's fundamental premise was correct: structured, supported access to psychedelic experience is feasible within a regulatory framework. What remains unresolved is how to design that framework to serve those who most need it — people without $300-2000 per-session access fees, people in rural areas, people whose mental health conditions create clinical need.

The Religious Freedom Argument: Sacred vs. Recreational

“Four organizations now have federal DEA exemptions for ayahuasca. The Churc…”policymysticism
“Four organizations now have federal DEA exemptions for ayahuasca. The Church of Gaia received the first-ever non-litigation DEA approval in May 2025. Huxley called the experience a sacrament. The law is slowly catching up.”

Huxley framed the mescaline experience in explicitly religious terms: a 'gratuitous grace,' a 'sacrament.' The Religious Freedom Restoration Act (1993) created the federal framework for this argument: it prohibits the government from substantially burdening a person's exercise of religion unless the government demonstrates a compelling interest by least restrictive means.

The Supreme Court applied RFRA to psychedelic religion in Gonzales v. O Centro (2006), unanimously holding the government could not prohibit the União do Vegetal's ayahuasca ceremonies. Four US organizations now hold confirmed federal DEA exemptions: the União do Vegetal (SCOTUS 2006), Santo Daime (9th Circuit 2009), the Iowaska Church of Healing (DEA settlement 2024), and the Church of Gaia — the first-ever non-litigation DEA approval, granted in May 2025.

Colorado's Proposition 122 addressed the limits of the religious institution model by allowing payment for 'spiritual and harm-reduction services' outside licensed healing centers — protecting indigenous ceremonial practice and access modalities that don't fit clinical or commercial frameworks.

The tension between institutional religious exemption and broader spiritual access remains the central unresolved question of psychedelic religious law. Huxley's 'gratuitous grace' was available, in his argument, regardless of denominational affiliation. The legal framework for psychedelic access that requires institutional religious structure creates exactly the kind of gatekeeping his democratic impulse resisted.

Who Gets Access: The Equity Problem in Psychedelic Medicine

“Huxley called the experience 'of inestimable value to everyone.' Oregon ses…”policyculture
“Huxley called the experience 'of inestimable value to everyone.' Oregon sessions cost $300-$2,000 out of pocket. These facts are in tension.”

In The Doors of Perception, Huxley argued that the experience of direct perception was 'of inestimable value to everyone.' The qualitative democracy of the claim is deliberate: not everyone who wants mescaline should have it, but the benefit of opening the reducing valve is not restricted to any class or education level.

The psychedelic therapy market as actually developed is not structurally democratic. In Oregon, a psilocybin session costs between $300 and $2,000 out of pocket, with no insurance coverage as of 2026. Clinical trials require specific diagnoses and geographic proximity. Ketamine infusion clinics cost $400-$800 per session, also typically without insurance.

The MAPS Policy Guidebook (2026) explicitly acknowledges this equity gap, noting the historical invisibility and exploitation of Indigenous people in the American narrative.

The racial equity dimension is sharpest in the cannabis parallel: communities most heavily criminalized under cannabis prohibition have not received commensurate benefit from legalization. Oregon's Measure 109 required an underserved community access program; Colorado's Proposition 122 included equity licensing provisions. Whether these provisions translate into meaningful equitable access or primarily function as symbolic concessions is the open empirical question.

The Long Road to Clinical Approval: From Weyburn to COMP360

“Hoffer and Osmond's 1961 paper showed roughly 50% sobriety rates in treated…”policytherapy
“Hoffer and Osmond's 1961 paper showed roughly 50% sobriety rates in treated alcoholics. COMPASS Pathways' NDA is targeted for Q4 2026. The interrupted clinical program is completing its interrupted work.”

When Osmond and Hoffer published their LSD alcoholism results in 1961, they were presenting a landmark finding: roughly half of treated alcoholic patients achieved lasting sobriety. The result exceeded anything available in 1961 psychiatry for alcohol use disorder. The finding did not lead to clinical approval — the Controlled Substances Act of 1970 ended the program.

The clinical research now reaching regulatory maturity uses psilocybin rather than LSD — structurally similar, pharmacologically analogous. COMPASS Pathways' COMP360 has completed two Phase 3 trials: COMP005 (June 2025) and COMP006 (February 2026), both hitting primary endpoints for treatment-resistant depression. The NDA submission is targeted for Q4 2026, with potential FDA approval in late 2026 or early 2027.

FDA's Breakthrough Therapy Designation for COMP360 (2018) provides intensive FDA guidance and rolling review eligibility. The DEA increased its 2026 psilocybin production quota to 50,000 grams — up from 30,000 in 2025 — citing expanded research and clinical trial needs. The Usona Institute's IPR001 program, testing psilocybin for major depressive disorder, received a National Priority Voucher accelerating FDA review.

What approval means: COMP360, if approved, would be the first FDA-approved psychedelic-assisted therapy. It would require certified clinical settings with trained therapists. The clinical model the FDA is approving is structurally what Osmond proposed in the 1950s: preparation, guided session, integration. The regulatory infrastructure for what Huxley called 'proper use' is, sixty-five years after the letters began, approaching completion.

Psychedelics and End-of-Life Care: A Policy Lag

“The evidence for psilocybin in end-of-life anxiety is among the strongest i…”policytherapy
“The evidence for psilocybin in end-of-life anxiety is among the strongest in all of psychedelic medicine. The policy response has been among the slowest.”

The 2016 Johns Hopkins and NYU studies of psilocybin for end-of-life anxiety in terminal cancer patients found that a single psilocybin session produced rapid and sustained reductions in depression and anxiety, with 80 percent showing clinically significant improvement at six months in both studies.

In the United States, psilocybin remains Schedule I — end-of-life psilocybin therapy is not accessible to dying patients outside clinical trials requiring specific eligibility and geographic proximity. Australia moved faster: in February 2023, the TGA approved psilocybin for treatment-resistant depression with provisions including palliative care contexts. Australia became the only country where licensed psychiatrists could prescribe psilocybin to dying patients as standard of care.

Oregon's Measure 109 permits end-of-life access — a person needs only to be 21 or older, without a diagnosis requirement. This means in Oregon, a dying person can legally access psilocybin at a service center, a flexibility the clinical trial infrastructure does not provide.

Huxley requested LSD on his deathbed in 1963. The clinical evidence for this use has been strong since 2016. The policy infrastructure to enable it broadly in the United States has still not arrived. The evidence is not the bottleneck.

What We Call Them: Vocabulary, Policy, and the Framing of Psychedelic Drugs

“The word 'psychedelic' was coined to replace 'psychotomimetic.' Regulators …”policyhistory
“The word 'psychedelic' was coined to replace 'psychotomimetic.' Regulators now use 'classical serotonergic psychedelics.' The vocabulary war continues to shape the policy.”

When Osmond coined 'psychedelic' in 1957 to replace 'psychotomimetic,' he was making a policy argument in the form of a word. 'Psychotomimetic' encoded a clinical framework: these substances mimic psychosis. Any research program premised on this word would investigate them as pathology simulators. 'Psychedelic' — mind-manifesting — encoded a different framework: these substances reveal what the mind contains. A research program premised on this word would investigate them as therapeutic tools.

The FDA's Breakthrough Therapy Designation for COMP360 psilocybin (2018) and MDMA (2017) represented regulatory acknowledgment that these substances might work through mechanisms unlike ordinary psychiatric drugs — not through chronic receptor modulation but through a single transformative experience. The designation implies a different pharmacological category from antidepressants, even if the regulatory pathway is the same.

The scientific literature has settled on 'classical serotonergic psychedelics' (Nichols, 2016) — technically precise but not politically neutral. 'Serotonergic' implies a specific receptor mechanism, pharmacological manageability, FDA-style drug approval as the appropriate regulatory model.

Osmond's vocabulary choice in 1957 shaped every subsequent regulatory discussion. The question of what these substances are doing to the mind is not separate from the question of how they should be governed. Vocabulary is policy, and the vocabulary is still contested.

Schedule I at Fifty-Five: The Science vs. the Scheduling

“LSD has been Schedule I for fifty-five years. Zero documented deaths from o…”policyhistory
“LSD has been Schedule I for fifty-five years. Zero documented deaths from overdose toxicity in eighty years of use. The WHO's 2019 Critical Review found no evidence supporting its current scheduling level.”

LSD has been Schedule I since the Comprehensive Drug Abuse Prevention and Control Act of 1970. Schedule I requires high abuse potential, no accepted medical use, and lack of accepted safety under medical supervision. These criteria have been disputed for fifty-five years.

The safety evidence: the 2016 Global Drug Survey (30,000+ drug users) found LSD had the lowest emergency medical treatment rate of any substance surveyed, lower than alcohol, cannabis, cocaine, and MDMA. Zero deaths from LSD overdose toxicity have been documented in eighty years of human use.

The WHO Expert Committee on Drug Dependence conducted a Critical Review of LSD in 2019 and found no evidence supporting the substance's current international scheduling level. The recommendation did not change the scheduling.

The FDA's Breakthrough Therapy Designation for psilocybin (2018) effectively acknowledged that classical psychedelics may have accepted medical use. COMPASS Pathways' NDA for COMP360 psilocybin, targeted Q4 2026, will be the first formal clinical approval application.

LSD is in Phase 2 clinical trials in Switzerland, Canada, and the UK. The regulatory pathway for LSD lags psilocybin by approximately five years for commercial rather than pharmacological reasons: no company has invested the Phase 3 infrastructure for LSD that COMPASS built for psilocybin. Hofmann proposed rescheduling in 1979. The current regulatory environment is approximately five years from implementing the proposal he always required.

“Hofmann synthesized LSD in 1943. COMPASS Pathways has filed patents on synthetic psilocybin formulations, dosing protocols, and therapy delivery. The enclosure of the psychedelic commons has begun.”

Albert Hofmann synthesized LSD-25 at Sandoz Laboratories. Sandoz held the pharmaceutical patents until they expired. Hofmann consistently argued LSD should be treated as a sacred drug, not a commercial product.

The current psychedelic patent landscape is substantially more aggressive. COMPASS Pathways has filed patents not only on its synthetic psilocybin formulation but on manufacturing processes, specific crystal polymorphs, and therapeutic protocols — including the specific combination of drug, therapist training, and environmental conditions constituting the COMP360 treatment system.

Researchers at Johns Hopkins established a defensive patent program in 2021 — filing patents on psychedelic compounds and protocols specifically to ensure prior art was in the public domain, preventing any single entity from monopolizing the space. The Usona Institute committed to non-exclusive licensing.

The indigenous knowledge dimension adds another layer: many compounds under patent consideration were used by indigenous communities for millennia. The ayahuasca patent case (US Patent 5,751,559, cancelled 2003 after indigenous challenge) established that prior art arguments can defeat patents on traditional plant knowledge.

Hofmann's problem child has become a commercial asset. Whether its therapeutic potential will be captured serving patients broadly or primarily shareholders is the central policy question of the current psychedelic industry.

Cluster Headaches and LSD: The Orphan Indication

“Cluster headache patients figured out that sub-hallucinogenic doses of LSD …”policypharmacology
“Cluster headache patients figured out that sub-hallucinogenic doses of LSD can abort cycles before any clinical trial tested it. The regulatory pathway has taken twenty years to formalize.”

Cluster headaches are called 'suicide headaches' by sufferers — orbital pain lasting 15 minutes to three hours, occurring multiple times daily. In online communities of sufferers in the early 2000s, an unusual pattern emerged: sub-hallucinogenic doses of LSD or psilocybin could abort active cluster cycles and extend remission significantly.

Andrew Sewell and colleagues published the first case series in Neurology in 2006, documenting 53 cluster headache patients who tried psilocybin or LSD. Both substances significantly shortened or aborted cluster periods in most respondents. The mechanism — hypothetically involving serotonergic effects on the trigeminal nucleus — is not fully understood.

No pharmaceutical company has sponsored a Phase 3 cluster headache trial for LSD or psilocybin. Cluster headache is rare (approximately 0.1% of population), limiting commercial incentive. The patient community has been vocal, but the regulatory pathway depends on commercial sponsorship that has not materialized.

This is Hofmann's problem child at its most ironic: a compound that patients are already using effectively, with a safety profile that supports use, and preliminary clinical evidence confirming efficacy, but that the regulatory system cannot fully approve because the commercial economics don't justify the Phase 3 investment. The problem child remains a partial orphan.

The Ecological Drug War: What Prohibition Costs the Planet

“McKenna's argument was ecological before it was pharmacological. The drug w…”policyculture
“McKenna's argument was ecological before it was pharmacological. The drug war and the environmental crisis have the same root: the dominator culture's relationship with the natural world.”

McKenna's argument in Food of the Gods is not primarily about drugs. It is about ecology. The suppression of plant medicines is one feature of a broader cultural pathology: the dominator culture's relationship with nature is extractive because the same culture that treats plants as objects treats consciousness as a territory to be conquered.

The Amazon has lost approximately 20 percent of its forest cover since 1992. The Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework (2022) commits signatories to protect 30 percent of global land by 2030 and includes specific provisions for indigenous-managed territories — recognizing that indigenous land management practices generally produce better conservation outcomes than state-managed protected areas.

The communities most effectively protecting biological diversity are the same communities that maintain plant medicine traditions. This connection is now embedded in mainstream conservation policy.

The policy implication is not that psilocybin legalization will save the Amazon. The policy implication is that the drug war's suppression of indigenous plant knowledge traditions has contributed to severing the ecological relationship McKenna identified as constitutive of healthy human culture. Restoration of legal access to plant medicines, within appropriate cultural frameworks, would serve ecological goals as well as therapeutic ones.

McKenna's argument provides no detailed policy blueprint, only the premise: these plants belong to the commons, not to the state or the corporation.

Food of the Gods is not a book about ibogaine. But its central argument — that psychoactive plants are medicine and that Western civilization has been impoverished by their suppression — has found unexpected expression in the most politically conservative corner of the current psychedelic policy landscape: veterans' PTSD treatment.

Ibogaine, derived from the iboga shrub of Gabon and Cameroon, produces a 12-36 hour experience characterized by intense autobiographical review and, in many reports, direct confrontation with consequences of one's actions. Small studies of veterans with PTSD and opioid use disorder have shown striking results that exceed available alternatives.

The political pathway for ibogaine has moved through veteran advocacy. Texas Governor Greg Abbott signed legislation in 2025 directing $50 million toward ibogaine clinical trials for veterans. Rick Perry — former Texas governor, Secretary of Energy under Trump — chairs Americans for Ibogaine. Mississippi's ibogaine research bill was signed in March 2026, coordinating with the Texas framework. Utah signed a veteran-focused psychedelic therapy research bill in March 2026.

The political dynamics are notable: these are conservative states with Republican governors, investing in psychedelic medicine research because the patient population is veterans. The bipartisan character of ibogaine advocacy is one of the clearest examples of how the policy landscape has shifted since McKenna wrote — not through countercultural arguments but through clinical evidence combined with a politically sympathetic patient population.

Decriminalization Models: Oregon, Colorado, and What Comes Next

“Oregon's Measure 110 decriminalized all personal drug possession in 2020. T…”policyhistory
“Oregon's Measure 110 decriminalized all personal drug possession in 2020. The legislature repealed it in 2024. The lesson: services without social investment cannot hold politically.”

Oregon passed two ballot measures in November 2020: Measure 109 (regulated psilocybin services) and Measure 110 (decriminalizing personal possession of all drugs). By 2024, Oregon's legislature had repealed Measure 110. The drug decriminalization portion collapsed under political pressure and implementation difficulties — the provision replacing criminal penalties with health assessments required social service infrastructure that was not ready when the law took effect.

Colorado's Proposition 122 attempted to combine both: regulated healing center access alongside personal decriminalization. Colorado's approach is still being implemented and has not faced the legislative reversal Oregon's decriminalization did.

As of mid-2026, psychedelic reform is advancing simultaneously in multiple states through multiple models. New Mexico's medical psilocybin program became operational in 2025 — the first to pass through a legislature rather than a ballot. New Jersey signed a $6 million psychedelic research initiative in January 2026. Massachusetts has multiple competing bills advancing. Alaska is gathering signatures for a 2026 ballot initiative.

The diversity of models is itself informative. The comparative data on outcomes will eventually produce a clearer evidence base for what works. McKenna's argument provides no blueprint, only the premise: these plants belong to the commons. The regulatory implementation of that premise requires environmental impact assessments and state licensing boards — which is not what he predicted, but is what is happening.

The Right to Alter Your Own Consciousness

“McKenna argued that the privacy of the individual mind is the most basic ci…”policyphilosophy
“McKenna argued that the privacy of the individual mind is the most basic civil liberty. The courts have not agreed. The legislature is beginning to.”

The psychedelic issue is a civil rights and civil liberties issue, McKenna wrote. It concerns the most basic of human freedoms: religious practice and the privacy of the individual mind.

The courts have been skeptical. No federal court has recognized a constitutional right to alter one's consciousness through controlled substances independent of religious context.

The legislature has been more receptive. Colorado's Proposition 122 is the most expansive implementation of McKenna's personal autonomy argument: decriminalized personal possession, cultivation, use, and social sharing of psilocybin, psilocyn, ibogaine, and mescaline (excluding peyote) for adults. The social sharing provision specifically protects informal, communal, and ceremonial use outside commercial or medical frameworks.

The Cato Institute's 2025 analysis argues for building on existing cannabis regulatory infrastructure rather than creating new regulatory agencies — using dispensaries, testing laboratories, and compliance frameworks already established for cannabis.

McKenna's framing — that the illegality of plants is obnoxious and ridiculous in the first place — captures what most policy advocates are more careful to avoid saying: the fundamental premise of drug prohibition, applied to plants humans have used for thousands of years, is philosophically incoherent. The plant does not become illegal because a legislature says so. The law making it illegal is the aberration.

The Fentanyl Crisis: What Hari's Framework Predicted and Didn't

“107,500 overdose deaths in 2023 — the highest in US history, primarily fent…”policypharmacology
“107,500 overdose deaths in 2023 — the highest in US history, primarily fentanyl. Hari's connection model predicted the social conditions driving addiction. It did not predict how prohibition-driven supply adulteration would accelerate mortality.”

Hari published Chasing the Scream in 2015, when US drug overdose deaths were approximately 52,000 annually. By 2023, overdose deaths had reached 107,500 — primarily attributable to illicit fentanyl and fentanyl analogs that had displaced heroin in the illegal drug market.

Hari's connection model correctly predicted that enforcement-focused policy would not reduce drug use or addiction rates. It did not specifically predict the mechanism by which the combination of increased enforcement and synthetic opioid availability would produce the mortality catastrophe of the 2020s.

The fentanyl crisis is in significant part a product of supply-side enforcement. Prohibition-driven pressure on heroin supply created market incentives for synthetic opioids that are more potent, more concentrated, easier to smuggle, and vastly more dangerous per unit. Fentanyl is approximately 50-100 times more potent than heroin by weight. The enforcement that was supposed to reduce drug supply has instead selected for more dangerous versions of the supply.

This pharmacological and economic argument complements Hari's social argument: prohibition does not eliminate drug markets; it selects for the most dangerous formats. Alcohol prohibition produced high-proof bootleg spirits. Heroin prohibition has produced fentanyl.

Portugal's harm reduction programs have had more limited impact on fentanyl-driven mortality precisely because fentanyl bypasses the social conditions approach: a person can be socially connected and still die from an accidental overdose of supply-contaminated product.

Harm Reduction in 2026: What Has Actually Changed

“OnPoint NYC reversed over 1,200 overdoses without a single on-site death be…”policytherapy
“OnPoint NYC reversed over 1,200 overdoses without a single on-site death between November 2021 and 2025. The US had no legal safe injection site for over forty years after the first opened in Canada.”

In November 2021, OnPoint NYC opened in East Harlem — the first legally sanctioned overdose prevention center in the United States. It serves an average of 500 clients daily and by 2025 had reversed over 1,200 overdoses through naloxone administration without a single on-site overdose death.

Harm reduction policy has expanded significantly since 2015. Naloxone availability has improved dramatically: available without prescription in every US state, with Narcan (nasal naloxone) receiving OTC approval in 2023. Fentanyl test strips, allowing users to check supply for the most dangerous adulterant, have been legalized in most states and distributed through syringe service programs.

What has not changed: the federal legal framework still classifies safe injection sites as illegal under the Controlled Substances Act's 'crack house' statute. The DOJ under the Trump administration did not challenge OnPoint NYC operationally, but the legal uncertainty has prevented most jurisdictions from opening similar facilities.

Hari's argument — that harm reduction is not only more humane but more effective than enforcement — has been confirmed by every facility permitted to operate. The policy constraint is not the evidence.

Hari's documentation of individual stories — Holiday, the communities he visited — is the human texture of what statistics describe. The policy debate often proceeds as if the racial targeting were incidental rather than central. The Ehrlichman quote is the evidence that it was not.

Decriminalization in America: Oregon's Reversal and What It Means

“Oregon's Measure 110 decriminalized all personal drug possession in 2020. T…”policyhistory
“Oregon's Measure 110 decriminalized all personal drug possession in 2020. The legislature repealed it in 2024. The lesson is not that decriminalization failed — it is that decriminalization without social investment cannot hold politically.”

Oregon's Measure 110 (November 2020) replaced criminal penalties for personal possession of all drugs with health assessments and referrals. The model was explicitly inspired by Portugal's 2001 decriminalization. By 2024, the Oregon Legislature had repealed Measure 110. The health assessment provisions had not been adequately implemented — the social service infrastructure required to make referrals meaningful did not exist in the communities where repeal of criminal penalties was most consequential.

Hari's account of Portugal's success was accurate for Portugal in the period he studied (2001-2015). What his account underweighted — as longer-term data has confirmed — is that Portugal's success depended on the social investment component, which austerity measures after the 2008 financial crisis eroded.

Oregon's reversal is instructive: decriminalization is necessary but not sufficient. Without corresponding investment in housing, employment, treatment capacity, and community services, decriminalization alone produces political vulnerability rather than public health improvement.

The lesson is not that Hari was wrong. It is that his framework is more demanding than 'stop arresting people.' Stop arresting people and provide meaningful alternatives to the conditions that drive drug use — that is the full policy, and it is considerably harder to implement than the arrest-and-incarcerate system it replaces.

Two Thousand Years of Suppression: Sacred Pharmacology and Legal Rights

“The Mysteries were abolished by state power in 392 CE because they competed…”policyhistory
“The Mysteries were abolished by state power in 392 CE because they competed with state religion. The US scheduling of psilocybin and LSD follows the same logic.”

In 392 CE, Emperor Theodosius issued edicts outlawing non-Christian religious practice throughout the Roman Empire. The Eleusinian Mysteries, which had operated continuously for approximately a thousand years, were formally prohibited. The political structure of the suppression is not obscure: a state religion that could not coexist with a competing institution offering direct, individual experience of the divine used state power to eliminate the competition.

Carl Ruck's scholarship places contemporary drug prohibition in this historical lineage: the recurring pattern in which institutions that manage access to the sacred suppress experiences that bypass their mediation. Psychedelic experience characteristically produces what William James called the 'noetic quality' — a sense of having directly received genuine knowledge. This is precisely what institutional religion claims to provide.

The Religious Freedom Restoration Act provides the current US legal framework for the argument that psychedelic experience deserves First Amendment protection. Gonzales v. O Centro (2006) applying RFRA to ayahuasca demonstrates legal traction. The Church of Gaia's May 2025 non-litigation DEA approval demonstrates the regulatory system can accommodate sincere religious psychedelic use.

But RFRA protection requires demonstrating sincerity of religious belief, creating institutional barriers. The Road to Eleusis scholarship's argument — that entheogenic religious practice is foundational rather than peripheral to Western civilization's religious history — is directly relevant to how these barriers should be evaluated.

The Eleusis Site: Heritage, Archaeology, and Pending Evidence

“Chemical residue analysis of excavated vessels could confirm or significant…”policyhistory

The archaeological site at ancient Eleusis — location of the Telesterion, the Sacred Way, and the sanctuary complex where two thousand years of Mystery initiations occurred — is a protected UNESCO-monitored zone in the municipality of Eleusis, approximately thirty kilometers from Athens. It is also adjacent to an operating oil refinery.

The Hellenic Ministry of Culture began a major excavation program in 2015. As of 2026, the excavation has produced new architectural documentation and ceramic finds, but the chemical residue analysis that would most directly test the Wasson-Hofmann-Ruck hypothesis has not been undertaken at the Eleusis site itself.

The 2026 Scientific Reports paper by Antonopoulos and Dadiotis explicitly calls for such analysis: 'Detailed archaeobotanical and chemical analyses of relevant vessels from the Eleusis sanctuary itself are necessary to confirm or refute the ergot alkaloid hypothesis.' The methods required are non-destructive for macroscopic residue analysis and minimally destructive for chemical sampling.

Eleusis's 2023 designation as European Capital of Culture brought significant international attention and EU funding, creating political conditions more favorable to innovative research. The research question is not whether the analysis should be done — it should — but whether institutional, political, and resource conditions will support it.

Carl Ruck was one of three authors of The Road to Eleusis (1978). A year later, he was one of five authors of a short paper in the Journal of Psychedelic Drugs proposing a new word for substances used in religious contexts: entheogen, from the Greek en theos — 'the divine within.'

The paper argued that 'hallucinogen' was inappropriate for substances used in genuine religious practice because it encoded the assumption that what was experienced was unreal. A new word was needed that accurately described the category: substances that occasion the experience of the divine, used within a framework that recognizes that experience as sacred.

'Entheogen' has significant uptake in ethnobotanical and religious studies contexts. The legal significance is not negligible. RFRA protection requires demonstrating that a substance is used for religious purposes as part of sincere religious belief. The word 'entheogen' describes a category of substance use that is, by definition, religious rather than recreational.

The Church of Gaia's May 2025 DEA approval was granted under the entheogenic religious use framework. Whether the framework will expand to cover substances beyond ayahuasca, or contexts beyond formally organized religious institutions, is the open regulatory question. The Road to Eleusis scholarship provides the historical argument for why it should.

This argument is in active litigation through RFRA cases. The Road to Eleusis scholarship and Muraresku's extension in The Immortality Key are being cited in these proceedings. MDMA's FDA Rejection: A 1968 Pattern in 2024

“In August 2024, the FDA rejected Lykos Therapeutics' MDMA-assisted therapy …”policyhistory
“In August 2024, the FDA rejected Lykos Therapeutics' MDMA-assisted therapy application for PTSD. The decision was not about efficacy — Phase 3 showed significant results. It was about trial design concerns.”

In June 2024, the FDA's Psychopharmacologic Drugs Advisory Committee voted 10-1 that the evidence did not show MDMA-assisted therapy was effective for PTSD. In August 2024, the FDA issued a Complete Response Letter denying the NDA.

The rejection surprised many. Phase 3 trial data showed 67-71 percent of PTSD patients who received MDMA-assisted therapy no longer met diagnostic criteria at follow-up, compared to approximately 32 percent in the placebo arm.

The FDA's concerns were methodological, not efficacy-based: trials could not adequately blind participants to whether they received active MDMA or placebo; therapist expectancy bias was not controlled; adverse events were inadequately characterized; and trial safety monitoring for drug misuse by therapists was insufficient. An additional Phase 3 trial was requested.

Jay Stevens documented the 1968 collapse of LSD research: a clinical program ended not because the evidence was wrong but because political and institutional conditions became untenable. The MDMA rejection follows a different but related pattern: genuine efficacy evidence found insufficiently methodologically rigorous to approve.

The FDA's request for an additional trial is not a refusal to engage with psychedelic therapy — it is an engagement demanding higher methodological standards than the program delivered. Whether this represents regulatory caution or obstruction depends on one's prior.

The Bipartisan Moment: Veterans, Ibogaine, and the New Political Map

“Texas signed $50M in ibogaine research funding. Colorado pardoned psychedel…”policyhistory
“Texas signed $50M in ibogaine research funding. Colorado pardoned psychedelic convictions. Utah signed veteran psychedelic therapy research. The political map has become genuinely bipartisan.”

Jay Stevens closed Storming Heaven in 1968 with the Schedule I classification as a politically driven suppression of clinical research. The political context was clear: the Nixon administration's drug war explicitly targeted anti-war protesters and Black communities.

The political context of the current psychedelic policy moment is substantially different. In 2025, Rick Perry — former Republican Governor of Texas, Secretary of Energy under Trump — became chairman of Americans for Ibogaine and advocated for ibogaine research funding to treat veterans. Texas Governor Greg Abbott signed legislation directing $50 million toward ibogaine clinical trials. Mississippi's Republican-led legislature passed an ibogaine research bill in March 2026.

Utah, with conservative political culture and a large veteran population, signed a veteran-focused psychedelic therapy research bill in March 2026. On the other side: Colorado Governor Polis (Democrat) pardoned people convicted of state psychedelic possession charges. Oregon's Democratic-led legislature passed technical fixes to the psilocybin services program.

Psychedelic reform is no longer a left-right issue. The patient population of veterans with PTSD has created a coalition including conservative military veterans, Republican governors, and libertarian advocacy organizations alongside progressive harm reduction advocates.

The drug war was built on political polarization. Psychedelic reform is, unexpectedly, being built on political convergence.

State vs. Federal: The Legal Landscape After Oregon and Colorado

“Psilocybin is Schedule I under federal law and legal in Oregon and Colorado…”policyhistory
“Psilocybin is Schedule I under federal law and legal in Oregon and Colorado. The same legal architecture that produced cannabis's state-federal conflict is now producing psychedelics' state-federal conflict.”

When Oregon's Measure 109 took effect in 2023, psilocybin became simultaneously Schedule I under federal law and regulated-legal under Oregon state law — the same legal architecture governing cannabis since Colorado and Washington's 2012 recreational legalization votes.

The psychedelic state-federal conflict is being managed through prosecutorial discretion: the DEA and DOJ have not challenged Oregon's psilocybin services program or Colorado's Natural Medicine Health Act. Over 100 service centers operate openly under Oregon state law without federal interference.

This arrangement is legally precarious: it depends on continued prosecutorial discretion, which could change with a new administration. The cannabis industry spent years seeking banking access and insurance coverage — complicated by the federal-state conflict. The psychedelic therapy industry will face the same complications unless federal law changes.

Federal psilocybin rescheduling — accompanying FDA approval of COMP360, if approved — would resolve the conflict for psilocybin in clinical contexts. It would not resolve the conflict for broader decriminalization provisions in Colorado and Oregon.

The Cato Institute's 2025 analysis argues state-level innovation should proceed regardless of federal action. The cannabis precedent supports this: state legalization preceded federal policy change and drove it. Stevens documented the 1968 federal destruction of psychedelic research; current states are building a record that may prevent a similar destruction.

Public vs. Private: Who Funds the Psychedelic Research Program

“In the 1950s, the CIA and NIH both funded psychedelic research simultaneous…”policyhistory
“In the 1950s, the CIA and NIH both funded psychedelic research simultaneously. In 2026, NIH contribution remains minimal. Private capital has filled the gap — and private capital has its own incentive structure.”

Stevens documented in Storming Heaven that the 1950s-1960s psychedelic research program had two simultaneous government funders: the CIA (through MK-Ultra, interested in weaponization) and the NIH (through legitimate research grants). Both ended with the 1968-1970 prohibition.

The current renaissance has been funded primarily by private capital rather than federal sources. COMPASS Pathways has raised over $300 million from venture capital and public markets. MAPS has raised over $100 million from philanthropic sources. The commercial pipeline of psychedelic biotech companies has attracted over $1 billion in investment since 2018.

NIH funding for psychedelic research has increased but remains a small fraction: approximately $20-30 million annually as of 2024-2025, compared to hundreds of millions from private sources. The research program is primarily driven by investors who need regulatory approval to generate returns.

This creates structural conditions Stevens identified as a risk: when financial interests drive the research agenda, questions being answered are those relevant to commercialization rather than the full range of therapeutic, cultural, and scientific applications. Cluster headaches — no large commercially attractive population — are not being funded. Indigenous ceremonial uses — no proprietary IP — are not being funded.

Osmond and Hoffer's Saskatchewan research was publicly funded provincial health research. The questions were driven by clinical need and scientific curiosity. The current program's questions are shaped by venture capital. The difference is not irrelevant.
