Was It Leary's Fault?

“Stevens is careful about assigning blame. Leary was not the only cause of t…”historyculture
“Stevens is careful about assigning blame. Leary was not the only cause of the 1968 collapse. He was the most visible accelerant.”

Jay Stevens does not write Timothy Leary as a villain in Storming Heaven. He writes him as a man of considerable intelligence who made a series of decisions that destroyed, in the short term, something more valuable than what he was building.

The chain of causation is more complex than 'Leary's fault.' The CIA's coercive research had already given prohibition its evidence. The counterculture's enthusiastic adoption of LSD had already created the political conditions for suppression. Anslinger's framework was already in place.

Leary did not create the conditions for the 1968 crackdown. He accelerated them.

What he did: he moved LSD from a clinical tool being carefully developed into a public symbol of rebellion against the social order. He made the connection between LSD and anti-war, anti-establishment politics explicit and theatrical. He gave the Nixon administration exactly the association they needed to make scheduling politically viable.

Huxley saw this coming. His letters to Osmond in the early 1960s include the warning that public advocacy would provoke a crackdown. He recognized the impulse as genuine. He was criticizing the strategy.

Stevens's judgment: the impulse was genuine and the strategy was catastrophic. What we cannot know is whether the crackdown would have come anyway, because the political conditions that made it possible were already present.

Sources

  • Stevens, Storming Heaven (1987)
Mini-EssayStorming Heaven190 words2 source entriesstatus: published

What the CIA Was Looking For

“The CIA spent a decade trying to weaponize LSD and produced nothing useful …”historyculture
“The CIA spent a decade trying to weaponize LSD and produced nothing useful except a casualty. The program's only lasting contribution was Ken Kesey.”

The CIA's interest in LSD was instrumental: could it extract information from unwilling subjects? Could it break down psychological resistance? Could it program behavior the subject wouldn't remember or resist?

The answer, after a decade of research including Operation Midnight Climax — in which unwitting subjects were dosed in San Francisco safe houses while agents watched through one-way mirrors — was no to all of the above.

What the program produced: in at least one documented case, a death. Frank Olson, the Army researcher secretly dosed by Sidney Gottlieb in 1953, fell from a New York hotel window.

The CIA program's ironic legacy is Ken Kesey. Kesey participated as a paid volunteer in a CIA-sponsored LSD study at the VA hospital in Menlo Park. He obtained LSD through the research network, formed the Merry Pranksters, organized the Acid Tests, and helped drive the counterculture's adoption of LSD — thereby providing the political conditions that made prohibition politically viable.

The CIA was looking for a weapon. What it found, through the pathway it inadvertently opened, was a movement that helped destroy the clinical research program it was simultaneously trying to weaponize.

Sources

  • Stevens, Storming Heaven (1987)
  • Marks, The Search for the Manchurian Candidate (1979)

Huxley's Warning: The Letter That Wasn't Heeded

“Huxley spent his final years trying to slow down what was coming. He failed…”historyculture
“Huxley spent his final years trying to slow down what was coming. He failed. The failure was not for lack of trying.”

By 1960, Aldous Huxley understood that Timothy Leary was going to destroy something valuable. He said so in letters to Osmond.

Huxley's argument: the experiences these substances provide are genuine and potentially transformative, but the social conditions for their beneficial use are fragile. They require careful preparation, experienced guidance, proper setting, and institutional distance from politics. Any association with public rebellion would give the government the excuse it needed.

Leary heard Huxley's concern and did not share it. He believed the experience was powerful enough to transform people regardless of context, and that democratizing access through public advocacy was more important than protecting the clinical research program.

Both men were right about different things. Huxley was right that the advocacy would provoke the crackdown. Leary was right that the experiences were powerful. Neither was entirely wrong about the other's concern.

What neither anticipated was the speed: the crackdown came within eight years. The clinical program that Osmond had spent fifteen years building was ended before it reached regulatory maturity.

Sources

  • Stevens, Storming Heaven (1987)
  • Huxley & Osmond, in Moksha (1977)

The Resumption: Picking Up Where 1968 Left Off

“Stevens documented the interruption. He could not have anticipated its end.…”historytherapy
“Stevens documented the interruption. He could not have anticipated its end. The end is happening now.”

Storming Heaven ends in despair. The clinical program that Hoffer, Osmond, Grof, and Pahnke had built was ended by a scheduling decision that had nothing to do with the evidence.

Stevens published in 1987. He did not know the interruption would end.

The ending is happening now. COMPASS Pathways has completed two Phase 3 trials for psilocybin in treatment-resistant depression. The NDA submission is targeted for Q4 2026. Johns Hopkins, NYU, Imperial College, and dozens of other institutions are running clinical trials. Australia approved psilocybin for clinical use in 2023. Oregon has a licensed psilocybin services program.

The specific clinical program Stevens mourned — Hoffer and Osmond's alcoholism protocol — has been reproduced with psilocybin. A 2022 NYU trial found that psilocybin-assisted therapy produced significantly better outcomes than placebo for alcohol use disorder.

Stevens wrote a history of an interruption. It has since become a history of an interruption that ended. That is, ultimately, a better story than the one he wrote.

Sources

  • Stevens, Storming Heaven (1987)
  • COMPASS Pathways Phase 3 (2025-2026)

The Two Worlds: Clinic and Culture Cannot Be Separated

“Stevens shows why the clinical and countercultural traditions cannot be sep…”historyculture
“Stevens shows why the clinical and countercultural traditions cannot be separated, no matter how hard each tries. They share a molecule.”

The central argument of Storming Heaven is about the impossibility of maintaining separation between clinical and countercultural psychedelic use. Osmond and Huxley tried. They built a careful, controlled clinical tradition that distinguished its use from recreational experimentation in every detail of protocol and intention.

The counterculture arrived anyway. Not because the clinical tradition failed — it was succeeding — but because the molecule was the same. The same compound that produced controlled therapeutic experiences in Weyburn and the Maryland Psychiatric Research Center produced the Acid Tests.

The compound couldn't be restricted to those who approached it correctly, because 'correctly' is not encoded in the chemistry.

This is the problem that the current psychedelic renaissance is also navigating. Every clinical trial takes place in a culture that already uses psilocybin recreationally. Every licensed service center operates in a state where psilocybin is simultaneously a therapeutic tool and a recreational substance.

Stevens documents the collapse of the attempt to separate them in the 1960s. The current movement is attempting to manage the relationship rather than enforce the separation — to build regulatory frameworks accommodating both therapeutic and adult-use contexts rather than insisting on one at the expense of the other.

Sources

  • Stevens, Storming Heaven (1987)

The $100,000 Challenge: Radical Transparency as Activism

“Herer offered $100,000 to anyone who could disprove his central claims and …”historyculture
“Herer offered $100,000 to anyone who could disprove his central claims and renewed the offer with every edition. The challenge was never met.”

The $100,000 challenge was both a rhetorical device and a genuine offer. Herer included it in every edition: if you can disprove my central claims about cannabis prohibition, hemp's industrial potential, and the suppressed medical literature, I will pay.

The challenge was never met. Nobody collected $100,000.

This does not mean every claim in the book is unassailable. Some of Herer's inferences — the specific DuPont orchestration thesis — exceed what the primary documents can support. But the challenge was carefully scoped to the central historical claims, which are substantially documented.

The challenge was also a way of forcing engagement. Herer understood that his audience would not believe him on authority — he had no institutional authority. What he had was documents. The $100,000 challenge was a dare: if you think these documents say something different from what I say they say, prove it.

No one did. The challenge sat unanswered across twelve editions and twenty-five years, which is itself a form of evidence. Not conclusive evidence — but it suggests that institutional opponents of cannabis legalization, who had every incentive to demolish Herer's argument if they could, were unable to do so from the available documentary record.

Sources

  • Herer, The Emperor Wears No Clothes (multiple editions)

Hemp for Victory: The Film That Was Hidden

“The US government denied the film existed. Then someone found it in the Lib…”historypolicy
“The US government denied the film existed. Then someone found it in the Library of Congress. The sequence is the argument.”

Hemp for Victory is a thirteen-minute film produced by the USDA in 1942. It urged American farmers to grow cannabis hemp for the war effort after the Japanese occupation of the Philippines cut off the supply of Manila hemp.

By the 1980s, the USDA denied the film existed. Library of Congress records did not list it.

Maria Farrow and Carl Packard searched the Library of Congress holdings anyway. They found the film in 1989. Herer announced the discovery. The Library of Congress subsequently acknowledged the film's existence.

The sequence is the argument, compressed to its essential structure. The government produced a film urging farmers to grow cannabis hemp as a patriotic duty in 1942. The same government subsequently denied that the film had ever been made. When the film was found, the government acknowledged it.

Herer used this sequence repeatedly, not because it proved the DuPont conspiracy thesis but because it demonstrated something simpler and more damning: the government had a documented relationship with industrial hemp that directly contradicted its official position on cannabis prohibition. This contradiction was on film.

The film is now on YouTube.

Sources

  • Herer, The Emperor Wears No Clothes (1985)
  • Wikipedia, Hemp for Victory

The Timing of Nylon

“Nylon was patented by DuPont in February 1938. The Marihuana Tax Act was si…”historypolicy
“Nylon was patented by DuPont in February 1938. The Marihuana Tax Act was signed into law in October 1937. Herer said this was not a coincidence.”

The Marihuana Tax Act was signed into law on October 1, 1937. DuPont patented nylon on February 16, 1938. Popular Mechanics published its 'New Billion-Dollar Crop' article describing hemp's industrial potential the same month.

Herer's argument: these are not independent events. DuPont needed hemp eliminated from the market to protect nylon's commercial position.

The correlation is real. Whether the correlation is causal is the question historians disagree about.

The case for causation: DuPont's financial institution was Mellon Bank. Andrew Mellon was Secretary of Treasury. Harry Anslinger was Mellon's relative and his appointee as FBN commissioner. DuPont had been briefing Treasury officials on the decorticator technology that threatened nylon. The legislation was drafted by Herman Oliphant, who received DuPont's briefings.

The case against simple causation: the racial panic around cannabis, immigration anxiety, and the moral reform movement were independently sufficient to produce prohibition legislation. DuPont may have benefited without orchestrating.

The honest assessment: DuPont almost certainly benefited from hemp prohibition. Whether it engineered the prohibition or exploited existing political conditions is not fully established. Herer presents the former as fact. The evidence supports the latter.

Sources

  • Herer, The Emperor Wears No Clothes (1985)
  • Popular Mechanics, New Billion-Dollar Crop (February 1938)

Anderson's Lesson: Why the Title Is Right

“In Andersen's tale, the emperor's nakedness is visible to everyone. The soc…”culturephilosophy
“In Andersen's tale, the emperor's nakedness is visible to everyone. The social pressure not to say so is what keeps the fiction functioning.”

Hans Christian Andersen's 1837 fairy tale is about the social mechanics of false consensus. Two swindlers sell the emperor clothes invisible to those who are incompetent or stupid. The emperor, unwilling to appear incompetent, admires the clothes he cannot see. His court follows. Only a child says what everyone can see: the emperor is wearing nothing.

Herer's title borrows this structure precisely. The emperor — cannabis prohibition — is wearing no clothes. The scientific evidence for the scheduling was fabricated or absent. The congressional hearings that produced it lasted two hours. The medical evidence supported the opposite conclusion from the one enacted.

The child who says what everyone can see is effective precisely because children have not yet learned the social pressure not to say obvious things. Herer cast himself in this role: the person who will say the thing that everyone with power has tacitly agreed not to say.

The analogy holds well. The emperor's nakedness — the absence of evidence for cannabis's Schedule I status — was visible to anyone who looked at the primary documents. Herer looked. He said what he saw. He printed it and sold it in head shops for thirty years.

The emperor is now partially clothed again, by rescheduling proceedings and medical cannabis markets. The clothes are still not what was claimed.

Sources

  • Herer, The Emperor Wears No Clothes (1985)
  • Andersen, The Emperor's New Clothes (1837)

Jack Herer: The Man Behind the Strain

“Herer was born in New York, served in Korea, and spent the rest of his life…”historyculture
“Herer was born in New York, served in Korea, and spent the rest of his life in documentation and activism. He died in 2010 having been proven substantially right.”

Jack Herer was born in New York City on June 18, 1939. He served in the Army as a military police officer in Korea. He encountered the California Marijuana Initiative in 1972 and discovered hemp's industrial potential. He spent the next thirty-eight years documenting the case that cannabis prohibition was an injustice, and he spent the last years of those thirty-eight years being substantially vindicated.

He was not a comfortable person to read or to know. He was loud, repetitive, sometimes imprecise, and cared about being right more than being polished.

It is also the foundational document of the modern cannabis legalization movement. The argument he assembled from government documents — that hemp prohibition was politically manufactured, that the medical evidence was suppressed, that the scheduling was scientifically unjustified — has been confirmed by the policy changes of the last decade.

He died in April 2010 having seen the beginning of what he had worked toward. He did not see the 2018 Farm Bill legalize industrial hemp. He did not see 24 states legalize recreational cannabis. He did not see the DOJ propose rescheduling.

He died with the strain that bears his name on dispensary menus across North America.

Sources

  • Jetty Extracts, Jack Herer Legacy (2026)
  • Wikipedia, Jack Herer

The Question That Remains Open

“In 80,000 plant species, indigenous peoples found the two whose combination…”ethnobotanyphilosophy
“In 80,000 plant species, indigenous peoples found the two whose combination creates oral DMT activity. The standard explanation — trial and error — is mathematically implausible.”

The combinatorial problem is the sharpest single challenge in the psychedelic literature to the assumption that Western science has a monopoly on reliable knowledge.

In an Amazon containing approximately 80,000 plant species, indigenous peoples across multiple independent cultures identified the same two plants: Banisteriopsis caapi and Psychotria viridis. Their combination creates oral DMT activity. Neither alone produces the sustained visionary state. The interaction requires knowing both plants and discovering that combining an oral MAO inhibitor with an orally inactive tryptamine produces hours of visionary experience.

The standard Western explanation is trial and error. Across 80,000 species, searching for the combination of two specific ones whose interaction only becomes apparent when both are consumed together. The combinatorial mathematics of this search space are forbidding.

All indigenous peoples asked about the discovery give the same answer: the plants told us. Narby spent a decade investigating what this answer might mean. He did not resolve it. He established that Western science's dismissal — 'hallucination, not information' — is itself a philosophical position rather than an empirical finding.

The question is real. The standard dismissal is inadequate. The correct answer is not known.

Sources

  • Narby, The Cosmic Serpent (1998)
  • Schultes & Hofmann, Plants of the Gods (1979)

The Double Helix and the Caduceus

“The medical symbol of the Western world is two serpents coiled around a sta…”historyphilosophy
“The medical symbol of the Western world is two serpents coiled around a staff. It is older than medicine. Narby says it represents DNA.”

The caduceus — two serpents coiled around a staff — is the symbol of Western medicine. It is ancient: Hermes carries it in Homer. Some form of the twin-serpent image appears in Sumerian iconography from the third millennium BCE.

Jeremy Narby's argument: the double helix of DNA and the twin serpents of the caduceus are the same image, arriving through different pathways. The shamanic visions in which serpents appear are, in his hypothesis, perceptions of the molecular level of life — specifically of DNA, which emits biophotons in the visible range and which, at the scale at which these biophotons might be perceived, would appear as luminous helical structures.

Kekule's Ouroboros is the supporting anecdote: a Western chemist solved the ring structure of benzene after a serpent dream. The convergence of shamanic vision imagery and Western chemical discovery in the same serpent image is the data point Narby emphasizes most.

The hypothesis is speculative but not empty. It is interesting in the specific sense that it generates testable predictions. That is more than most speculation offers.

The Ashaninca Answer

“When Narby asked how his hosts had learned the medicinal properties of plan…”indigenousphilosophy
“When Narby asked how his hosts had learned the medicinal properties of plants, they answered without hesitation: by drinking a hallucinogenic brew.”

The anecdote Narby opens with is the book's engine.

An Ashaninca man tells him that his people learned the medicinal properties of plants by drinking ayahuasca. Narby, trained in social science, interprets this as metaphor — a culturally embedded explanation for systematic empirical observation.

But the man is not speaking metaphorically. He is making a literal claim: the plants teach us about the plants. The ayahuasca experience provides direct information about the pharmacological properties of other plants.

Narby spends a decade trying to dismiss this answer and eventually concludes that he cannot. Not because he accepts it uncritically — he does not — but because no alternative explanation is adequate to the phenomenon being explained.

The specific phenomenon: indigenous Amazonian pharmacological knowledge is systematically accurate. The compounds isolated from plants Schultes documented have produced medical treatments. The knowledge works.

If the knowledge works, and if the people who hold it say it came from the plants, the scientific response should be to take this seriously as data — not to accept it uncritically, but to design investigation around it rather than dismissing it before investigation.

The Sacred Is Not for Sale

“Narby reports a principle found in every shamanic tradition he studied: the…”indigenouspolicy
“Narby reports a principle found in every shamanic tradition he studied: the sacred is not for sale. The use of spiritual knowledge for personal accumulation is, by definition, black magic.”

'In shamanic traditions, it is invariably specified that spiritual knowledge is not marketable. The sacred is not for sale; the use of this knowledge for the accumulation of personal power is the definition of black magic.'

Narby is reporting a consistent finding, not editorializing. The rule is definitional to shamanism: what distinguishes the healer from the sorcerer is not the knowledge but the orientation toward it. Knowledge used for the community is healing. Knowledge used for personal power is sorcery.

The global ayahuasca economy has not been built on this principle. Retreat centers sell access to ayahuasca ceremonies. Traditional designs appear on products without benefit-sharing. Shamanic healing frameworks are marketed to Western wellness consumers.

This is not Narby's main argument — he makes it as a description of what the traditions themselves say. But the principle he reports is the most direct possible challenge to the psychedelic retreat industry's business model.

If the sacred is not for sale, then the $500-per-night ayahuasca retreat is, by the tradition's own definition, not engaged in healing. It is engaged in something the tradition calls black magic. Whether this framing should shape policy is debated. That Narby was reporting it accurately is not.

Knowledge Without Mechanism: What Narby Gets Right

“The most defensible claim in The Cosmic Serpent is the simplest: indigenous…”philosophyethnobotany
“The most defensible claim in The Cosmic Serpent is the simplest: indigenous pharmacological knowledge is reliably accurate. How it was acquired is the open question.”

The critics of The Cosmic Serpent are right that Narby's DNA-serpent-biophoton hypothesis is speculative and that he moves too readily from correlation to causation. They are wrong if they take this criticism to undermine the book's central argument.

The central argument is not about DNA. It is about epistemology: Western science has a standard of evidence that it applies inconsistently. Evidence that indigenous pharmacological knowledge is reliably accurate would, in any other domain, trigger serious investigation of how that knowledge was acquired. In this domain, it triggers dismissal of the explanation the knowledge holders provide — on the grounds that the explanation involves experiences that are epistemologically inadmissible.

The inadmissibility is a prior, not a finding. Western science has not found that ayahuasca visions cannot convey accurate pharmacological information. It has assumed they cannot, dismissed the testimonies that claim they do, without investigation.

The most defensible version of the Cosmic Serpent argument is not the DNA hypothesis but the epistemological challenge: 'We don't know how they knew' is a different statement from 'they didn't know.' The conflation of these two statements is not science. It is the refusal of a question.

The Aspirin Pill: Schultes's Most Prescient Observation

“In 1967, Schultes said the greatest enemy of ethnopharmacological research …”ethnobotanyhistory
“In 1967, Schultes said the greatest enemy of ethnopharmacological research was the aspirin pill. He was right. The pill is cheap; the knowledge is not.”

'Perhaps the greatest enemy of ethnopharmacological research is the arrival and cheap availability of the aspirin pill.'

Schultes said this at the NIMH symposium in 1967, and it has become one of the most quoted observations in ethnobotany. Its truth has not diminished.

The mechanism is simple: when aspirin becomes available in a community that previously used plant-based pain relief, the plant-based practices begin to atrophy. The motivation to maintain and transmit the knowledge diminishes when a cheaper, more reliable alternative is available. The apprenticeship is long, the knowledge is complex, and the aspirin pill is easier.

This process has been documented across the world. The young people who might have become traditional healers choose other paths because Western medicine is available and the plants require decades of study.

What is lost with each atrophied knowledge tradition is not replaceable by the archive. Schultes's herbarium specimens are dried plant matter. They preserve the plant's chemistry but not the knowledge of dose, preparation, context, contraindication, and ceremonial integration that makes the plant useful. The knowledge requires a living person who learned it from another living person in a specific ecological and cultural context.

The aspirin pill continues to arrive.

Why the Suit Mattered

“Schultes wore a suit and tie in the field for fifty years. This was not ecc…”historyculture
“Schultes wore a suit and tie in the field for fifty years. This was not eccentricity. It was a statement about how he understood his relationship with the communities he worked with.”

The image of Richard Evans Schultes in a suit and tie in the Colombian Amazon has become legendary in ethnobotany — partly because it is genuinely remarkable, partly because Wade Davis described it in One River with enough specificity that anyone who read the book will never forget it.

The suit was not about fashion. It was about how Schultes understood the ethics of his fieldwork.

The standard anthropological approach of his era was either colonial (the scientist extracts knowledge and leaves) or romantic (the scientist goes native, adopts local dress and customs). Schultes did neither. He went to communities as a scientist — with notebooks, botanical presses, and the apparatus of professional inquiry — but he also took those communities seriously as holders of systematic knowledge.

The suit communicated: I am here to do professional work. Your knowledge is professional knowledge. I am not a tourist, and I am not going to pretend to be you. I am going to be myself, and I expect you to be yourselves, and we are going to learn from each other as professional equals.

The communities Schultes worked with were not confused about what he was. He was not confused about what they were. The suit was the sartorial expression of that clarity.

How Schultes Found the Mushrooms

“Schultes identified the sacred mushrooms of Mexico in 1938. He sent specime…”historyethnobotany
“Schultes identified the sacred mushrooms of Mexico in 1938. He sent specimens to Hofmann's laboratory. Hofmann isolated psilocybin. The collaboration made Plants of the Gods possible.”

When Gordon Wasson published his Life magazine article about the Mazatec mushroom ceremony in 1957, he was not the first Westerner to have identified the sacred mushrooms. That was Schultes, who had traveled to Oaxaca in 1938 — nearly twenty years earlier — and had identified the mushrooms used in Mazatec ceremony, collected specimens, and sent them for analysis.

The 1938 identification was not widely publicized, partly because Schultes was at the time a graduate student without the institutional platform that would later give his findings wider reach.

When Wasson's 1957 article created widespread interest, Schultes had the relevant botanical documentation already in his archives. He facilitated the exchange that led to Hofmann receiving specimens and isolating psilocybin and psilocin in 1958.

The collaboration between Schultes and Hofmann that produced Plants of the Gods twenty years later was the culmination of a two-decade relationship that had started with mushroom specimens from Oaxaca. The field knowledge and the laboratory analysis had been in dialogue since 1938 — the book was the record of that dialogue.

The Urgency Is Still Real

“Schultes called the investigation urgent in 1967. Fifty-seven years later, …”ethnobotanypolicy
“Schultes called the investigation urgent in 1967. Fifty-seven years later, the urgency has not decreased.”

'In the search for new hallucinogens, we have much to do and little time in which to do it.'

Schultes said this in 1967. He was describing a race between documentation and destruction — a race he knew he was losing.

In 2026, the urgency he described has not diminished. The Amazon has lost approximately 20 percent of its forest cover since Schultes made this statement. An estimated language — the primary carrier of ethnobotanical knowledge — is lost every two weeks globally.

What has changed is the response. Mark Plotkin's Amazon Conservation Team, the ICEERS Foundation, the Society of Ethnobiology, and dozens of other organizations are working to document, protect, and transmit the knowledge that Schultes identified as endangered. The Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework (2022) includes specific provisions for indigenous-managed territories.

This is progress. It is not sufficient. The race Schultes was watching in 1967 is still being lost at the macro scale, while individual documentation and protection efforts slow it in specific places.

Plants of the Gods was published as an emergency document. It remains one.

The Riddle Schultes Couldn't Answer

“Schultes spent twelve years in the Amazon and documented the ayahuasca prep…”ethnobotanyphilosophy
“Schultes spent twelve years in the Amazon and documented the ayahuasca preparation in systematic detail. He never answered the question of how it was discovered. He didn't pretend to.”

Schultes documented the ayahuasca preparation more systematically than any previous Western researcher. He identified the botanical species, the preparation methods, the regional variations, the ritual contexts, and the pharmacological properties.

He did not explain how it was discovered.

In twelve years of fieldwork, Schultes heard the same answer Narby would hear twenty years later: we were taught by the plants. He recorded this in his field notes without elaboration. He was a botanist, not a philosopher of knowledge. The question of how indigenous peoples had identified the two specific plants in a forest of 80,000 species whose combination created an effect that neither plant alone produced was, to Schultes, an interesting question beyond his ability to answer.

He was honest about this in a way that subsequent commentators often are not. The standard 'trial and error over millennia' explanation is not one Schultes endorsed — he knew too much about the pharmacology and the search space to find it convincing. But he did not substitute a better explanation. He documented what was there and moved on.

Narby's Cosmic Serpent is, in part, the attempt to construct the explanation that Schultes declined to attempt. Whether it succeeds is debated. That the attempt was necessary — that the question Schultes declined to answer was real and important — is not.

Sources

  • Schultes & Hofmann, Plants of the Gods (1979)
  • Narby, The Cosmic Serpent (1998)

Huxley's Reducing Valve: The Verdict Is In

“Huxley proposed a mechanism in 1954. Carhart-Harris and Friston named it in…”neuroscienceconsciousness
“Huxley proposed a mechanism in 1954. Carhart-Harris and Friston named it in 2019. The gap between them was sixty-five years of neuroscience arriving at the same place.”

The claim: Huxley argued in 1954 that the brain functions primarily as a 'reducing valve,' filtering out most of what could be perceived and allowing through only what is biologically useful. Mescaline works by impairing this valve.

The evidence: The REBUS model (Relaxed Beliefs Under Psychedelics), published in Nature Reviews Neuroscience by Carhart-Harris and Friston in 2019, provides a rigorous computational account of exactly this mechanism. In predictive coding theory, the brain generates predictions about incoming sensory data and suppresses signals that match predictions. Psychedelics reduce the 'precision weighting' of these top-down predictions — allowing more bottom-up sensory information into awareness.

This is Bergson's reducing valve, translated into the vocabulary of computational neuroscience. The mechanism Huxley described intuitively maps precisely onto what fMRI studies verify: psychedelics systematically suppress the default mode network, the system most associated with self-referential filtering, increasing global brain entropy and cross-network connectivity.

A December 2025 Cell paper confirmed structural correlates: a single dose of psilocybin triggers activity-dependent rewiring of dendritic spines in the medial frontal cortex in mice, with the structural remodeling detectable weeks later. This is the neural substrate for what Huxley described phenomenologically as the opening of the valve — lasting changes in synaptic architecture from a single experience.

Verdict: Was right. The metaphor was accurate. The mechanism it described is confirmed by fMRI, by predictive coding theory, and by structural neuroimaging at single-synapse resolution.

Sources

  • Huxley, The Doors of Perception (1954)
  • Carhart-Harris & Friston, REBUS, Nature Reviews Neuroscience (2019)
  • Shao et al., Neuron (2021)

Hofmann's Sacred Drug Hypothesis: Mystical Experience as Mechanism

“Hofmann argued LSD works by providing access to mystical experience. The cl…”neurosciencetherapy
“Hofmann argued LSD works by providing access to mystical experience. The clinical literature now confirms mystical experience quality predicts therapeutic outcomes better than drug dose alone.”

The claim: Hofmann argued throughout My Problem Child that LSD's therapeutic benefit derives from its ability to produce genuine mystical experience — a direct encounter with what he called the sacred — and that the drug should be understood as a 'sacred drug' rather than merely a pharmacological agent.

The evidence: The Mystical Experience Questionnaire (MEQ30), derived from philosopher Walter Stace's phenomenological analysis, now measures mystical experience reliably in clinical trial participants. Multiple studies have found that MEQ30 score predicts therapeutic outcomes across conditions — depression, alcohol use disorder, end-of-life anxiety — better than drug dose alone.

Griffiths et al. (Johns Hopkins, 2006) established this with psilocybin in healthy volunteers. Barrett and Griffiths (2018) confirmed that complete mystical experiences (MEQ30 score above 60%) are specifically associated with sustained therapeutic benefit. The COMPASS Pathways Phase 3 trials (COMP005, June 2025; COMP006, February 2026) produced data consistent with this: 25% of participants showing clinically meaningful depression reduction maintained that response through 26 weeks — and the quality of the experience, not only the dose, is a key predictor.

Hofmann's insistence on the word 'sacred' was not religious in the denominational sense — it was a claim that the compound acts through a specific quality of consciousness, not through receptor pharmacology alone. The MEQ30 is measuring this claim. It is confirmed.

Verdict: Was right. The mechanism Hofmann proposed — therapeutic benefit through mystical experience quality — is now the primary mechanistic hypothesis in clinical psychedelic research. The word 'sacred' has been replaced by 'mystical experience score,' but the underlying claim is the same.

  • Griffiths et al., Psychopharmacology (2006)
  • Barrett & Griffiths, Pharmacol. Biochem. Behav. (2018)
  • COMPASS Pathways Phase 3 Results (2025-2026)

The Stoned Ape: What the Evidence Actually Shows

“The neuroplasticity mechanism McKenna proposed is partly confirmed. The spe…”neurosciencehistory
“The neuroplasticity mechanism McKenna proposed is partly confirmed. The specific evolutionary timeline is not. The interesting question he opened remains open.”

The claim: Psilocybin mushrooms catalyzed human cognitive evolution in East Africa. At low doses, they enhanced visual acuity (useful for hunting). At medium doses, they increased sexual arousal and group bonding. At high doses, they produced ego dissolution and expanded social and symbolic consciousness. These effects, applied to ancestral hominids, drove language, religion, and brain growth.

The neuroplasticity evidence: Shao et al. (Yale, Neuron 2021) showed that a single psilocybin dose induces rapid and persistent growth of dendritic spines in the frontal cortex of mice, with effects lasting at least a month. A 2025 Frontiers in Systems Neuroscience review confirmed psilocybin increases dendritic spine density and complexity in both the hippocampus and frontal cortex. A December 2025 Cell paper demonstrated activity-dependent rewiring of large-scale cortical networks following a single psilocybin dose.

These findings confirm that psilocybin produces lasting changes in synaptic architecture — exactly the kind of change that could, in principle, produce cognitive enhancement if applied to organisms capable of learning from altered states.

What is not confirmed: Any archaeological evidence of psilocybin use by early hominids at the relevant scale. The presence of Psilocybe cubensis in East Africa during the critical period of human cognitive evolution. The specific three-stage dose-response mechanism McKenna described. The causal chain from mushroom consumption to brain size increase.

What remains genuinely open: Whether the long-term human relationship with psychoactive plants — which is universal across known cultures — had any effect on human cognitive development. This is a real scientific question that the stoned ape hypothesis raises, even if it does not answer it.

Verdict: Remains unresolved. The neuroplasticity mechanism is real; the specific evolutionary claim is unsupported. The underlying question — what role did psychoactive plants play in human evolution? — is genuine and uninvestigated.

The Opposite of Addiction Is Connection: Verdict

“The connection model correctly identified social environment as a major dri…”pharmacologytherapy
“The connection model correctly identified social environment as a major driver of addiction. It overstated the degree to which connection overrides pharmacology.”

The claim: 'The opposite of addiction is connection.' Addiction is primarily driven by social disconnection, trauma, and lack of meaningful purpose — not by pharmacological dependence. Bruce Alexander's Rat Park experiments demonstrated this in animals; the Vietnam natural experiment demonstrated it in humans.

What is confirmed: Social environment modulates drug-seeking behavior reliably across species. The Rat Park finding — that social enrichment dramatically reduces morphine consumption — holds conceptually across subsequent enrichment paradigms, even if the specific experimental results have not been directly replicated. Lee Robins's Vietnam data remains the strongest human evidence: 95% of heroin-addicted soldiers stopped using upon returning home, without formal treatment, because their environment changed radically.

The fentanyl complication: Hari published in 2015 when overdose deaths were approximately 52,000 annually. By 2023, they had reached 107,500 — primarily fentanyl. The fentanyl crisis demonstrates a limitation of the connection model: even socially connected people die from adulterated supply. The connection model addresses addiction vulnerability; it does not address supply contamination risk.

What is overstated: The claim that connection almost completely overrides pharmacological dependence. Opioid withdrawal is a genuine physiological process. A 2020 review by Gage and Sumnall found the Rat Park effect is real but not as absolute as the original data suggested. Neurobiological evidence (Koob & Volkow) confirms that chronic drug use produces lasting receptor changes independent of social environment.

Verdict: Partially right. The connection model correctly identified social environment as a major variable — more important than purely pharmacological models had acknowledged. It overstated the degree to which environment overrides pharmacology. The most accurate model includes both.

Sources

  • Hari, Chasing the Scream (2015)
  • Gage & Sumnall, Addiction (2020)
  • Koob & Volkow, Neuropsychopharmacology (2016)

The Ergot-Eleusis Hypothesis: Status in 2026

“Forty-eight years after publication, the hypothesis has moved from speculat…”pharmacologyhistory
“Forty-eight years after publication, the hypothesis has moved from speculative to experimentally feasible and archaeologically evidenced at an affiliated cult site. The direct test at Eleusis has not yet been done.”

The claim: The kykeon drink at the heart of the Eleusinian Mysteries contained ergot alkaloids — specifically water-soluble lysergic acid derivatives from Claviceps purpurea contaminating the barley — that produced the visionary experiences initiates described.

The 2019-2020 evidence: Bioarchaeologist Jordi Juan-Tresserras's analysis of material from Mas Castellar de Pontós — an ancient Catalan site associated with the Demeter cult — found apparent ergot alkaloids in dental calculus from a woman buried at the site (third to second century BCE) and in a sealed ritual vessel with beer-making residue. This is the first physical evidence of ergot use at an Eleusinian-affiliated site.

The 2026 experimental evidence: Antonopoulos and Dadiotis (National Kapodistrian University of Athens, Scientific Reports, February 2026) demonstrated experimentally that lye — readily available in antiquity as wood ash solution — converts toxic ergotamine and ergotoxine alkaloids into water-soluble lysergic acid amide derivatives at concentrations achievable through ancient preparation methods. The specific chemical transformation that would make ergot psychoactive in the kykeon without causing ergotism has been demonstrated in the laboratory.

What remains unconfirmed: Ergot residue at the Eleusis Telesterion site itself. The 2026 Scientific Reports paper explicitly calls for chemical analysis of vessels from the Eleusis sanctuary. This analysis has not been done. Access to the site involves institutional, political, and preservation constraints.

Verdict: Gaining support. In 1978, the hypothesis was speculative. In 2026, it is experimentally feasible (the chemistry has been demonstrated) and archaeologically evidenced at an affiliated cult site. The direct confirmation at Eleusis itself — the most decisive possible test — awaits analysis that is technically possible and institutionally pending.

  • Wasson, Hofmann & Ruck, The Road to Eleusis (1978)

Set and Setting: The Clinical Evidence for Osmond's Framework

“Osmond developed the set and setting framework from clinical observation in…”therapyneuroscience
“Osmond developed the set and setting framework from clinical observation in Saskatchewan in the 1950s. A 2024 systematic review confirmed it predicts outcomes across 75 clinical trials.”

The claim: Osmond and Huxley argued through their correspondence that the same substance produces dramatically different outcomes depending on the mindset of the person taking it (set) and the physical and social context (setting). Preparation, guidance, environment, and integration are not peripheral to the pharmacology — they are constitutive of the therapeutic outcome.

The clinical evidence: A 2024 review by Borkel et al. in Expert Review of Clinical Pharmacology analyzed set and setting variables across independent samples and found they predict psychopathology, wellbeing, and meaningfulness of psychedelic experiences. A 2024 systematic review by Thal and Lommen (Clinical Psychology & Psychotherapy) synthesized 75 clinical trials of psychedelic-assisted therapy and found therapeutic alliance, preparation quality, and integration session quality were significant predictors of outcome across conditions.

The 2008 safety guidelines published by Johnson, Richards, and Griffiths at Johns Hopkins — which are now the baseline protocol for every clinical psychedelic trial — formalize exactly what Osmond and Huxley worked out empirically: therapeutic alliance must be established before dosing; monitors must be present throughout sessions; integration sessions are required; adverse event protocols must be in place. These are Osmond's clinical observations, operationalized.

A 2025 Frontiers in Psychology paper (Zamaria) examined the ongoing controversy about whether psychotherapy is necessary alongside the drug, or whether the drug does the work independently. The tentative answer: the preparation-session-integration structure significantly modulates outcomes, and separating drug and structure in a powered RCT has not been done.

Verdict: Was right. The set and setting framework, developed from clinical observation in Saskatchewan in the early 1950s, has been confirmed by 75-study systematic reviews and is now mandatory infrastructure for clinical psychedelic research.

McKenna's Machine Elves: What the Research Has Found

“McKenna's description of the machine elves has been independently corrobora…”neuroscienceconsciousness
“McKenna's description of the machine elves has been independently corroborated by thousands of users. Imaging has mapped DMT's global brain effects but has not yet isolated entity contact. What the entities are remains open.”

The claim: McKenna described 'merry elfin, self-transforming, machine creatures' encountered during high-dose DMT experiences. He argued their consistency across users suggested something was genuinely being encountered — not simply hallucination in the dismissive sense.

The consistency data: A 2020 Johns Hopkins survey (Davis et al., J. Psychopharmacol. 34(9):1008-1020) of 2,561 people who had already had a DMT entity encounter described their encounters in a 2020 Johns Hopkins survey (Davis et al., J. Psychopharmacol. 34(9)). It documents the phenomenology in detail but sets no prevalence rate, because every respondent was recruited for having had an encounter; the 97% figure often attached to it appears in no published paper. The most common entity types — small, humanoid or non-humanoid, apparently intelligent, apparently communicating — substantially match McKenna's original description. The survey found most respondents rated the encounters as among the most meaningful experiences of their lives.

The neuroscience: A 2023 Imperial College London fMRI study (Timmermann et al., PNAS 120(13)) mapped DMT's global brain effects — large increases in global functional connectivity, network disintegration and desegregation, and compression of the principal cortical gradient. It did not isolate entity contact as a distinct neural signature, and no published imaging study yet has: the phenomenology is well documented, the neural specificity is not. Entity contact is not a uniform feature of DMT; it is a specific experience with specific neural correlates.

What the neuroscience does not resolve: Whether entities are projections of the unconscious, products of the brain's pattern-recognition systems applied to an unusually rich signal, or something that requires a different explanatory framework. The consistency of the report — across cultures, decades, and thousands of independent subjects — is established. The mechanism and meaning of that consistency are not.

McKenna's epistemic position — he reported the phenomenon without claiming certainty about its ontological status — has proven to be the scientifically appropriate one. The phenomenon he described is real in the sense of being consistently reported. What it represents remains open.

Verdict: Phenomenologically confirmed, explanation unresolved. McKenna accurately reported a consistent phenomenon and correctly held open the question of what it means. The neuroscience has confirmed the phenomenon's consistency and identified its neural correlates. The explanation awaits frameworks that do not yet exist.

Narby's DNA Hypothesis: What Has Been Tested

“Narby's central claim — that shamans access molecular-level information thr…”neuroscienceethnobotany
“Narby's central claim — that shamans access molecular-level information through ayahuasca — has not been tested. His subsidiary claims about plant intelligence have been substantially validated by mainstream science.”

The central claim: Shamans access information at the molecular level — specifically DNA — through ayahuasca visions. The twin-serpent imagery universal in shamanic traditions represents the double helix. Biophoton emission from DNA may be the physical mechanism by which plant information reaches human consciousness.

What has been tested: The biophoton hypothesis — that DNA emits ultra-weak photons in the UV/visible range — is scientifically established. Whether these biophotons serve an informational function in the way Narby suggests has not been tested experimentally.

The plant intelligence subsidiary claims: Monica Gagliano's 2014 study (Oecologia) demonstrated that Mimosa pudica plants can learn to habituate to a stimulus and retain this learning for weeks. Suzanne Simard's mycorrhizal network research, widely replicated since 1997, showed trees communicate, share resources, and respond to each other's distress through underground fungal networks. Both findings vindicate Narby's 2005 argument in Intelligence in Nature that plant intelligence is a legitimate research object — at the time, a fringe claim.

The combinatorial problem: The core puzzle Narby raises — how indigenous peoples discovered the ayahuasca combination across an 80,000-species search space — remains scientifically unresolved. No proposed mechanism (trial and error, chemical ecology, sensory identification, or ayahuasca-mediated plant communication) has been established as the explanation.

Verdict: Partially supported, core mechanism untested. Narby's subsidiary arguments about plant intelligence have been substantially vindicated by mainstream research (Simard, Gagliano). His epistemological critique — that Western science dismisses indigenous pharmacological knowledge without adequate investigation — is correct. His specific DNA-biophoton-serpent hypothesis has not been experimentally tested and remains speculative.

Schultes's Urgency: Has the Race Been Lost?

“Schultes said in 1967 that ethnopharmacological research was racing against…”ethnobotanyhistory
“Schultes said in 1967 that ethnopharmacological research was racing against time. The Amazon has since lost 20% of its forest cover. The race has not been won.”

The claim: 'In the search for new hallucinogens, we have much to do and little time in which to do it.' Schultes argued in 1967 that the aspirin pill, the mission school, and the road were destroying indigenous plant knowledge traditions faster than they could be documented.

The Amazon data: The Brazilian Amazon has lost approximately 20% of its original forest cover since Schultes made this statement. An estimated language — the primary carrier of ethnobotanical knowledge — is lost every two weeks globally. Communities that maintained the psychoactive plant knowledge traditions Schultes documented have been disrupted by Western medicine, economics, religion, and legal systems at an accelerating pace.

The response: The field Schultes established has expanded dramatically since 1967. The Society of Ethnobiology, the Amazon Conservation Team (founded by his student Mark Plotkin), ICEERS, and dozens of academic programs now work on documentation and preservation. The Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework (2022) commits signatories to protect 30% of global land by 2030 with specific provisions for indigenous-managed territories.

The asymmetry: Individual documentation and protection efforts have been substantial. They have not matched the scale of loss. The communities whose knowledge Schultes documented have not been reconstituted. The plants he described are in many cases rarer or locally absent. The practitioners who held the knowledge have in many cases died without successors.

Verdict: Was right — and the urgency has increased. Schultes identified in 1967 what is now a mainstream conservation argument: that indigenous knowledge and biological diversity are inseparable, and that losing one loses the other. The race he described is still being lost at the macro scale. The institutions he inspired have slowed but not stopped the loss.

Sources

  • Schultes & Hofmann, Plants of the Gods (1979)
  • INPA Amazon Reports (2023)

Herer's Prohibition Theory: What Was Right and What Was Wrong

“The core argument — that cannabis scheduling was scientifically unjustified…”historypolicy
“The core argument — that cannabis scheduling was scientifically unjustified and served specific corporate interests — has been confirmed. The specific DuPont orchestration thesis exceeds what the documents prove.”

The core claim: Cannabis's Schedule I classification was not based on scientific evidence of harm. It was driven by corporate interests (DuPont's synthetic fibers, Hearst's timber paper), racial targeting, and political expediency. The medical evidence supported cannabis's therapeutic applications, which were systematically suppressed.

What has been confirmed: The WHO Expert Committee on Drug Dependence conducted a Critical Review of cannabis in 2019 and recommended reclassification, finding that the current scheduling is not justified by the pharmacological evidence. The DOJ's proposed rescheduling (May 2024) from Schedule I to Schedule III represents the federal government's own acknowledgment that the 'no accepted medical use' criterion is no longer supported.

The ACLU's 2020 enforcement data confirmed racial targeting: Black Americans are 3.73 times more likely to be arrested for marijuana possession despite similar use rates. Ehrlichman's 2016 Harper's admission confirmed that the Nixon drug war was explicitly designed to target Black communities and anti-war protesters. The racial targeting argument Herer made in 1985 is now documented at the highest level.

What was overstated: The specific DuPont conspiracy thesis — that DuPont orchestrated the Marihuana Tax Act to eliminate hemp as a competitor to nylon — exceeds what the available documents can establish. The corporate interests existed; whether DuPont specifically orchestrated the legislation, as opposed to benefiting from it, is not conclusively proven. Historians including Campos have shown that racial panic and moral reform movements were independently sufficient to produce the legislation.

Verdict: Substantially vindicated, some overreach. The core claims — scientifically unjustified scheduling, corporate benefit, racial targeting — have been confirmed. The specific conspiracy framing of DuPont-as-orchestrator goes beyond what the evidence establishes.

Sources

  • Herer, The Emperor Wears No Clothes (1985)
  • WHO ECDD Critical Review Cannabis (2019)
  • DOJ NPRM Cannabis Rescheduling (May 2024)
  • ACLU, A Tale of Two Countries (2020)

Stevens's Thesis: Was the 1968 Prohibition Evidence-Based?

“Stevens argued the 1968 scheduling was politically driven, not evidence-dri…”historypolicy
“Stevens argued the 1968 scheduling was politically driven, not evidence-driven. The WHO Critical Review, the FDA Breakthrough Therapy designations, and the Phase 3 clinical results have all confirmed this.”

The claim: The 1968 Staggers-Dodd Act and the 1970 Controlled Substances Act's Schedule I classification of LSD ended a clinical research program that had produced genuine evidence of therapeutic efficacy — not because the evidence was wrong but because the political and institutional conditions had become untenable. The scheduling was political, not scientific.

The evidence that the scheduling was not scientific: The WHO Expert Committee on Drug Dependence conducted a Critical Review of LSD in 2019 and found no evidence supporting the substance's current international scheduling level. The FDA's Breakthrough Therapy Designation for psilocybin (2018) — a compound with nearly identical pharmacological mechanism to LSD — effectively acknowledged that classical psychedelics may have accepted medical use, contradicting the Schedule I criterion.

The resumption confirms what was interrupted: The COMPASS Pathways Phase 3 trials (2025-2026) produced statistically significant results for psilocybin in treatment-resistant depression. A 2012 meta-analysis by Krebs and Johansen of six randomized controlled trials of LSD for alcoholism from the 1960s-70s found a statistically significant positive effect on drinking behavior. The clinical evidence that existed in 1968 was real.

The LSD safety data: The 2016 Global Drug Survey found LSD had the lowest emergency medical treatment rate of any substance surveyed. Zero overdose deaths from LSD toxicity have been documented in eighty years of use. The pharmacological evidence for Schedule I's 'high abuse potential, no accepted medical use' designation was absent in 1968 and remains absent.

Verdict: Was right. The 1968 scheduling was not driven by evidence of harm or lack of efficacy. It was driven by the political association of LSD with the counterculture, by Ehrlichman's explicitly racially targeted drug war strategy, and by the institutional desire to control what could not be controlled. The clinical research that resumed fifty years later is confirming what was interrupted.

Sources

  • Stevens, Storming Heaven (1987)
  • WHO ECDD Critical Review LSD (2019)
  • COMPASS Pathways Phase 3 (2025-2026)
  • Krebs & Johansen, J. Psychopharmacol. (2012)

Passage: The Bicycle Ride

“I had the impression of being unable to move from the spot, although my ass…”historypharmacology
“I had the impression of being unable to move from the spot, although my assistant told me later that we had cycled at a good pace.”

The passage: 'On the way home, my condition began to assume threatening forms. Everything in my field of vision wavered and was distorted as if seen in a curved mirror. I also had the sensation of being unable to move from the spot, although my assistant told me later that we had cycled at a good pace.'

Why this passage: It is the founding document of modern psychedelic pharmacology, and its most important feature is the contrast between subjective and objective experience that Hofmann captures in a single sentence.

Hofmann had the impression of standing still. His assistant confirmed they had been moving at a good pace. The subjective experience of temporal distortion — which was overwhelming and convincing from the inside — was simply false as a report about the external world. He was moving; he felt motionless.

This contrast became one of the most clinically important observations in the history of LSD research. It established that the subjective experience of LSD is not merely a distortion of external reality but a reorganization of the brain's processing of temporal and spatial information. The brain, under LSD, is doing something different — not reporting external reality incorrectly by accident, but processing the same external reality through a different filter.

The 2017 crystal structure of LSD bound to the 5-HT2A receptor (Wacker et al., Cell) explains why the experience lasted so long and was so disorienting: LSD's molecular shape fits the receptor so precisely that a protein lid traps it inside for hours. The 'good pace' that Hofmann could not perceive was being generated by the same body whose sensory experience had been completely reorganized.

Sources

  • Hofmann, LSD: My Problem Child (1979)

Passage: Television as Dominator Drug

“Television is by nature the dominator drug par excellence. Control of conte…”culturephilosophy
“Television is by nature the dominator drug par excellence. Control of content, uniformity of content, repeatability of content make it inevitably a tool of coercion.”

The passage: 'Television is by nature the dominator drug par excellence. Control of content, uniformity of content, repeatability of content make it inevitably a tool of coercion, brainwashing, and manipulation. Television induces a trance state in the observer that is analagous to hypnosis. Preferences and values are subtly imposed... it saps individual autonomy, creates passivity, and makes for spectator culture.'

Why this passage: Written in 1992, three years before the World Wide Web became publicly available and twenty years before the algorithmic social media feed, it anticipates with remarkable precision the mechanism of what would become the attention economy.

McKenna's specific claims: control of content (editorial gatekeeping), uniformity (same programming for mass audiences), repeatability (content that can be replicated identically). These are the mild version of what followed. The algorithmic feed does not merely control content — it individually optimizes content for each viewer's psychological vulnerabilities. It is not uniform — it is precisely nonuniform, serving each person what will maximize their engagement. And it is not merely repeatable — it is infinite, without the natural endpoint of a television schedule.

Sean Parker, founding president of Facebook, confirmed in 2017 that the platform was deliberately designed to exploit psychological vulnerabilities: 'How do we consume as much of your time and conscious attention as possible?' This is the dominator drug thesis stated explicitly by one of its engineers.

McKenna was writing about NBC. The technology he was warning about had not yet been invented. Every sentence has become more accurate.

Sources

  • McKenna, Food of the Gods (1992)

Passage: Billie Holiday on Addiction

“Imagine if the government chased sick people with diabetes, put a tax on in…”historypolicy
“Imagine if the government chased sick people with diabetes, put a tax on insulin and drove it into the black market, told doctors they couldn't treat them — then sent them to jail.”

The passage: 'Imagine if the government chased sick people with diabetes, put a tax on insulin and drove it into the black market, told doctors they couldn't treat them — then sent them to jail. If we did that, everyone would know we were crazy. Yet we do practically the same thing every day in the week to sick people hooked on drugs.'

Why this passage: Holiday wrote this in 1956, the same year Osmond was introducing the word 'psychedelic' to the scientific literature. She was not a pharmacologist or a policy analyst. She was a woman who had been directly targeted by Harry Anslinger's Federal Bureau of Narcotics, who had had her New York cabaret license revoked and been denied the ability to work in the city where her career was centered, who had been arrested, imprisoned, and under federal surveillance for years.

From inside this experience, she produced one of the clearest arguments in the addiction policy literature: the analogy between insulin-dependent diabetes and heroin addiction. Both involve a body that has become physiologically dependent on a compound. The moral framework applied to each is completely different.

The analogy is not perfect — diabetes is not caused by voluntary behavior in the way heroin dependence begins, and the social determinants of the two conditions differ significantly. But as a description of how the same pharmacological process — dependency — is treated differently depending on who has it and what they're dependent on, it is precise and devastating.

Holiday understood in 1956 what the policy literature would not fully acknowledge for another sixty years: the drug war's target was not the drug. Hari quotes this passage because it says in one paragraph what his book takes three hundred pages to establish.

Sources

  • Hari, Chasing the Scream (2015)
  • Holiday, Lady Sings the Blues (1956)
Passage SpotlightMoksha: Letters of Huxley & Osmond247 words2 source entriesstatus: published

Passage: The Naming Couplets

“To fathom Hell or soar angelic, / just take a pinch of psychedelic. — Osmon…”historyphilosophy
“To fathom Hell or soar angelic, / just take a pinch of psychedelic. — Osmond wins.”

The exchange: In 1956, Osmond and Huxley were corresponding about what to call these substances. Both submitted rhyming couplets as proposals.

Huxley: 'To make this trivial world sublime, / take half a gram of phanerothyme.' Osmond: 'To fathom Hell or soar angelic, / just take a pinch of psychedelic.'

Osmond's won. He introduced 'psychedelic' formally in a 1957 paper in the Annals of the New York Academy of Sciences.

Why this passage: Because the choice between the two words was the choice between two philosophical positions, and the winning position shaped everything that followed.

Huxley's phanerothyme ('making the spirit manifest') located the substance's action in a spiritual register: what becomes visible is the spirit, the divine capacity of the human person. The word assumes an anthropology in which spirit exists and is ordinarily hidden.

Osmond's psychedelic ('mind-manifesting') located the action in a psychological register: what becomes manifest is the mind itself. The word does not assume a spirit. It assumes a mind that contains more than ordinary consciousness reveals.

Osmond's couplet also contains the bipolar truth Huxley's doesn't: 'fathom Hell or soar angelic.' The choice of words acknowledged the negative possibility — that what the mind contains includes Hell, not only the divine — in a way that Huxley's 'trivial world sublime' did not. This acknowledgment would prove clinically crucial: set and setting matter precisely because the experience can go in either direction.

The word that won was slightly less philosophically precise but slightly more pharmacologically honest.

Sources

  • Huxley & Osmond, in Moksha (1977)
  • Osmond, Ann. N.Y. Acad. Sci. (1957)

Passage: The First Description of Machine Elves

“Merry elfin, self-transforming, machine creatures — looking like self-dribb…”consciousnessphilosophy
“Merry elfin, self-transforming, machine creatures — looking like self-dribbling Fabergé eggs on the rebound, they had surrounded me and tried to teach me the lost language of true poetry.”

The passage: 'During my own experiences smoking synthesized DMT in Berkeley, I had had the impression of bursting into a space inhabited by merry elfin, self-transforming, machine creatures. Dozens of these friendly fractal entities, looking like self-dribbling Fabergé eggs on the rebound, had surrounded me and tried to teach me the lost language of true poetry.'

Why this passage: It is the founding phenomenological document of the entity contact literature. McKenna wrote this description approximately twenty years after the original experiences (the DMT experiments in Berkeley began in the mid-1960s). It entered wide cultural circulation with the publication of True Hallucinations in 1993.

The description's vocabulary is notable: merry, elfin, self-transforming, machine, fractal, friendly. Each term carries specific information. Merry and friendly establish the emotional tone of most — though not all — entity encounters. Elfin and fractal attempt to capture the appearance. Self-transforming is the quality most consistently reported across independent accounts: the entities are in constant motion, changing form continuously. Machine suggests mechanical intelligence rather than biological organic life.

The 'lost language of true poetry' — the entities attempting communication through visible language, through objects made of meaning rather than words — is the feature McKenna returned to most obsessively. He believed the entities were demonstrating a mode of communication that preceded and exceeded verbal language.

A 2019 Johns Hopkins survey of 2,561 DMT users found this description substantially corroborated by people who had not encountered it before their experiences. The specific vocabulary varies; the underlying phenomenology does not. Self-transforming entities that seem to be communicating something are the most reported feature of high-dose DMT. McKenna described it first and best.

Sources

  • McKenna, True Hallucinations (1993)
  • Sexton et al., J. Psychopharmacol. 33(9) (2019)
Passage SpotlightThe Cosmic Serpent263 words1 source entrystatus: published

Passage: The Plants Told Us

“The first time an Ashaninca man told me that he had learned the medicinal p…”indigenousphilosophy
“The first time an Ashaninca man told me that he had learned the medicinal properties of plants by drinking a hallucinogenic brew, I thought he was joking. But he was not smiling.”

The passage: 'The first time an Ashaninca man told me that he had learned the medicinal properties of plants by drinking a hallucinogenic brew, I thought he was joking. But he was not smiling.'

Why this passage: It is one of the most important sentences in the ethnobotanical literature, because it marks the moment when an epistemological collision between two knowledge systems becomes visible.

Narby is a Stanford-trained anthropologist. He has been trained to identify what cultural informants mean versus what they say — to find the rational empirical process that underlies mythological explanation. When an Ashaninca man says 'we learned from the plants,' the standard interpretive move is to understand this as: 'we learned from careful observation of plant effects over many generations, and we have encoded this knowledge in a narrative framework that attributes it to the plants themselves.'

But the man is not using a mythological framework. He is making a literal claim. And Narby, precisely because he is trained to hear the difference, notices: this is the literal claim.

The passage is important because it marks the beginning of a decade of investigation that The Cosmic Serpent documents. Narby does not accept the claim uncritically. He also cannot, after years of fieldwork, dismiss it as metaphor. The combinatorial pharmacology of ayahuasca — the identification of two specific plants from 80,000 candidates whose combination creates oral DMT activity — is not adequately explained by 'careful observation over many generations.'

The man was not joking. He was reporting what he knew. The question the book investigates is what his knowledge means.

Sources

  • Narby, The Cosmic Serpent (1998)
Passage SpotlightPlants of the Gods264 words2 source entriesstatus: published

Passage: The Aspirin Pill Warning

“Perhaps the greatest enemy of ethnopharmacological research is the arrival …”ethnobotanyhistory
“Perhaps the greatest enemy of ethnopharmacological research is the arrival and cheap availability of the aspirin pill.”

The passage: 'Perhaps the greatest enemy of ethnopharmacological research is the arrival and cheap availability of the aspirin pill.'

Why this passage: Schultes delivered this line at the NIMH symposium in San Francisco in 1967 — the same year as the Summer of Love, the same year Leary's public advocacy was peaking, the same year the counterculture was beginning to engage with the plant knowledge that Schultes had spent two decades documenting.

He was not talking about aspirin's pharmacology. He was talking about the economics of knowledge transmission. The mechanism is simple: when a cheap, reliable Western pharmaceutical becomes available in a community that has used plant-based medicine for generations, the motivation to maintain and transmit the traditional knowledge declines. The apprenticeship to learn the knowledge is long. The aspirin pill is short, cheap, and available at the nearest shop.

The aspirin pill is a stand-in for the entire Western pharmacopeia — for the economic and cultural conditions of modernity that make traditional knowledge less necessary at exactly the moment when Western science has the tools to verify its accuracy and the urgency to preserve it before it disappears.

Schultes was describing an irreversible process. Once a knowledge tradition is disrupted — once the practitioner dies without transmitting what they know — what is lost cannot be recovered from herbarium specimens. The chemistry of the plant survives. The knowledge of how to use it does not.

This sentence was the distilled anxiety of twelve years in the Amazon, watching the world Schultes had documented being replaced, too quickly, by a world he had not.

Sources

  • Schultes, NIMH Symposium (1967)
  • Schultes & Hofmann, Plants of the Gods (1979)

Passage: The Day the Research Stopped

“The research stopped. Over a thousand scientific papers, forty thousand pat…”historypolicy
“The research stopped. Over a thousand scientific papers, forty thousand patients, fifteen years of accumulated clinical practice — stopped.”

The moment: October 6, 1968. The Staggers-Dodd bill signed into law, making LSD possession a federal misdemeanor. The Controlled Substances Act of 1970 completing the classification: Schedule I.

Stevens writes the ending of the research with documentary precision and without editorializing. The numbers speak: over a thousand published scientific papers. More than forty thousand patients who had received LSD-assisted therapy. Fifteen years of refinement — better protocols, better patient selection, better understanding of what the drug was doing and in what conditions it was most useful.

All of it stopped.

Why this passage matters: Not because of what it says about 1968 but because of what it says about how institutions end promising research. The research did not stop because it failed. The evidence from the Hoffer-Osmond alcoholism trials, from Grof's work at the Maryland Psychiatric Research Center, from the end-of-life anxiety studies — all of it pointed toward genuine therapeutic application.

The research stopped because the political costs of continuing exceeded the institutional capacity to absorb them. Leary had made LSD a symbol of anti-establishment rebellion. The Nixon administration had made the counterculture an explicit enemy. The clinical researchers — who had never endorsed recreational use, who had spent fifteen years building careful protocols — could not separate their work from its appropriation.

The Storming Heaven's deepest lesson is institutional: scientific evidence is not sufficient to protect research from political suppression. What protects research is institutional durability — the kind that the current psychedelic renaissance is explicitly trying to build, having read the history.

Sources

  • Stevens, Storming Heaven (1987)
  • Cambridge HPS Medical History dissertation (2007)

Passage: Hemp for Victory, 1942

“'Hemp for Victory' was the title of a 1942 USDA film urging farmers to grow…”historypolicy
“'Hemp for Victory' was the title of a 1942 USDA film urging farmers to grow cannabis hemp as a patriotic duty. The same government denied the film's existence in the 1980s.”

The film: Hemp for Victory, produced by the USDA in 1942, thirteen minutes long, distributed to American farmers across the Midwest. Its message: grow cannabis hemp for the war effort. The Philippines had fallen to Japan, cutting off the supply of Manila hemp critical for military rope, rigging, and parachute webbing. The government needed domestic production. It distributed 400,000 pounds of cannabis seed to farmers and made a film encouraging them to grow the plant.

The denial: When Herer began citing the film in Emperor, the USDA denied it had ever been made. Library of Congress records did not list it. Archivists told researchers there was no such film.

The recovery: Maria Farrow and Carl Packard searched the Library of Congress holdings and found it in 1989. Herer announced the discovery. The Library of Congress subsequently acknowledged the film's existence.

Why this passage matters: The Hemp for Victory sequence is Huxley's most compressed argument. It is not a conspiracy theory — it is a documentary record. The US government produced a film urging patriotic cannabis hemp cultivation in 1942. Four years earlier, the same government had passed legislation eliminating the same crop on the grounds that it was a dangerous narcotic. After the war, the same government returned to prohibition.

The contradiction is on film. The film is in the Library of Congress. The government denied the film existed. Then acknowledged it.

Herer assembled documents, and the documents made the argument. This sequence — the film's existence, the government's denial, the discovery, the acknowledgment — is the structure of the book in miniature.

Sources

  • Herer, The Emperor Wears No Clothes (1985)
  • Wikipedia, Hemp for Victory

The Biophoton Question: What DNA Actually Emits

“DNA emits ultra-weak photons in the UV and visible range. This is establish…”neurosciencepharmacology
“DNA emits ultra-weak photons in the UV and visible range. This is established biophysics. Whether these biophotons serve an informational function in the way Narby proposes is untested.”

Every living cell emits ultra-weak photons — light in the UV and visible range produced as a byproduct of metabolic processes. The phenomenon was first systematically documented by Fritz-Albert Popp in the 1970s and confirmed repeatedly since. Biophoton emission from DNA is established biophysics.

Jeremy Narby built his central hypothesis on this foundation: if DNA emits biophotons, and if the brain under ayahuasca becomes unusually sensitive to internal signals, the visionary content of the DMT state might represent perception of biophoton emission from DNA at the cellular level. The luminous, serpentine imagery consistent across shamanic traditions would be, in this account, the visual signature of DNA itself.

The hypothesis is specific enough to be tested and has not been. Cifra and Pospíšil's 2014 review in the Journal of Photochemistry and Photobiology B systematically examined biophoton research and found no evidence that biophoton emission serves a communication function in the way Narby proposes. The photons are real; their informational role is not established.

What Narby's hypothesis correctly identifies is that the brain is not a closed system — it is bathed in internally generated photons as well as receiving signals from outside. Whether this creates any pathway between cellular molecular processes and conscious experience is the genuine open question his work raises. The answer is not known. The question is legitimate.

Sources

  • Popp et al., J. Photochem. Photobiol. (1992)
  • Narby, The Cosmic Serpent (1998)
  • Cifra & Pospíšil, J. Photochem. Photobiol. B (2014)
