The Wood Wide Web: What Simard's Research Actually Shows

“Simard showed that trees share carbon through mycorrhizal networks, prefere…”neuroscienceculture
“Simard showed that trees share carbon through mycorrhizal networks, preferentially supporting kin. This is not metaphor. It is documented carbon transfer. The question is what it means for how we understand intelligence.”

Suzanne Simard's 1997 Nature paper is the most cited paper in plant communication research. It showed that Douglas fir and paper birch trees growing together exchange carbon through mycorrhizal fungal networks — the fir sending carbon to the birch in summer when the birch is shaded, the birch returning carbon to the fir in autumn. The exchange is bidirectional, responsive to seasonal conditions, and follows kin recognition patterns: mother trees preferentially allocate carbon to their own seedlings through the network.

This finding is empirically robust and has been replicated in multiple forest systems. What it means conceptually is more contested. Simard uses the language of communication and intelligence; critics argue the word 'communication' implies intentionality that the mechanism doesn't support — the carbon transfer is a consequence of mycorrhizal fungal behavior, not necessarily coordinated by the trees themselves.

A 2023 review by Karst et al. in New Phytologist engaged this debate directly, arguing that the 'wood wide web' framing has outpaced the evidence — that many popular accounts of inter-tree communication describe a degree of coordination and intentionality that the underlying mechanism doesn't require.

For Narby's argument, the Simard finding matters as one of several empirical pillars supporting the claim that plant intelligence is a legitimate research object. Whether the specific mechanism is 'communication' in a strong sense matters less than the fact that plants are embedded in information-exchanging systems that Western science had previously overlooked entirely.

Sources

  • Simard et al., Nature (1997)
  • Simard, Finding the Mother Tree (2021)
  • Karst et al., New Phytologist (2023)
Deep DiveThe Cosmic Serpent531 words4 source entriesstatus: published

Two Epistemologies in the Same Forest: Science and Shamanism as Knowledge Systems

“The question is not whether ayahuasca visions are 'real.' The question is w…”philosophyethnobotany
“The question is not whether ayahuasca visions are 'real.' The question is what epistemological framework is adequate to the evidence of what indigenous pharmacological knowledge has achieved.”

Jeremy Narby's central epistemological move in The Cosmic Serpent is modest but consequential: he distinguishes between 'we don't know how' and 'it didn't happen.' Western science has consistently conflated these two statements when evaluating indigenous pharmacological claims. The conflation is not a finding — it is a prior.

The distinction matters because the evidence demands it. Indigenous Amazonian pharmacological knowledge is reliably accurate. The compounds isolated from the plants Schultes and others documented have produced working pharmaceuticals — curare as a surgical muscle relaxant, quinine as antimalarial, dozens of compounds still in clinical trials. The knowledge works. Western science has not produced an adequate explanation of how it was acquired.

The standard explanation — systematic trial and error over millennia — is less satisfying the more closely you examine it. The ayahuasca case is the sharpest challenge. In a forest containing approximately 80,000 plant species, indigenous peoples across multiple unconnected cultures identified the same two specific plants whose combination creates oral DMT activity. Neither plant alone produces the sustained visionary state. The pharmacological interaction — MAO inhibition enabling DMT oral bioavailability — requires knowledge of both plants simultaneously. The search space for this combination by random trial and error is forbidding.

Narby's response is not to claim that shamans access DNA through biophoton perception — though he proposes this as a hypothesis. His response is prior to the hypothesis: the indigenous explanation (the plants told us) deserves investigation as data, not dismissal as superstition. This is a methodological claim, not a metaphysical one.

Philosopher of science Paul Feyerabend made a structurally similar argument in Against Method (1975): that the demarcation between science and non-science is not epistemologically principled, and that alternatives to the dominant method have historically produced genuine knowledge. Helen Longino in Science as Social Knowledge (1990) showed that scientific knowledge is always produced within social contexts that shape which questions get asked and which evidence is considered admissible.

Applied to Narby's argument: Western science has operated with a prior that excludes visionary states as a source of accurate information about the physical world. This prior is not based on empirical investigation of the claim — it is based on a theory of mind that says conscious experience cannot be a reliable guide to molecular reality. That theory of mind is not established by evidence; it is a commitment.

The plant intelligence research of the last thirty years has chipped at this commitment from a different angle. If plants can learn (Gagliano 2014), if mycorrhizal networks transfer resources in ways that follow kin recognition (Simard 1997), if forests are embedded in chemical communication systems that respond to damage, stress, and seasonal change — then the assumption that plants are passive objects without any form of information processing has been empirically undermined.

Narby's book is most valuable not as a specific hypothesis about DNA and biophotons but as a sustained argument for intellectual humility about the epistemological status of indigenous knowledge. The argument is: a knowledge system that reliably produces accurate pharmacological results deserves investigation of its methods, not dismissal of its framework. This argument is now mainstream in ethnobotany, anthropology, and philosophy of biology. The specific biophoton hypothesis remains untested.

Sources

  • Narby, The Cosmic Serpent (1998)
  • Longino, Science as Social Knowledge (1990)
  • Feyerabend, Against Method (1975)
  • Gagliano et al., Oecologia (2014)

After Nagoya: What Benefit-Sharing Actually Requires

“The Nagoya Protocol exists. 138 countries have ratified it. Its enforcement…”policyindigenous
“The Nagoya Protocol exists. 138 countries have ratified it. Its enforcement is weak, its scope excludes prior exploitation, and the communities it's designed to protect remain largely unaware of its provisions.”

The Nagoya Protocol on Access and Benefit-Sharing entered into force in October 2014 after four years of negotiation under the Convention on Biological Diversity. As of 2026, 138 countries have ratified it. Its core obligation: companies and researchers who access genetic resources or traditional knowledge associated with genetic resources from signatory countries must share benefits with the provider country and, where applicable, the indigenous communities of origin.

The Protocol is the international legal implementation of the argument Narby makes in The Cosmic Serpent: that indigenous communities have a legitimate claim to benefit from commercial exploitation of knowledge they developed and stewarded.

The gap between the Protocol and its implementation is large. A 2018 review by Wynberg and Laird in Ambio examined Nagoya's first four years and found: most provider countries lacked the domestic legislation to implement its provisions; most companies remained unaware of or non-compliant with their obligations; indigenous communities in most signatory countries had received no benefit-sharing payments under the Protocol despite continued commercial exploitation of traditional knowledge.

The Protocol explicitly does not apply retroactively — it covers access and exploitation that occurs after its entry into force. This means that the decades of ethnobotanical exploitation that produced current pharmaceutical products, including the ayahuasca-derived compounds in clinical development, are outside its scope. Historical exploitation is not addressed.

For the psychedelic industry specifically: the compounds in clinical development (psilocybin, ibogaine, DMT-based ayahuasca) are all derived from or structurally related to compounds used by indigenous communities for millennia. The Nagoya Protocol's benefit-sharing requirements apply to new commercial development of these compounds where traditional knowledge is accessed. Enforcement of these requirements in practice has been minimal.

Narby's argument — that the sacred cannot be sold without cost to the communities that stewarded it — has partial legal expression in the Nagoya Protocol. The distance between the legal expression and the practical reality is the ongoing policy failure that the Protocol was designed to address.

Sources

  • Nagoya Protocol on ABS (2010, in force 2014)
  • Wynberg & Laird, Ambio (2018)
  • UNCTAD, Access and Benefit Sharing in Practice (2023)

The Emperor's New Industry: Cannabis at $40 Billion

“The legal cannabis industry is worth $40 billion. The communities most harm…”policyhistory
“The legal cannabis industry is worth $40 billion. The communities most harmed by prohibition have received a small fraction of its benefit. Herer's vision — distributed hemp economies empowering small farmers — has not materialized.”

Jack Herer published The Emperor Wears No Clothes in 1985 with a specific political economy in mind. Cannabis legalization would distribute economic power to small farmers, local processors, and community businesses. Industrial hemp would replace petrochemical products, paper pulp, and synthetic fibers. The decriminalization of cannabis would restore dignity and economic opportunity to communities destroyed by a century of racially targeted prohibition.

The legal cannabis industry that actually emerged is measurable. By 2025, the combined US legal cannabis market — medical and recreational — was valued at approximately $40 billion annually. Employment in the legal cannabis industry exceeded 400,000 full-time equivalent positions. Tax revenue from cannabis sales across legal states exceeded $15 billion cumulatively since 2014.

These are large numbers. They do not describe Herer's political economy.

Consolidation has proceeded rapidly in every state that has legalized recreational cannabis. The initial wave of small operators — often the activists and advocates who drove legalization — has been largely displaced by multi-state operators (MSOs) with access to capital markets, real estate, and regulatory expertise. California's cannabis market, the largest in the US, consolidated so aggressively that by 2024 most small dispensaries were operating at a loss or had closed. The craft cannabis sector, analogous to craft brewing, exists in some markets but at a small fraction of industry revenue.

Equity provisions in legal cannabis markets have been systematically underfunded. Illinois passed one of the most ambitious social equity frameworks, allocating a percentage of cannabis tax revenue to communities disproportionately impacted by prohibition. By 2024, the program had distributed a fraction of its intended funding due to administrative bottlenecks and legal challenges from non-equity operators.

The racial equity gap has not closed. The ACLU's 2023 analysis found that Black Americans continued to be arrested for marijuana possession in legal states at higher rates than white Americans despite equivalent use rates — the disproportion narrowed but did not disappear. The communities most targeted by the drug war have not received proportionate economic benefit from legalization.

The hemp market, which Herer identified as the most important industrial opportunity, has developed in a different direction from his vision. The 2019-2020 CBD extraction bubble overproduced massively, crashed prices, and eliminated most small hemp farmers. By 2024, the hemp market had restabilized around larger operators with processing infrastructure. Hempcrete is a real product used in some construction projects. Hemp textiles are a small but growing market. Hemp biofuel has not scaled.

The honest assessment: Herer was right that cannabis prohibition was unjust, that the scheduling was scientifically unjustified, and that industrial hemp had commercial potential. He was wrong that legalization, when it came, would empower the communities and create the distributed economic model he envisioned. The industry that emerged is substantially corporate, substantially concentrated, and substantially failing to deliver the social equity that provided the political momentum for legalization in the first place.

Sources

  • MJBizDaily State of the Cannabis Industry (2025)
  • ACLU, Cannabis Legalization and Social Equity (2023)
  • Herer, The Emperor Wears No Clothes (1985)
  • Brightfield Group, Hemp Market Report (2024)

Island and Its Limits: Huxley's Utopia Evaluated

“Island is Huxley's answer to Brave New World: the same pharmacological tool…”culturephilosophy
“Island is Huxley's answer to Brave New World: the same pharmacological tools used for liberation rather than control. The novel's failure as fiction is part of its value as argument.”

Aldous Huxley published Island in 1962, his final novel, eleven months before his death. It is widely considered his weakest novel and his most important philosophical document. The two judgments are related.

Pala, the island of the title, is a small nation that has integrated Eastern contemplative practice with Western science and Tantric sexuality into a genuinely functional society. The moksha-medicine — a psilocybin-like substance derived from a local mushroom — is used by Palanese at key life transitions: adolescence, serious illness, death. The drug is not recreational. It is sacramental in precisely the sense Huxley meant by 'gratuitous grace': a tool for opening the reducing valve at moments when the reduction is most costly.

The novel fails as fiction because Huxley cannot sustain the dramatic tension required. Pala is too good; the protagonist's cynicism converts too readily; the ending — Indonesian invasion destroys the utopia just as the protagonist achieves enlightenment — arrives as an imported tragedy rather than one grown from the novel's own logic.

But Island is doing something different from what novels usually do. It is a worked example: if you actually designed a society around the principles Huxley developed in The Perennial Philosophy (1945) and The Doors of Perception (1954), what would it look like? How would childhood education work? How would dying work? What would the relationship between science and contemplative practice look like? How would the sacramental use of consciousness-expanding substances be integrated into ordinary life?

These questions are not answered by The Doors of Perception, which describes an experience, not a social structure. Island is the social structure. Its failure as a novel is the price of its success as a thought experiment — characters who exist to demonstrate social arrangements cannot also be psychologically complex in the way that dramatic fiction requires.

The correspondence in Moksha contains Huxley's own uncertainty about whether Island was achieving what he wanted. He writes to Osmond about the difficulty of dramatizing states of consciousness that are, by definition, not reducible to the dramatic. The letters around Island's composition are more philosophically interesting than most of the novel.

Sources

  • Huxley, Island (1962)
  • Huxley & Osmond, in Moksha (1977)
  • Horgan, Rational Mysticism (2003)

The Sandoz Years: How a Pharmaceutical Company Handled a Sacred Drug

“Sandoz distributed LSD to researchers worldwide at minimal cost from 1947 t…”historypharmacology
“Sandoz distributed LSD to researchers worldwide at minimal cost from 1947 to 1966. This was pharmaceutical generosity without precedent. What it meant about Sandoz's understanding of what it had synthesized is worth examining.”

In 1947, Sandoz Laboratories released LSD under the trade name Delysid — a 25-microgram tablet and 0.1% solution for injection — as a tool for psychiatric research. The pricing was minimal: Sandoz supplied Delysid to qualified researchers at essentially no cost, treating it as a contribution to science rather than a commercial product.

This decision shaped everything that followed. Because LSD was freely available to researchers, the 1947-1966 period produced over 1,000 scientific papers, treated approximately 40,000 patients in clinical programs, and established a research base that — despite the 1968 scheduling — could not be fully erased. The knowledge existed in published form.

Hofmann's memoir reveals his ambivalence about this period. He was proud of LSD's research applications and troubled by its counterculture appropriation. He understood that Sandoz's generous distribution had enabled both.

In 1963, under pressure from the US Food and Drug Administration, Sandoz began restricting distribution — requiring institutional affiliation and research protocols. In 1966, facing the US Congressional hearings on LSD and the wave of negative publicity driven by Leary's public advocacy, Sandoz withdrew Delysid from the market entirely and ceased distribution.

The withdrawal ended the clinical research program. It also ended the period in which a pharmaceutical company had voluntarily restrained commercial impulses in the belief that a substance required special handling. Hofmann consistently praised this restraint. He argued that LSD needed to be treated as a sacred drug — carefully, with appropriate protocols, without commercialization — and that Sandoz had, for nearly twenty years, honored this requirement.

The contrast with the current psychedelic industry is stark. COMPASS Pathways, MindMed, Cybin, and dozens of other companies have built commercial pipelines around psychedelic compounds. The Sandoz model — provide it freely, don't commercialize it, restrict access to qualified researchers — has no analog in the 2020s landscape. Whether this represents necessary adaptation to regulatory reality or a failure of the field's founding values is a question Hofmann's memoir raises implicitly throughout.

Sources

  • Hofmann, LSD: My Problem Child (1979)
  • Lee & Shlain, Acid Dreams (1985)
  • Stevens, Storming Heaven (1987)

The Australian Model: What Happens When a Country Actually Approves

“Australia approved psilocybin for treatment-resistant depression and MDMA f…”policytherapy
“Australia approved psilocybin for treatment-resistant depression and MDMA for PTSD in February 2023. It is the only country to have done so. The implementation has revealed problems the approval process did not anticipate.”

On February 3, 2023, the Australian Therapeutic Goods Administration (TGA) amended the Poisons Standard to allow authorized psychiatrists to prescribe MDMA for post-traumatic stress disorder and psilocybin for treatment-resistant depression. Australia became the first country in the world to approve psychedelic-assisted therapy as standard of care rather than experimental intervention.

The approval created a framework: licensed psychiatrists could apply for Authorized Prescriber status from the TGA, allowing them to prescribe these substances to eligible patients outside a clinical trial. The framework required that sessions be conducted with trained therapists present and that patients receive appropriate preparation and integration support.

Implementation has been slower and more complicated than the approval announcement suggested. By mid-2024, fewer than 100 psychiatrists had received Authorized Prescriber status nationally. The compound costs — legally produced pharmaceutical-grade psilocybin and MDMA — were high: a full treatment course cost between AUD $25,000 and $35,000 per patient, with no Medicare coverage. Patients were primarily wealthy and privately funded.

A 2025 report from the Australian Healthcare and Hospitals Association identified the central equity problem: the world's first legal psychedelic therapy program was accessible almost exclusively to people with significant private means. The communities with the highest rates of treatment-resistant depression and PTSD — Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander communities, veterans, people with histories of trauma — were the least likely to access the approved treatment.

The Australian experience is the most important policy evidence available for what happens after approval. The lesson: approval of the treatment does not solve the access problem. A regulatory framework that permits prescription by authorized psychiatrists at unsubsidized cost produces a boutique treatment for the wealthy. The Australian government is aware of this and working on Medicare coverage pathways; as of mid-2026, coverage has not been established.

For the US approval process: the Australian experience suggests that FDA approval of COMP360 psilocybin, when it comes, will produce an initial market serving a narrow population. Whether the equity framework develops from there, or whether the Australian model of expensive boutique treatment becomes the US default, is the most important downstream policy question.

Sources

  • TGA Australia, MDMA and Psilocybin Approval (February 2023)
  • Therapeutic Goods Administration, Authorized Prescriber Scheme Reports (2024-2025)
  • Australian Healthcare & Hospitals Association, Psychedelic Therapy Implementation (2025)

The Students of Schultes: What the Next Generation Found

“Schultes trained a generation of ethnobotanists who went back to the commun…”ethnobotanyhistory
“Schultes trained a generation of ethnobotanists who went back to the communities he had documented. What they found was a race against time that Schultes had warned about and no one had adequately funded.”

Richard Evans Schultes trained more than the 3,000 undergraduates who passed through his Harvard Economic Botany course. He trained a generation of field ethnobotanists who took his methods and his urgency into the field: Wade Davis, Mark Plotkin, Glenn Shepard, William Milliken, among others. Their fieldwork, conducted primarily in the 1980s and 1990s, extended Schultes's documentation project into the period when the race he had described in 1967 was visibly being lost.

Mark Plotkin's Tales of a Shaman's Apprentice (1993) documented his work with the Tirio people of Suriname and Brazil. What Plotkin found was Schultes's aspirin-pill problem in acute form: young Tirio men were choosing to train as health workers in the Western medical system rather than as traditional plant medicine practitioners. The knowledge was not being transmitted. The healer Plotkin had apprenticed himself to had no successor in the traditional sense.

Wade Davis's One River (1996) reconstructed Schultes's Amazon expeditions through Davis's own fieldwork in the same regions, twenty years later. What Davis documented was both the persistence of the knowledge and its precarity — specific villages still had healers with specific knowledge, but the healers were old, the apprentices were fewer, and the botanical contexts were under pressure from agricultural expansion, mining, and road development.

The Amazon Conservation Team, founded by Plotkin in 1996, developed a documentation methodology — community-controlled mapping projects that recorded traditional knowledge in formats the communities themselves owned — that has become a model for ethnobotanical preservation. By 2025, the ACT had supported territory mapping and knowledge documentation projects in more than 70 indigenous communities across the Amazon basin.

What the students of Schultes found, collectively, is that documentation is necessary but not sufficient. The knowledge does not survive in an archive — it survives in people, and people survive in communities, and communities survive on territories. The ethnobotanical preservation project is inseparable from the land rights project.

Sources

  • Davis, One River (1996)
  • Plotkin, Tales of a Shaman's Apprentice (1993)
  • Amazon Conservation Team Reports (2020-2025)

The Peyote Exemption: How Indigenous Rights Shaped Drug Law

“The 1994 AIRFA amendments created a specific federal exemption for NAC peyo…”policyindigenous
“The 1994 AIRFA amendments created a specific federal exemption for NAC peyote use. This is the only federally recognized right to use a Schedule I substance for religious purposes that was not created by litigation.”

The Native American Church's use of peyote in religious ceremonies has been legally protected since the 1994 amendments to the American Indian Religious Freedom Act — but the road to that protection was neither simple nor complete.

In 1990, the Supreme Court in Employment Division v. Smith held that the First Amendment does not require religious exemptions from neutral laws of general applicability. The case involved Alfred Smith and Galen Black, Native American members of the NAC who were fired from drug counseling jobs and denied unemployment benefits after testing positive for peyote following a religious ceremony. The Smith decision effectively removed constitutional protection for peyote use in NAC ceremonies.

Congress responded with the Religious Freedom Restoration Act (1993) and then specifically with the 1994 AIRFA amendments, which added a provision explicitly protecting the use, possession, transportation, and sale of peyote for bona fide religious ceremonies of the Native American Church. This created a statutory exemption — not a constitutional right — for NAC peyote use.

The exemption is NAC-specific. Non-Native practitioners who use peyote for spiritual purposes do not receive the same protection, even within the same ceremony. The Peyote Way Church of God, a predominantly non-Native organization that uses peyote sacramentally, challenged this restriction and lost in the Fifth Circuit in 1991: the court held that the racial classification of the NAC exemption served the compelling government interest of protecting Native American culture.

Colorado's Proposition 122 (2022) navigated this history by decriminalizing mescaline but explicitly excluding peyote from the decriminalization. The drafters made a deliberate choice: the conservation status of peyote and the specific interests of the NAC warranted keeping the plant outside a broader decriminalization framework.

Schultes documented the Huichol peyote pilgrimage with care and respect. The legal history of peyote's status reveals how complicated the relationship between indigenous plant medicine rights and broader drug policy reform has been — and continues to be.

Sources

  • American Indian Religious Freedom Act Amendments (1994)
  • Employment Division v. Smith (1990)
  • Peyote Way Church of God v. Thornburgh (5th Cir. 1991)
  • Colorado Proposition 122 (2022)

The Archive and the Fire: Ethnobotany in the Extinction Era

“We are losing knowledge faster than we can document it. The documentation p…”ethnobotanypolicy
“We are losing knowledge faster than we can document it. The documentation projects are real and insufficient. What Schultes called urgency in 1967 is now crisis.”

In 1967, Richard Evans Schultes told the NIMH symposium in San Francisco that ethnopharmacological research was racing against time. The aspirin pill was arriving. The mission school was transmitting different values. The road was bringing the market. The race to document indigenous plant knowledge before it disappeared was urgent.

Fifty-seven years later, the race he described has not been won. The question is whether it can still be won in meaningful form, or whether the knowledge systems Schultes dedicated his career to documenting are now too damaged to restore.

The evidence: the global language extinction rate — relevant because language is the primary carrier of traditional ecological knowledge — has accelerated. Linguist David Harmon's work with Loh (Bioscience, 2010) found that languages and biodiversity are correlated geographically and decline together. The regions with the greatest biological diversity contain the most linguistic diversity; both are under the most pressure. An estimated one language is lost every two weeks, each taking with it specific knowledge of local ecology, plant uses, and the social context in which that knowledge was transmitted.

The IPBES Global Assessment (2019), the most comprehensive scientific review of biodiversity loss, found that indigenous and local knowledge is declining rapidly alongside the biodiversity it describes. The assessment identified indigenous-managed territories as the most effective conservation units on the planet while documenting the legal and economic pressures that are displacing indigenous peoples from those territories.

The documentation response has been substantial: the Biodiversity Heritage Library has digitized over 60 million pages of botanical literature. The Global Biodiversity Information Facility aggregates millions of specimen records. Ethnobotanical databases at Kew, the Missouri Botanical Garden, and Harvard contain structured records of plant uses across cultures. Schultes's own 24,000 specimens are curated and accessible.

What these archives cannot preserve is what Schultes's colleague Paul Alan Cox called 'the living laboratory of indigenous medicine': the dynamic, context-dependent, community-embedded knowledge that determines when a plant is appropriate, how it is prepared for a specific condition, what spiritual or ceremonial context surrounds its use, and what contraindications experienced practitioners recognize. This knowledge is transmitted person-to-person, in specific landscapes, over years of practice. No database can hold it.

Mark Plotkin's Amazon Conservation Team developed community-controlled knowledge mapping as a partial response: the communities themselves decide what is documented, in what format, and with what access restrictions. The mapped knowledge stays with the community; the ACT provides technical support and legal protection for the territories in which the knowledge is embedded. This approach has documented knowledge in 70+ communities over 30 years.

The limitation: documentation preserves a record of what was known. It does not preserve the capacity to use that knowledge — the trained practitioner who can apply it, the ecological context in which the plants grow, the social institutions that structured its transmission. Schultes's herbarium is one of the most valuable botanical collections in the world. The communities that helped him fill it are smaller, more fragmented, and under more pressure than when he visited them.

The honest assessment of where ethnobotany stands in 2026: the field has done more than Schultes could have imagined in 1967 to document what exists. The forces he identified as threatening — the aspirin pill, the road, the market — have accelerated beyond what the documentation projects can match. The knowledge is being preserved in archives at roughly the same rate as it is being lost from communities. This is not sufficient, and everyone in the field knows it.

Sources

  • Schultes, NIMH Symposium (1967)
  • Harmon & Loh, Bioscience (2010)
  • Brondizio et al., IPBES Global Assessment (2019)
  • Biodiversity Heritage Library, Annual Report (2024)

Who Owns the Pharmacopoeia: Intellectual Property and Sacred Plants

“Schultes documented 24,000 specimens. The communities who guided him have n…”policyindigenous
“Schultes documented 24,000 specimens. The communities who guided him have no legal claim to the 78 pharmaceutical compounds derived from his work. The Nagoya Protocol covers new exploitation. It does not remedy old exploitation.”

Richard Evans Schultes's Amazon herbarium represents one of the world's most valuable repositories of traditional botanical knowledge in Western scientific format. The 24,000 specimens he collected, the detailed field notes, the chemical analyses conducted with Hofmann and others — this archive has been the foundation for botanical, pharmacological, and ethnopharmacological research for fifty years.

Seventy-eight pharmaceutical compounds have been derived from or developed in response to plants documented in the ethnobotanical tradition that Schultes represented. The communities whose knowledge guided the documentation have received no systematic benefit from these compounds.

The intellectual property framework that governs this situation has two parts. The first part — historical exploitation — is outside the reach of any current international agreement. The Nagoya Protocol on Access and Benefit-Sharing covers new commercial exploitation of genetic resources and traditional knowledge, not exploitation that occurred before its entry into force in 2014. The debt to the communities whose knowledge produced the pharmacopoeia has no legal mechanism for remediation.

The second part — new exploitation — is theoretically covered by Nagoya, but implementation is weak. A 2025 Global Health Innovation Center analysis found that the majority of pharmaceutical companies with products derived from traditional plant knowledge had not conducted the prior informed consent and benefit-sharing negotiations Nagoya requires. Enforcement is left to national authorities who frequently lack the capacity or political will to pursue multinational pharmaceutical companies.

The psychedelic industry presents a specific current case. Psilocybin is derived from mushrooms documented extensively by Schultes and others from indigenous Mexican traditions. Ibogaine is derived from the iboga shrub of the Gabonese Bwiti tradition. Both are now the subject of commercial pharmaceutical development programs with patent portfolios and investor backing. Neither program has established benefit-sharing relationships with the communities of origin that would meet the Nagoya standard.

Schultes's work was conducted in the colonial scientific tradition — take specimens, take knowledge, publish in Western journals, build careers at Western institutions. He was personally respectful of the communities he worked with and documented their knowledge with more care than most of his contemporaries. But the structural arrangement was extractive regardless of his personal intentions. The communities remain outside the benefit stream.

Sources

  • Schultes & Hofmann, Plants of the Gods (1979)
  • Nagoya Protocol (2010)
  • Swanson, Biotechnology and the Problem of Property (1994)
  • Global Health Innovation Center, Traditional Knowledge and IP (2025)

MDMA After the Rejection: What the 2024 FDA Decision Actually Means

“The FDA rejected the first psychedelic NDA in August 2024. The reasons were…”policytherapy
“The FDA rejected the first psychedelic NDA in August 2024. The reasons were methodological, not efficacy-based. Whether this is regulatory caution or regulatory failure is the most important contested question in the field.”

In June 2024, the FDA's Psychopharmacologic Drugs Advisory Committee voted 10-1 that the evidence did not support approval of MDMA-assisted therapy for PTSD. In August 2024, the FDA issued a Complete Response Letter declining to approve Lykos Therapeutics' NDA — the first formal application to approve a psychedelic-assisted therapy.

The data: the Phase 3 trials (MAPP1 and MAPP2) enrolled 263 participants with severe PTSD. In MAPP1, 67% of the MDMA group no longer met PTSD diagnostic criteria at follow-up, compared to 32% of placebo. In MAPP2, 71% versus 48%. The treatment differences were statistically significant. The effect sizes were large by psychiatric standards.

The FDA's concerns were not about whether MDMA helped participants. They were about whether the trials demonstrated that MDMA specifically — independent of the intensive psychotherapy surrounding it — was responsible for the benefit, and whether the safety characterization was adequate.

The unblinding problem: participants who receive active MDMA know they've received it — the phenomenological effects are unmistakable. This breaks the double-blind standard that FDA drug approvals depend on. If participants know they've received the active drug, therapist and patient expectancy effects cannot be controlled. The measured treatment difference might be partly or largely attributable to expectancy rather than pharmacology.

The committee was also concerned about therapist boundary violations: reports of therapists engaging in inappropriate conduct with MDMA-treated patients during sessions, including the high-profile accusations against therapists at several trial sites. The FDA found that the safety monitoring for therapist behavior was inadequate.

The FDA's position, as expressed in the Complete Response Letter, was not that MDMA doesn't help people with PTSD. It was that the current trial design cannot demonstrate what specifically causes the benefit in a way that meets FDA standards for drug approval.

David Yaden and colleagues at Johns Hopkins published a perspective in Nature Mental Health (2024) arguing that the FDA's methodological standards were appropriate and that the field needed to develop better trial designs — including active placebos that mimic some phenomenological features of MDMA without the therapeutic effects, and more careful separation of drug and psychotherapy components.

MAPS and others have argued the opposite: that the FDA's standards are impossible to meet for a drug whose mechanism of action involves the subjective experience itself, and that the unblinding problem is a feature of the treatment rather than a methodological flaw to be designed around.

Jay Stevens wrote in Storming Heaven about a research program ended not by scientific failure but by political conditions. The MDMA situation is structurally different: the political conditions in 2024 are more favorable to psychedelic therapy than they were in 1968. The challenge is methodological, not political. But the result — a promising clinical program unable to achieve approval despite positive efficacy data — has structural similarities.

As of mid-2026, Lykos is working on the design of an additional Phase 3 trial that addresses the FDA's methodological concerns. Whether an adequate design is possible, and whether the company can fund it, are open questions. MDMA remains Schedule I in the US while Australia has approved it for clinical use. The gap between the evidence and the approval will persist until the methodological problem is solved or the approval standard is revised.

Sources

  • FDA AdCom Briefing Documents, Lykos MDMA-AT NDA (June 2024)
  • Mithoefer et al., Lancet Psychiatry (2018)
  • Mitchell et al., Nature Medicine (2021)
  • Yaden et al., Nature Mental Health (2024)

Rick Strassman's DMT Trials: The First Controlled Research

“Strassman administered IV DMT to 60 participants in 400 sessions at the Uni…”neurosciencepharmacology
“Strassman administered IV DMT to 60 participants in 400 sessions at the University of New Mexico from 1990 to 1995. He documented entity contact in the majority of sessions. He didn't know what to do with the data.”

Rick Strassman's DMT research program at the University of New Mexico was the first controlled clinical study of a classic psychedelic in the United States in over twenty years. From 1990 to 1995, working under DEA Schedule I researcher registration and IRB approval, Strassman administered intravenous DMT to 60 participants in approximately 400 sessions.

The primary published findings concerned dose-response relationships, cardiovascular safety, endocrine effects, and subjective experience ratings (using the Hallucinogen Rating Scale). These findings, published in Archives of General Psychiatry in 1994 and subsequent journals, established that IV DMT produced rapid, intense, brief (15-30 minute) experiences with a manageable safety profile at doses up to 0.4mg/kg.

What the published papers did not fully capture — and what Strassman's 2001 book DMT: The Spirit Molecule communicated to a general audience — was the consistency of entity contact across participants. In the majority of high-dose sessions, participants reported encountering autonomous entities: beings who seemed to be present in a real place, who sometimes communicated, who were experienced as independent rather than as products of the participant's imagination.

Strassman describes his own disorientation at this finding: his training had not prepared him to take entity contact seriously as a phenomenon requiring explanation, yet the consistency of the reports across participants with no prior psychedelic experience — and the specificity of their descriptions — made dismissal difficult.

The 2023 Imperial College fMRI study (Timmermann et al., PNAS 120(13)) mapped DMT's global brain effects — large increases in global functional connectivity, network disintegration and desegregation, and compression of the principal cortical gradient. It did not isolate entity contact as a distinct neural signature, and no published imaging study yet has: the phenomenology is well documented, the neural specificity is not. The phenomenon is real in the sense of having consistent neural correlates. Strassman spent twenty years wondering what it meant. The neuroscience has now confirmed what he observed; the interpretation remains open.

Sources

  • Strassman, DMT: The Spirit Molecule (2001)
  • Strassman et al., Arch. Gen. Psychiatry (1994)
  • Timmermann et al., PNAS 120(13) (2023)

The Ayahuasca Churches: From Brazil to the Supreme Court

“The União do Vegetal won at the Supreme Court in 2006. The case was unanimo…”policyhistory
“The União do Vegetal won at the Supreme Court in 2006. The case was unanimous. The opinion was written by Chief Justice Roberts. It is the most important legal precedent for psychedelic religious freedom in American history.”

The União do Vegetal (UDV) is a Brazilian syncretic religion founded in 1961 by José Gabriel da Costa, known as Mestre Gabriel, in Porto Velho. Its sacrament is hoasca — ayahuasca — consumed in ritual ceremonies presided over by trained mestres. The UDV has approximately 20,000 members in Brazil and several thousand in the United States.

In 1999, DEA agents raided the UDV's New Mexico temple and seized hoasca, charging the organization with violation of the Controlled Substances Act. The UDV sued, arguing that the Religious Freedom Restoration Act (RFRA) protected their sacramental use of hoasca.

The case reached the Supreme Court as Gonzales v. O Centro Espirita Beneficente Uniao do Vegetal. On February 21, 2006, the Court ruled unanimously in favor of the UDV. Chief Justice John Roberts wrote the opinion: the government had not demonstrated a compelling interest that overrode the UDV's sincere religious use of hoasca under RFRA. The government's arguments — that DMT is Schedule I and that allowing UDV use would undermine drug control generally — were rejected as insufficient to meet RFRA's compelling interest standard.

The Gonzales ruling is the bedrock of American psychedelic religious freedom law. It established that RFRA protects sincere religious psychedelic use from the Controlled Substances Act, and that the government must demonstrate a compelling interest by least restrictive means before overriding such use.

As of 2026, four US organizations have DEA exemptions for ayahuasca: the UDV (SCOTUS 2006), Santo Daime (9th Circuit 2009), the Iowaska Church of Healing (DEA settlement 2024), and the Church of Gaia (first non-litigation DEA approval, May 2025). All other ayahuasca ceremonies in the US operate without federal legal protection, though prosecution is rare. McKenna's DMT visions, which he described in True Hallucinations, are the experiential territory these legal battles have been fought over.

Sources

  • Gonzales v. O Centro Espirita Beneficente Uniao do Vegetal (2006)
  • Beyer, Singing to the Plants (2009)
  • Mindmedicinelaw.com, Psychedelic Legal Status (2026)

Psychedelic Science 2025: The Field Comes Back Together

“Psychedelic Science 2025 drew 12,000 attendees to Denver in June 2025. It w…”historyculture
“Psychedelic Science 2025 drew 12,000 attendees to Denver in June 2025. It was the largest psychedelic conference in history. The field that had been underground for fifty years assembled publicly.”

The Psychedelic Science 2025 conference, held in Denver in June 2025, drew approximately 12,000 attendees over five days — researchers, clinicians, policymakers, advocates, facilitators, investors, journalists, and curious members of the public. It was the largest gathering in the history of psychedelic science.

The content spanned the full range of the field: Phase 3 clinical results, regulatory strategy, indigenous knowledge and ethics, harm reduction, business development, veteran advocacy, religious freedom law, and the political coalition that had produced $50 million in Texas ibogaine research funding. Colorado Governor Jared Polis announced pardons for people convicted of state psychedelic possession charges.

The conference captured the field's current character: genuinely bipartisan, genuinely complex, and in some tension with itself. The researchers presenting Phase 3 clinical data were sharing space with advocates for decriminalization and with indigenous leaders arguing that commercialization of plant medicines without benefit-sharing was a continuation of colonial extraction.

Rick Perry — former Republican Governor of Texas, Secretary of Energy under Trump — was there, speaking about ibogaine for veterans. Rick Doblin — MAPS founder, psychedelic activist for forty years — was there, still arguing for the therapeutic framework after the FDA rejection of MDMA. Shipibo-Conibo healers were there, expressing concern about the commodification of their traditions.

This is the world McKenna was trying to describe when he talked about the Archaic Revival: a moment when psychedelic plant knowledge returned to public discourse, when the institutions that had suppressed it could no longer ignore it, when the culture was reconsidering its relationship to consciousness. Whether the conference represented the Archaic Revival or its co-optation is the question McKenna's framework asks — and which Psychedelic Science 2025 did not resolve.

  • Colorado Sun, Psychedelic Policy Reform (July 2025)

Scheduling Endogenous Compounds: The DMT Paradox

“The human body produces DMT. The compound is detectable in blood and urine …”policypharmacology
“The human body produces DMT. The compound is detectable in blood and urine under normal physiological conditions. Its Schedule I status — 'no accepted medical use, high abuse potential' — applies to a compound the body makes.”

Dimethyltryptamine is Schedule I under the US Controlled Substances Act. It has been since the Controlled Substances Act of 1970. Schedule I status means: high potential for abuse, no currently accepted medical use, lack of accepted safety for use under medical supervision.

DMT is also produced by the human body. Barker et al.'s 2012 review in Psychopharmacology established that DMT is detectable in human blood, urine, and cerebrospinal fluid under normal physiological conditions. It is produced by the lung, retina, and likely other tissues from the amino acid tryptophan through the enzyme aromatic amino acid decarboxylase. The human body manufactures a Schedule I controlled substance as part of normal metabolism.

This creates a legal paradox that has no clean resolution. The Controlled Substances Act schedules chemical compounds; it does not create an exception for endogenous production. The DEA's enforcement focus is on the manufacture, distribution, and possession of DMT in quantities and forms associated with deliberate use — not on the trace amounts found in blood under normal conditions. But the legal distinction between endogenous and exogenous DMT is not written into the law.

The clinical significance: Rick Strassman's hypothesis — that the pineal gland produces elevated DMT during near-death experiences, deep meditation, and REM sleep — has not been confirmed. Strassman documented the hypothesis in DMT: The Spirit Molecule (2001) and has advocated for research to test it. The specific claim about pineal production is disputed; the broader claim about endogenous DMT as a component of altered states remains an active research area.

Colorado's Proposition 122 decriminalized personal possession of DMT alongside psilocybin, ibogaine, and mescaline. The decriminalization applies to the compound as it appears in plant preparations — ayahuasca, for example — and in synthetic form. It does not change the federal Schedule I status. McKenna's account of DMT experiences in True Hallucinations describes encounters with the Schedule I version. Whether they engaged the same system the body uses endogenously is a question the law cannot answer and science has not yet resolved.

Sources

  • Strassman et al., Arch. Gen. Psychiatry (1994)
  • Barker et al., Psychopharmacology (2012)
  • Colorado Proposition 122 (2022)
  • Mindmedicinelaw.com (2026)

The Hemp Economy Herer Predicted: Industrial Cannabis in 2026

“Herer was right that hemp had substantial industrial potential. He was wron…”policyhistory
“Herer was right that hemp had substantial industrial potential. He was wrong that it would undercut petrochemicals, synthetic fibers, and timber paper. The market that emerged is real and modest. It is not the revolution he described.”

Jack Herer's 1985 argument rested on a specific empirical claim: that industrial hemp — Cannabis sativa grown for fiber, seed, and stalk rather than cannabinoid content — was the most versatile industrial crop in agricultural history, capable of replacing petrochemical plastics, synthetic fibers, timber paper, and fossil fuels if prohibition were lifted. He documented this claim with historical sources, scientific studies, and the 1942 US government film Hemp for Victory, which had urged American farmers to grow hemp for the war effort before prohibition resumed afterward.

The Agricultural Improvement Act of 2018 — the Farm Bill — removed hemp from the Controlled Substances Act, defining hemp as Cannabis sativa with THC content below 0.3% by dry weight. This ended eighty years of federal prohibition on hemp cultivation in the United States. By 2025, hemp was being grown commercially in approximately 35 states.

The hemp economy that emerged is real. It is not the one Herer described.

The 2018-2020 CBD extraction bubble was the first major commercial wave. Farmers planted hemp for CBD extraction — the cannabidiol compound extracted from the flowers — responding to a perceived consumer demand for CBD wellness products. The market overproduced massively. By 2020, CBD hemp was selling for less than the cost of processing it. Thousands of farmers lost money. The CBD extraction market has since stabilized at a smaller scale, dominated by larger operators with processing infrastructure rather than the small family farms Herer's vision implied.

Industrial hemp fiber and seed markets have developed more steadily. Hemp textiles are a growing category, with brands including Patagonia and Levi's incorporating hemp fiber blends. Hempcrete — a building material combining hemp hurds (the woody core of the stalk) with lime — is used in a small number of construction projects and has attracted architectural interest for its carbon-sequestering properties. Hemp seed oil and hemp seed protein are established food market categories. Hemp-derived CBD gummies are available in gas stations across America.

What has not developed: hemp biofuel at commercial scale. Hemp-derived plastic replacing petroleum plastic at commercial scale. Hemp paper replacing timber paper at commercial scale. The industrial hemp economy Herer described — in which hemp's superior yield per acre would make it economically irresistible as a replacement for less efficient crops and petrochemical products — has not materialized in the seven years since re-legalization.

The reasons are structural. Industrial hemp processing requires infrastructure — decorticators for separating fiber from stalk, retting facilities, specialized equipment — that was dismantled or never built during the prohibition decades. Rebuilding that infrastructure requires capital investment that takes time and carries risk. Petrochemical supply chains are deeply embedded with cost structures that hemp cannot undercut in the near term even with equivalent performance. Timber paper production has its own entrenched infrastructure.

Herer's claim about hemp's potential was not fabricated. The historical record he documented — hemp as a significant American agricultural product before prohibition, capable of producing fiber, fuel, paper, and medicine — is accurate. His claim that re-legalization would produce rapid industrial transformation underestimated the structural inertia of existing supply chains and the infrastructure gap created by eighty years of prohibition.

The honest assessment in 2026: industrial hemp is a real and growing market, probably reaching $10-15 billion annually within the next decade. It is a specialty agricultural category, not an industrial revolution. Herer was right about the prohibition being unjust and right about the agricultural potential. He was optimistic about the pace and scale of the transformation.

Sources

  • Herer, The Emperor Wears No Clothes (1985)
  • USDA Hemp Crop Report (2025)
  • Brightfield Group, Hemp Market Report (2024)
  • Vote Hemp, Annual Report (2025)

The Ayahuasca Science Since Narby: What Twenty-Five Years of Research Has Found

“Narby published in 1998, when there was almost no controlled research on ay…”neurosciencepharmacology
“Narby published in 1998, when there was almost no controlled research on ayahuasca. There is now. The combinatorial problem he posed remains open. Everything else is better understood.”

When Jeremy Narby published The Cosmic Serpent in 1998, controlled clinical research on ayahuasca was essentially nonexistent in Western scientific literature. He was writing about a phenomenon — the pharmacological effects and cultural context of ayahuasca — that had been documented by ethnobotanists and anthropologists but not studied in clinical settings. The Hoasca Project (1993), a collaboration between Brazilian and American researchers studying União do Vegetal members, was the first controlled study of long-term ayahuasca use, and it had only recently been published.

Twenty-five years later the research landscape is substantially different. The mechanism is well characterized. The therapeutic applications are actively studied. The phenomenology has been measured in hundreds of subjects. The combinatorial problem Narby posed remains open. Everything else is better understood.

THE PHARMACOLOGY

Ayahuasca is a brew prepared from Banisteriopsis caapi (a vine containing β-carboline alkaloids — harmine, harmaline, tetrahydroharmine) and Psychotria viridis or Diplopterys cabrerana (leaves containing N,N-dimethyltryptamine). The β-carbolines are monoamine oxidase inhibitors that prevent the gut and liver from metabolizing DMT before it reaches the central nervous system. Without MAO inhibition, orally ingested DMT is pharmacologically inactive. The combination produces 4-6 hour psychedelic experiences with a characteristic phenomenology.

The specific 5-HT2A receptor binding that drives the psychedelic effects is now characterized at atomic resolution. The contribution of each alkaloid to the overall experience — harmine's mild stimulant effect, tetrahydroharmine's serotonin reuptake inhibition, DMT's primary hallucinogenic action — is reasonably well understood at the receptor level.

THERAPEUTIC RESEARCH

Fernando Dos Santos and colleagues at the University of São Paulo have conducted the most systematic review of ayahuasca's therapeutic potential, synthesizing studies across depression, substance use disorder, and trauma. Their 2016 Psychopharmacology review found consistent evidence of antidepressant effects in both controlled and naturalistic studies, with effects observable within hours of administration and persisting for weeks. The neuroplasticity mechanism — BDNF upregulation, dendritic spine growth — provides a pharmacological explanation for both the rapid onset and the lasting duration.

A 2019 Frontiers in Psychiatry systematic review by Hamill et al. identified 28 studies of ayahuasca in mental health contexts, with consistent positive findings for depression, anxiety, and PTSD. The evidence base is substantially weaker than for psilocybin (fewer RCTs, smaller samples, more heterogeneous preparation) but points in the same direction.

THE ENTITY CONTACT QUESTION

Narby's specific focus — the consistency of serpentine imagery and entity contact across shamanic traditions — has been empirically confirmed in a way he could not have anticipated. Timmermann et al.'s 2023 PNAS paper, using simultaneous EEG-fMRI during IV DMT administration, mapped DMT's global brain effects — large increases in global functional connectivity, network disintegration and desegregation, and compression of the principal cortical gradient. It did not isolate entity contact as a distinct neural signature, and no published imaging study yet has: the phenomenology is well documented, the neural specificity is not. The consistency of the report is established. The neural correlates are beginning to be characterized. The interpretation — whether entities are produced by the brain or perceived through the brain — is not settled by neuroscience.

THE COMBINATORIAL PROBLEM

Narby's core puzzle — how Amazonian peoples identified the specific combination of these two plants from 80,000 candidate species in the absence of any obvious single-session discovery mechanism — remains without an accepted scientific explanation. No controlled research has addressed the acquisition question. The pharmacological interaction is understood; its discovery by human beings without the tools of Western pharmacology is not. This remains the most genuinely open question Narby raised.

Sources

  • Narby, The Cosmic Serpent (1998)
  • Dos Santos et al., Psychopharmacology (2016)
  • Frecska et al., J. Psychoactive Drugs (2016)
  • Hamill et al., Frontiers in Psychiatry (2019)
  • Timmermann et al., PNAS 120(13) (2023)

Peyote Under Pressure: Conservation, Native Rights, and the Psychedelic Industry

“Peyote is not a recreational drug that happens to be used ceremonially. It …”policyethnobotany
“Peyote is not a recreational drug that happens to be used ceremonially. It is a sacrament under ecological pressure from the same forces that benefit financially from other psychedelics becoming legal. This is the most acute ethical contradiction in the current psychedelic moment.”

Richard Evans Schultes documented peyote ceremonies with the Huichol (Wixáritari) people of central Mexico in the 1930s and 1940s — the weeks-long pilgrimage to Wirikuta, the sacred desert where peyote grows; the careful harvesting protocol that leaves the root system intact; the prayers that accompany each cut. He was observing a practice continuous for at least 5,000 years, possibly much longer. Peyote use is documented in the archaeological record of northeastern Mexico at least from 3780-3660 BCE.

As of 2026, Lophophora williamsii — peyote — is listed as vulnerable on the IUCN Red List. Its range in Texas and northern Mexico has contracted by more than 30% since the 1970s due to habitat loss, agricultural expansion, ranching, and overharvesting. The conservation crisis Schultes warned about has materialized.

The NAC DIMENSION

Approximately 250,000-500,000 members of the Native American Church use peyote ceremonially in the United States. The legal protection for this use — established by the 1994 AIRFA amendments after the Supreme Court's 1990 Employment Division v. Smith decision removed constitutional protection — is specific to Native American Church members and bona fide ceremonial use. Non-Native ceremonial use of peyote is not federally protected.

The NAC does not buy peyote from commercial distributors. It sources it from licensed distributors in Texas — the only US state where peyote grows commercially — who harvest from private ranchlands under DEA license. The supply is constrained by the limited range, the slow growth rate of the plant (it takes 10-20 years to reach harvestable size), and the increasing demand from a growing NAC membership base.

The NAC has explicitly requested that peyote be excluded from psychedelic decriminalization and legalization measures. Colorado's Proposition 122 honored this request — it decriminalized mescaline while specifically excluding peyote. Oregon's Measure 109 does not address peyote. The NAC's concern is straightforward: any expansion of legal access to peyote beyond current NAC ceremonial use will increase harvesting pressure on a plant already under conservation threat, and will appropriate a sacred practice without the cultural context that gives it meaning.

THE INDUSTRY CONTRADICTION

The psychedelic industry's relationship to peyote is the most acute ethical contradiction in the current moment. Mescaline — the active compound in peyote — is of commercial interest as a therapeutic compound. Several companies have filed patents for mescaline derivatives and synthetic mescaline production processes. Synthetic mescaline, produced in a laboratory, would not require peyote harvesting and would not raise conservation concerns. The NAC has not objected to synthetic mescaline research.

The objection is to the cultural context: the use of peyote or its derivatives in therapeutic or recreational frameworks that extract the pharmacological compound from the ceremonial tradition that developed it, stewarded it, and protected it through a century of criminalization. From the NAC's perspective, the psychedelic industry's interest in mescaline-derived compounds is another form of the extraction that has characterized Indigenous-Western relations for five centuries — taking the useful part without acknowledging the source.

Schultes's documentation of the Huichol peyote pilgrimage in Plants of the Gods was careful and respectful. He understood that the ceremony was inseparable from the plant's meaning. The current psychedelic industry's engagement with mescaline and peyote derivatives is largely divorced from that understanding — focused on the pharmacological mechanism, not the cultural context.

THE CONSERVATION PATH

Several conservation projects are attempting to address the peyote shortage. The Multidisciplinary Association for Psychedelic Studies (MAPS) has supported peyote cultivation research. The Cactus Conservation Institute documents peyote populations. Some NAC members and affiliated organizations have established small-scale cultivation operations. The growth rate of the plant — the same characteristic that Schultes documented in Huichol harvesting protocols — makes scaling cultivation difficult. A peyote cactus planted today will not be harvestable for a decade.

The conservation problem and the cultural appropriation problem are connected: the resolution that serves both is synthetic mescaline for non-Native therapeutic use, combined with legal protection for NAC ceremonial use of natural peyote, combined with funded conservation of wild peyote populations. This framework has been articulated by the NAC and has not been implemented at policy level.

Sources

  • Schultes & Hofmann, Plants of the Gods (1979)
  • Labate & Cavnar, Peyote: History, Tradition, Politics, and Conservation (2016)
  • Gehr, Drugs of the Dreamtime (2021)
  • Native American Church of North America, Conservation Statement (2023)

The Doors of Perception223 words

Why Huxley Reached for Vermeer

The specific art historical comparison Huxley made under mescaline tells you more about the experience than any of his philosophical claims.

In the pharmacy, looking at an art book under mescaline, Huxley looked at a Botticelli and said yes. He looked at a Van Gogh and said no. He thought of a Vermeer and said: this is the standard.

The Van Gogh judgment is the interesting one. Van Gogh is the painter most associated with ecstatic visual experience. If mescaline produces ecstatic visual experience, Van Gogh should be its validation, not its failure.

But Huxley's complaint is precise: Van Gogh's flowers are symbols of flowers, not flowers. They carry the weight of the painter's feeling about flowers. They point at something beyond themselves. Under mescaline, this additional weight makes them less rather than more.

Vermeer, by contrast, is the painter who disappears into the thing he is looking at. The light on the wall, the woman at the window — these are not expressions of anything. They are presences. The light is exactly light.

This is what Huxley experienced: not a transformation of the flowers into symbols of something else, but the flowers being present as themselves, at a density that ordinary perception reduces.

The specific art historical preference he formed under mescaline follows from the phenomenology. The reducing valve, when it opens, reveals not more meaning but more being — and Vermeer is the painter who most consistently painted being rather than meaning.

The Doors of Perception179 words

Soma vs. Mescaline: The Two Huxleys

Brave New World's soma makes people comfortable. Doors of Perception's mescaline makes people see. Huxley wrote both, and he knew the difference.

Twenty-one years separate Brave New World from The Doors of Perception, and those years are the distance between two different theories of what drugs are.

Soma is a sedative. It produces contentment and eliminates anxiety. It makes the social order acceptable by making its inhabitants too comfortable to notice its constraints — 'Christianity without tears.'

Mescaline does the opposite. It removes the filters that make ordinary existence tolerable. It produces not comfort but clarity — a quality of perception so acute that ordinary management strategies stop working.

Huxley wasn't changing his mind between 1932 and 1953. He was specifying. Brave New World was always a satire about the wrong use of consciousness-alteration — the use that produces compliance. What he found in May 1953 was the right use — the use that produces genuine perception.

Soma and mescaline are opposite ends of the same axis: one drug that makes you less conscious, one that makes you more. The political argument between the two books is about which kind of consciousness-alteration a society should value and which it should suppress.

The Doors of Perception172 words

The Gratuitous Grace: On Not Needing It

Huxley's most careful qualifier is also his most useful one. The experience is not necessary. It is available. The distinction is everything.

Huxley borrowed 'gratuitous grace' from Catholic theology, where it refers to gifts given not for personal sanctification but for the community's good — extraordinary capacities that don't indicate holiness in the recipient.

He applied this to mescaline deliberately. Not a necessary grace — not required for enlightenment. Not a sure sign of spiritual progress. But potentially helpful, to be accepted thankfully if offered.

This qualifier prevents Doors of Perception from becoming a cult founding text. The experience is not necessary. People have achieved genuine mystical realization without any chemical assistance. The reducing valve can be opened by other means: meditation, crisis, love, grief.

What mescaline offers is reliable access. Not guaranteed depth or wisdom — but reliable access to a quality of perception that is otherwise very difficult to produce deliberately.

The current clinical research has confirmed this framing. Psilocybin reliably produces mystical experience in a high proportion of participants in appropriate conditions. The mystical experience, when it occurs, is associated with therapeutic benefit. The drug is a tool, not a destination.

The Doors of Perception206 words

Words and Things: Huxley's Epistemological Complaint

The deepest argument in Doors of Perception is about language. Mescaline was the evidence; the real subject was what words cost us.

Huxley's education argument, buried in the final pages of Doors, is more radical than his neuroscience argument. The reducing valve claim is an empirical hypothesis. The education claim is a value judgment: we have organized formal education entirely around the verbal-conceptual mode of experience, and this systematically impoverishes people.

'Every individual is at once the beneficiary and the victim of the linguistic tradition into which he has been born.' The benefit is access to accumulated human knowledge. The cost is the habituation to mistaking the word for the thing.

Under mescaline, this mistake briefly became impossible. The flowers were the flowers, not concepts of flowers. The difference between these two modes is, Huxley argues, incalculable.

What he is not arguing is that words are bad. He is arguing that words without training in what words cannot do produce a specific pathology: the inability to distinguish between map and territory. Education that teaches only the map, and never teaches that the map is not the territory, produces people who have genuinely forgotten the territory exists.

This complaint is still unmade in most educational theory. The contemplative education movement has partially implemented it. The full implementation — an educational system explicitly cultivating both modes — does not exist.

The Doors of Perception193 words

Eight Hours That Changed Everything

The entire argument of The Doors of Perception is based on eight hours in May 1953. The specificity of the claim is its strength.

Everything in The Doors of Perception is based on a single day. May 4, 1953. A Los Angeles living room. Four-tenths of a gram of mescaline administered at 11 AM.

Huxley was 58 years old. He had been nearly blind since his teens, had watched two world wars, had written the most famous dystopian novel in English. He had read everything about mescaline that existed. He had the conceptual tools — Bergson's reducing valve, the perennial philosophy — to place what happened in context.

And still the flowers surprised him. Still the folds of grey flannel trousers were more interesting than he had predicted. Still the Vermeer judgment emerged from the experience itself, not from prior theory.

This is the value of the specific and the particular. Not 'mescaline produces interesting perceptual phenomena' — every account says that. But this specific observation, by this specific person, on this specific afternoon: the world looks like this. The is-ness of things. The flowers as they are.

The argument of the book earns its authority from the specificity of its evidence. One day, one person, four-tenths of a gram. That's what it rests on. That's enough.

Moksha: Letters of Huxley & Osmond208 words

Why the Letters Matter More Than the Books

The published books are performances. The letters are thought in progress. Moksha is where you see two minds actually working.

Huxley published The Doors of Perception knowing it would be read by a general audience — knowing it was an argument, a frame, a position he was defending. The prose is beautiful precisely because he was shaping it.

The letters to Osmond don't have that shape. They were written quickly, in the middle of thinking, to someone who would understand without explanation. When Huxley writes to Osmond the day after a session, he is reporting, not explaining.

The result is that the letters contain things the books don't. The admission of apprehension before the May 1953 session. The slightly surprised quality of what followed. The uncertainty about whether the next session will be as good. The worry about Leary. The rueful awareness that the counterculture is going to make the careful clinical work untenable.

Huxley in the letters is a different person from Huxley in Doors — not more honest, exactly, but less performed. The philosophical framework is the same. The emotional texture is different. And the emotional texture is where the most useful information lives.

Moksha is the primary source from which Doors was refined. The letters are the laboratory; Doors is the publication. Reading the publication without the laboratory is reading the conclusion without the experiment.

Moksha: Letters of Huxley & Osmond184 words

Humphry Osmond's Underrated Legacy

Osmond coined the word, ran the clinical program, gave Huxley his mescaline, and designed the first psychiatric hospital informed by psychedelic phenomenology. He is consistently the least famous person in any room he enters.

Humphry Osmond coined 'psychedelic.' He ran the most successful LSD alcoholism treatment program in history. He gave Aldous Huxley his mescaline and thereby produced The Doors of Perception. He coined 'sociofugal' and 'sociopetal' and contributed to the design of the first psychiatric hospital informed by psychedelic phenomenology.

He is consistently the least famous person in any room he enters.

This is partly geographical — Osmond spent his career in provincial Saskatchewan, far from the centers of attention where Huxley, Leary, and Kesey operated. And partly temperamental — he was careful, clinically focused, and rigorous in ways that don't generate compelling personal narrative.

What he left is the clinical foundation of everything that has followed. The preparation-session-integration model that every Phase 3 psychedelic trial now mandates is Osmond's model, built at Weyburn in the early 1950s. The word he coined shapes every regulatory and public discussion. The hospital he designed with Izumi is still studied in architectural history.

The letters in Moksha reveal a man of uncommon intelligence and unusual moral seriousness. He deserves to be read as a primary thinker, not as Huxley's supplier.

Moksha: Letters of Huxley & Osmond164 words

The Couplet That Won: Notes on Psychedelic

A word was chosen in a rhyming competition between a novelist and a psychiatrist. The word shaped everything that came after.

The competition between 'psychedelic' and 'phanerothyme' is a competition between two theories of what these substances do.

Huxley's phanerothyme means 'making the spirit visible' — it emphasizes the spiritual capacity, the revelation of something hidden.

Osmond's psychedelic means 'mind-manifesting' — it locates the manifestation in the mind rather than the spirit. One implies a psychological process; the other a spiritual one.

Osmond's winning couplet also contained an acknowledgment that Huxley's didn't: 'To fathom Hell or soar angelic' — the recognition that the territory was bipolar. Hell was available, not only the angelic. Huxley's 'trivial world sublime' implies uniformly positive transformation. Osmond knew that wasn't reliable.

The winning word has served well. Mind-manifesting is accurate and non-pejorative. It does not encode that what is revealed is unreal, that it simulates psychosis, or that it is pharmacologically specific.

The losing word might have been better philosophy. But Huxley's couplet lost, and fifty years of regulatory and cultural discourse have been shaped by the word that won.

Moksha: Letters of Huxley & Osmond204 words

Try to Be a Little Kinder

The conclusion of ten years of correspondence about consciousness, God, mescaline, and the future of civilization was three words.

'It is a bit embarrassing to have been concerned with the human problem all one's life and to find, at the end, that one has no more to offer by way of advice than try to be a little kinder.'

After a decade of sustained intellectual effort about consciousness, the reducing valve, the gratuitous grace, and the proper use of a sacred drug, Huxley arrived at kindness.

The conclusion sounds obvious — trivially available to anyone who has read the Sermon on the Mount. Why did it take mescaline and ten years of letters?

Because kindness, as Huxley is using the word, is not the ordinary sentimental thing. It is the practice of seeing other people as they are — with the same direct perception that mescaline temporarily makes possible — rather than as they are useful or threatening to one's purposes.

The direct perception of things as they are, which mescaline enables briefly and which sustained spiritual practice cultivates gradually, produces, when applied to other people, what we call kindness but which is more precisely accuracy — seeing someone as themselves rather than as a function in your life.

The three words are not a disappointment. They are the completion of the argument.

Moksha: Letters of Huxley & Osmond234 words

Laura's Words at the End

The words Laura spoke to Aldous as he died had been written in his own novel two years before. He thought of everything.

Aldous Huxley's final novel, Island (1962), contains a scene in which moksha-medicine is given to a dying person, and the guide speaks to them through the passage. The words were written by Huxley as what he thought the right words were.

On November 22, 1963, Laura Huxley used those words. She had given Aldous 100 micrograms of LSD at 11:20 AM, as he had requested in writing when he could no longer speak. She spoke to him for several hours as his breathing changed and finally stopped.

Huxley had written the template for his own death in his final published work. He had thought, in his usual systematic way, about what dying with LSD should look like — and had put the conclusion in a novel two years before he needed to use it.

This is either moving or calculating, depending on your disposition. It is both. Huxley was a man who thought about everything, including how to die, and who had the unusual advantage of having found, in his late fifties, a substance and a partner willing to implement what he had worked out.

Laura's letter to Osmond, written within days of Aldous's death, is the final letter in a correspondence that began with Osmond's mescaline session in 1953 and ended with Aldous's death in 1963. Ten years. The correspondence produced a word, a clinical framework, three books, and a blueprint for dying.
