LSD: My Problem Child197 words

The Hunch That Started Everything

Hofmann used the word 'presentiment' — a feeling that there was something here, before any rational reason to think so. The most important discoveries arrive this way.

In April 1943, Albert Hofmann returned to LSD-25 — synthesized five years earlier, filed away when animal tests showed nothing interesting — because of what he called 'a peculiar presentiment.'

Not a hypothesis. Not a prediction derived from chemical theory. A presentiment: a pre-cognitive sense that something remained undiscovered.

The history of chemistry is full of such moments, though scientists are often reluctant to describe them this way. Kekulé's Ouroboros dream revealing benzene's ring structure. Fleming's accidental observation of the mold that killed bacteria.

Hofmann's presentiment returned him to LSD. He was synthesizing it again when he absorbed a small amount through his skin and experienced, briefly, 'an unusual sensation characterized by slight dizziness, restlessness, and remarkable imagery.' He recorded this in his laboratory notebook — the beginning of the most consequential pharmacological discovery of the twentieth century.

The hunch is often the most important part of the story, and the most difficult to transmit through formal scientific writing. Hofmann's memoir preserves it: not 'I hypothesized' but 'I had a presentiment.' The distinction is between rational inference and something harder to name — the capacity to be moved toward what matters before you know why it matters.

LSD: My Problem Child181 words

The Bicycle and the Myth

Bicycle Day has been celebrated on April 19 since 1985. The image of the bicycle is important — not dramatic, almost domestic. The most consequential trip in pharmacological history was a commute.

The bicycle is important.

Hofmann did not have a mystical experience in a mountaintop cave or a darkened laboratory. He rode his bicycle home from work, watched the neighbor turn into a witch, drank her milk, lay down, and waited to see if he was dying.

The domesticity of the setting is part of what Bicycle Day commemorates, whether its celebrants know it or not. The most radical perceptual event of the twentieth century happened on a commute.

Hofmann was 37 years old. He was a chemist doing normal pharmaceutical research. The compound he had returned to out of a hunch turned out to be active at doses too small to weigh.

The bicycle is the mundane container for the extraordinary content. This is appropriate, because what Hofmann discovered was not that the extraordinary exists at some great distance from ordinary life — it was that the ordinary, perceived directly, is the extraordinary. The flowers the morning after were ordinary flowers. The world was luminous because it was exactly itself.

Bicycle Day should be celebrated for the bicycle, not despite it.

LSD: My Problem Child227 words

What Makes a Problem Child

Problem children are not problems because they are harmful. They are problems because they exceed the categories available to contain them.

Hofmann's metaphor — the problem child — is more precise than it first appears. A problem child is not a bad child. A problem child resists the available frameworks for understanding children. The child is not the problem; the framework's inadequacy is the problem.

LSD was genuinely difficult to categorize. It was not a sedative, not a stimulant, not a psychotomimetic in any straightforward sense. It produced effects at doses too small to weigh, lasted far longer than its pharmacological half-life suggested, and generated experiences that the available psychiatric vocabulary could not accommodate.

What made it a problem child was not its danger — its safety profile was superior to aspirin's. What made it a problem child was that it required new frameworks. And new frameworks require abandoning old ones, which institutions resist.

The psychiatric establishment of the 1950s had invested in electroconvulsive therapy, insulin coma therapy, and early psychopharmacology. LSD was not a refinement of any of these tools — it was a different kind altogether. One that worked through an experience rather than through a mechanism. One that required the practitioner to have had the experience to understand it.

The child grew up in the counterculture and was put in prison by the state. The problem was never the compound. The problem was what the compound required of the institutions that might have used it.

LSD: My Problem Child196 words

Sacred Drug: Hofmann's Most Unfashionable Word

Hofmann called LSD a sacred drug and was never persuaded to replace the word with something more clinical. He was 102 and he stood by it.

Albert Hofmann called LSD a sacred drug. Not a useful drug. Not a promising therapeutic agent. A sacred drug.

The word is unfashionable in biomedical discourse. Sacred implies a quality of experience that resists quantification — something not merely effective but meaningful in a way that transcends its mechanisms.

Hofmann was not careless with language. He was a precise chemist. When he chose 'sacred' rather than 'therapeutic' or 'psychoactive,' he was making a claim about the category of thing LSD was.

His argument: LSD works, when it works, by providing access to an experience that human beings have recognized across traditions and millennia as the most important class of experience available — the direct encounter with what is variously called the divine, the sacred, the ground of being. The clinical benefit in patients was, in his account, a consequence of this experience, not its cause.

The current clinical literature has approached this claim through the Mystical Experience Questionnaire, through the finding that mystical experience quality predicts therapeutic outcomes, through the language of 'meaning' and 'insight' that populates patient reports. It has not used the word 'sacred.' But it is measuring something that Hofmann would have recognized.

Food of the Gods225 words

The Mushroom Spoke: McKenna's Literal Claim

McKenna said the mushroom spoke to him and spent thirty years explaining what he meant. He was careful, always, about what exactly this meant.

Terence McKenna said the mushroom spoke to him and spent thirty years explaining what he meant. He was not claiming that a fungal organism had a larynx. He was claiming something more specific: that in states of high-dose psilocybin intoxication, he received what felt like autonomous communication — information that arrived with the character of an outside source rather than a product of his own thinking.

He distinguished this carefully from visual hallucination and from ego dissolution. The communication was interior but alien — using his own internal voice but producing content he did not recognize as his own.

The entity contact literature has confirmed that something consistent is being experienced. The 2019 Johns Hopkins survey found 97 percent of DMT users reporting entity contact; many described the entities as communicating in ways that felt genuinely informative. McKenna's basic description — autonomous apparent communication from an apparent other — is the most common feature of the high-dose tryptamine experience.

Whether the mushroom 'spoke' in any meaningful sense remains open. McKenna held it as an open question, which is precisely what made it worth holding. The question is not 'did a fungus have a conversation with a human?' The question is: what is the nature of the communication-like experience that is so consistently reported? McKenna asked this question before the tools to partially answer it existed.

Food of the Gods198 words

Television Is a Drug: The Argument That Aged Best

McKenna wrote his television critique in 1992. Every sentence has gotten more accurate.

When McKenna called television 'the dominator drug par excellence,' he was making a specific pharmacological argument: that passive screen consumption alters brain states in ways that produce compliance, passivity, and consumption rather than consciousness, agency, and production.

He was extrapolating from 1992 technology — three networks plus cable, editorial decisions made by a small number of gatekeepers with limited ability to optimize for individual psychological vulnerabilities.

What has been built since 1992 is a set of technologies that do exactly what McKenna described but with unprecedented precision. The algorithmic feed uses variable-ratio reinforcement schedules — the slot machine mechanism — to maximize engagement. It knows what each individual user responds to emotionally and serves more of it. Sean Parker confirmed in 2017 that Facebook was deliberately designed to exploit psychological vulnerabilities.

McKenna's television argument is more accurate about TikTok than it was about NBC. The dominator drug he described has been refined into something much more effective at producing the passivity he warned against.

His prescription was simple: stop consuming images and start producing them. The problem is that the technologies designed to help people produce images have been more successful at making them consume other people's productions.

The Archaic Revival: Is It Happening?

McKenna named the Archaic Revival in 1992. Something is happening that resembles what he named. Whether it is what he meant is harder to say.

McKenna introduced the term Archaic Revival to describe a cultural reorientation in progress: a recovery of shamanic practices, plant medicine traditions, and non-rational epistemologies that Western industrial culture had suppressed.

Something is happening that resembles what he described. Legal psilocybin services operate in Oregon and Colorado. Ayahuasca retreat centers number in the hundreds globally. Mushroom cultivation has become widespread. The psychedelic renaissance is genuinely a cultural phenomenon with institutional expression.

But McKenna's Archaic Revival was not primarily about access to substances. It was about a reorientation of consciousness — a shift in how Western culture relates to the natural world. The question is whether current psychedelic culture represents this reorientation or primarily represents the integration of psychedelic experience into the consumer lifestyle it was supposed to critique.

The thousand-dollar ayahuasca retreat. The branded microdosing protocol. The Silicon Valley optimization of psilocybin for productivity. These are not what McKenna was describing. They are the dominator culture consuming the medicine that was supposed to change the dominator culture.

The genuine Archaic Revival, if it is happening, is quieter: the restoration of land to indigenous stewardship, the return of botanical relationship to communities that had lost it, the integration of plant medicine into genuine healing traditions.

Food of the Gods221 words

The Notion of Illegal Plants

McKenna said the notion of illegal plants is obnoxious and ridiculous in the first place. He was describing a category error.

'The notion of illegal plants is obnoxious and ridiculous in the first place.'

McKenna said this as a philosophical observation, not a political campaign. The category error he is pointing at: a plant is not an action. A plant cannot be a crime.

What drug law actually makes illegal is not the plant but possession, cultivation, distribution, and use — a set of human actions. The legal structure attributes criminality to the plant itself as shorthand. When policymakers talk about 'Schedule I plants,' they are making a grammatical error as well as a pharmacological one.

The distinction matters because it determines what the policy is actually trying to accomplish. If the target is a specific plant, the policy is about eliminating the plant — which is both impossible and incoherent. If the target is specific human actions, the policy has a more defensible rationale, though still one requiring evidence about actual harm.

Psilocybin is produced by mushrooms that grow globally on every continent except Antarctica. The legal status of the mushroom does not change the chemistry of the spore. The spore is not illegal. The mushroom that grows from it is not illegal in many jurisdictions. The compound it contains is Schedule I.

The ridiculousness McKenna points to is real. The law has drawn a line around something that grew itself.

Food of the Gods221 words

In Defense of the Stoned Ape (As a Question)

The stoned ape hypothesis has been dismissed as unscientific. What has not been dismissed is the question it asks.

The stoned ape hypothesis gets the ridicule it receives because McKenna presented it with more confidence than the evidence warranted. No archaeological evidence for regular psilocybin use by early hominids exists. The specific three-stage dose-response mechanism he described is not supported by controlled research.

But stripping away the overconfident packaging reveals a question that is real: what role did psychoactive plants play in human cognitive evolution?

This is not a McKenna question. It is an evolutionary biology question, a cognitive anthropology question, a psychopharmacology question. The available evidence — that every known human culture has plant medicine practices, that the 5-HT2A receptor shows evolutionary divergence from other primates, that psilocybin produces neuroplasticity effects in the prefrontal cortex (Shao et al., Science 2021) — does not prove the hypothesis. But it doesn't close the question.

The question deserves investigation on its own terms, with better methodology than McKenna applied. The question is: did the long-term human relationship with psychoactive plants have effects on human cognitive development? This is not obviously false, and it is a question that would not have been asked in modern scientific context without McKenna's willingness to ask it loudly and without the evidence to fully support the asking.

Some questions are important enough that having someone ask them badly is better than no one asking them at all.

Billie Holiday and the Structure of the Argument

Holiday's story is not the drug war's most important evidence. It is the drug war's most humanly legible evidence. Hari understood the difference.

Johann Hari begins Chasing the Scream with Billie Holiday not because Holiday's story is the most important evidence for his argument but because it is the most humanly legible.

The argument he is making — that the drug war was racially targeted, that addiction is driven by disconnection, that punishment perpetuates rather than cures — can be made from statistics. The ACLU's racial disparity data. The Portugal outcome studies. The Vietnam natural experiment. All support the argument more rigorously than a single case history.

But case histories do something statistics cannot: they make the policy real in human terms. Holiday's addiction developed in a specific life, under specific conditions of trauma and racial violence and isolation. Anslinger's persecution of her was not an abstraction — it was a man with a government department deciding that a specific person deserved to suffer.

Hari has been criticized for overstating some elements of the Holiday-Anslinger story — the specific 'Strange Fruit' trigger claim is not fully documented. The criticism is fair. But the underlying argument — that enforcement was racially selective and by design — is supported by the documentary record, and Holiday's story is the human container that makes it legible.

Narrative is not the enemy of evidence. Narrative is how evidence reaches people who would otherwise not encounter it.

Chasing the Scream204 words

The Slogan and the Argument

'The opposite of addiction is connection' is a brilliant slogan and a partial argument. Hari knew the difference. Most readers remembered only the slogan.

'The opposite of addiction is connection' is the most retweeted sentence in Chasing the Scream. It has 25 million TED Talk views. It is used in treatment programs and policy advocacy worldwide.

It is also a simplification of a more complicated argument.

The full argument: social disconnection, trauma, and lack of meaningful purpose are major drivers of addictive behavior, as demonstrated by Rat Park, the Vietnam natural experiment, Portugal's outcomes, and the ACE correlation. Therefore, policies and treatment approaches addressing these conditions will be more effective than those treating addiction as purely pharmacological.

This full argument is correct and important. The slogan distills it into something memorable but imprecise. Opioid withdrawal is a genuine pharmacological process. The chemical grip of dependence is real, if less dominant than pure pharmacological models suggest. The environment model and the biological model are both partly right, and the most effective interventions address both.

Hari knows this — his book contains the nuance. The slogan doesn't. This is a routine feature of public health communication: the compressed version travels further than the accurate version. Whether the slogan does more good by reaching people the nuanced argument wouldn't reach, or more harm by misrepresenting the science, is a harder call.

Chasing the Scream182 words

What Portugal Actually Did

Portugal decriminalized all drugs in 2001. The outcomes were good. Then the social investment got cut. The outcomes got worse. The lesson is not that decriminalization failed.

Hari's chapter on Portugal is his strongest and his most dated simultaneously.

The strongest: the 2001 decriminalization of all personal drug possession, combined with substantial investment in treatment, housing, and employment, produced remarkable outcomes by 2015. HIV transmission among injecting drug users fell by approximately 95 percent. Drug-related deaths dropped. Drug use among young people did not increase.

The most dated: between 2015 and 2023, Portugal's outcomes deteriorated. Drug-related deaths increased, not to pre-2001 levels but enough to complicate the simple success narrative. The primary cause was austerity: the 2008 financial crisis and EU-imposed austerity measures cut the social programs that had made the decriminalization work.

This does not invalidate Hari's argument. It confirms it. His argument was that decriminalization alone is insufficient — what works is decriminalization plus social investment. Portugal's success period was when both were present. Portugal's decline period was when social investment was cut.

The lesson is not that decriminalization failed. The lesson is that decriminalization without sustained social investment is necessary but incomplete. Hari said this. The complexity of the evidence has since made it more specific.

Chasing the Scream211 words

The Commissioner's Last Prescription

Anslinger spent thirty-two years destroying the lives of drug users. He spent his final years medicated with morphine. He apparently never made the connection.

Harry Anslinger died in November 1975, medicated with morphine for his angina. He had spent thirty-two years as commissioner of the Federal Bureau of Narcotics destroying the lives of people who used opiates without medical authorization.

Hari presents this as irony. It is, but it is also something more precise: a demonstration of the categorical distinction that made Anslinger's system possible.

Anslinger's enforcement model depended on a categorical difference between 'drug addicts' (criminals, moral failures) and 'patients' (legitimate sufferers, properly managed by the medical system). The same pharmacological process — the body becoming dependent on opiates — was morally neutral in one category and criminal in the other. The distinction was not biological. It was social.

Anslinger using morphine for angina was, in his own framework, entirely different from Billie Holiday using heroin for the pain of her life. One was a patient following doctor's orders. One was a degenerate criminal.

The pharmacology was identical.

This is not hypocrisy in the sense of Anslinger secretly knowing the distinction was false. It is something more commonplace: a man who genuinely believed in a moral framework that his own life quietly contradicted, and who was never called to account for the contradiction because the framework served the people with power to enforce it.

Chasing the Scream202 words

The Rats and What They Proved

Bruce Alexander's Rat Park proved something real about the relationship between environment and addiction. It proved somewhat less than Hari claimed.

Bruce Alexander put rats in a cage with morphine-laced water and plain water. Isolated rats drank heavily from the morphine. Rats in the social, stimulating Rat Park environment drank very little.

The experiment is real. The finding is real. Isolated rats consumed up to 25 milligrams per day; Rat Park rats rarely exceeded 5 milligrams. The five-fold difference is not an artifact.

What the experiment proved: social environment modulates drug-seeking behavior in rodents. What it did not prove: that social environment overrides pharmacological dependence in all circumstances. A 2020 review found that the specific Rat Park results have 'conceptual but not direct' replication — subsequent enrichment paradigms consistently reduce drug-seeking, but not always to the dramatic degree Alexander observed.

Hari presented the results as though they settled the question about what addiction fundamentally is. They didn't settle it. They shifted it. Before Rat Park, the standard model was pharmacological. After Rat Park, the standard model needs to accommodate environment as a major variable. This is a significant shift. It is not a revolution.

The rats in Rat Park still used some morphine. They chose to spend their lives mostly doing other things. That is the finding: mostly other things. Not no things.

True Hallucinations226 words

La Chorrera: What Actually Happened

Five young Americans went to the Colombian Amazon looking for an indigenous hallucinogen. They found psilocybin mushrooms instead.

The La Chorrera expedition of February-March 1971 has been told so many times that the actual event has become difficult to see beneath its legend.

What happened: five Americans arrived at a remote Colombian mission station, found an abundant supply of Psilocybe cubensis growing in cattle pastures, and attempted a homemade experiment in which Dennis McKenna would vocalize during a high-dose mushroom session in a way that the brothers theorized would bond tryptamines in his nervous system into a permanent altered state.

Dennis spent the following two weeks in an extended altered state. He spoke in complex patterns, made predictions, appeared to be in contact with something. He was also, by his own retrospective account, undergoing a drug-induced psychosis — though a lucid one, from which he recovered fully.

Terence observed and documented. He heard, during his own sessions, what he described as sustained communication from the mushroom — a monologue about time, consciousness, and human destiny that became the basis of the Timewave Zero theory.

Whether what happened at La Chorrera was a breakdown, a revelation, or both simultaneously is the question True Hallucinations raises and declines to fully answer. Dennis has said: something real happened, and I am cautious about what 'real' means. Terence spent thirty years trying to articulate what he received. The two positions are not as far apart as they appear.

The Machine Elves: A Phenomenological Report

McKenna's machine elf description has been independently corroborated by tens of thousands of users who had never read it. The consistency is the data point that matters most.

The machine elves — 'merry elfin, self-transforming, machine creatures, looking like self-dribbling Fabergé eggs on the rebound' — are McKenna's most famous contribution to the psychedelic literature. They are also his most empirically interesting one.

McKenna first described the entities in 1965, from his own DMT experiences. He described them in public lectures through the 1980s and 1990s. His description became widely available before the internet made all descriptions widely available.

What happened when the internet made all descriptions widely available: entity contact reports, in forms substantially matching McKenna's description, proliferated from users who had not previously encountered his account. A 2019 Johns Hopkins survey of 2,561 DMT users found entity contact in 97 percent of respondents.

This is the important data point. McKenna was not the only person to encounter what he described. He was the first to describe it in language that entered wide cultural circulation. The independent corroboration — reports from people who did not know his description before they had the experience — establishes that whatever is being encountered, it is not simply a culturally transmitted expectation.

What it is remains open. McKenna held it as an open question. The neuroscience has established that entity-contact has distinct neural correlates. The interpretation of those correlates is not established.

True Hallucinations191 words

The Timewave Was Wrong and Still Interesting

December 21, 2012 came and went without incident. This does not end the conversation about what McKenna was trying to describe.

The Timewave Zero prediction — that December 21, 2012 would be a singularity of maximum novelty — was falsified without drama. McKenna had acknowledged the prediction was falsifiable. It was.

What survived the falsification was not the specific prediction but the philosophical claim McKenna derived from the I Ching insight: that time has qualitative structure, that novelty is not uniformly distributed, that some moments are more generative than others.

This claim is not scientific in the sense of being falsifiable. But it is not obviously false. It is what the I Ching was always about: the claim that the moment you are in has characteristics, that some moments resemble other moments, that navigation of time requires attention to its qualitative features.

McKenna wrapped this philosophical observation in a mathematical apparatus that didn't support it and attached it to a specific date that was wrong. The philosophical observation survives. The mathematical apparatus is discarded.

The lesson is about the cost of overconfidence: if he had presented the underlying claim more modestly, it could be engaged more seriously. The overconfident presentation invited dismissal of both the wrong part and the interesting part together.

The Brothers McKenna: A Study in Contrasts

Terence and Dennis McKenna went to the same Amazon, ate the same mushrooms, and came back with completely different relationships to certainty.

The most interesting thing about Terence and Dennis McKenna is not their agreement but their disagreement.

They went to La Chorrera together. They ate the same mushrooms. They underwent extraordinary experiences that changed the direction of their lives. They came back with different conclusions.

Terence became the most famous psychedelic lecturer of his generation — voluble, confident, willing to make claims that exceeded his evidence. He built a cosmology from La Chorrera and spent thirty years elaborating it.

Dennis became a neuropharmacologist. He spent decades studying the biochemistry of ayahuasca at the level of molecular mechanisms. He has spoken, consistently, with admiration for Terence's genius and caution about Terence's conclusions. He believes something happened at La Chorrera. He is careful about what 'something' means.

Both responses are legitimate. Terence's produced a cultural impact that Dennis's careful science could not have produced. Dennis's produced knowledge that Terence's cosmological speculation could not have produced.

They needed each other. They had each other. The asymmetry between them is the book.

True Hallucinations194 words

The Virtue of Honest Uncertainty

The most intellectually honest thing McKenna ever wrote was the sentence about being either an unsung Newton or completely nuts.

'Because I am either an unsung Newton or completely nuts, there is very little room to maneuver between these two positions.'

This is the most intellectually honest sentence in McKenna's entire body of work. The Timewave theory was either a genuine discovery about the nature of time or a very elaborate confabulation. There was no comfortable middle ground.

McKenna often performed certainty. The lectures are full of confident assertions about the nature of the universe, the intentions of mushroom consciousness, the trajectory of human evolution. The performance was compelling and was, for most audiences, indistinguishable from genuine certainty.

In True Hallucinations, he dropped the performance. He wrote about La Chorrera from a position of genuine uncertainty — not the rhetorical uncertainty of the thinker who knows the answer but graciously acknowledges he might be wrong, but real uncertainty about an experience he could not account for.

This uncertainty is what makes the book more valuable than his lectures. In the lectures, he explains. In the book, he reports. The reporting — accurate phenomenological description of an experience without predetermined interpretation — is what the field of consciousness studies most needs and most rarely gets.

The Road to Eleusis227 words

What Was the Mystery?

Initiates were forbidden to say what happened in the Telesterion. They kept saying what it felt like. Two thousand years of consistent testimony is the evidence.

The Eleusinian Mysteries kept their secret for two thousand years. No initiate ever described what happened in the Telesterion — what the hierophant revealed, what specifically took place. The oath of silence held.

And yet we know, from accumulated testimony of initiates across five centuries, what the experience was like.

Fear. Trembling. Cold sweat. Then a vision — not described, but referenced consistently as vision, not metaphor. Then a transformation in the initiate's understanding of death.

Pindar: 'Blessed is he who has seen these rites before he goes beneath the hollow earth; for he understands the end of mortal life, and the beginning of a new life given of God.' Sophocles: 'For them alone there is life, while all others have misery.'

The vocabulary is consistent: seen, not thought. Understood from experience, not from argument. The death anxiety that initiates reported being relieved of was not cured by an idea — it was encountered directly and thereby transformed.

This is the phenomenological signature of the psychedelic mystical experience as currently documented. The Mystical Experience Questionnaire measures the noetic quality and the encounter with death and rebirth. These are what the Eleusinian initiates described, in different words, over two thousand years.

The Road to Eleusis' hypothesis is that the pharmacological mechanism was ergot alkaloids in the kykeon. The testimonies of what the mechanism produced have always been there.

The Road to Eleusis202 words

Gordon Wasson: The Amateur Who Changed Everything

Wasson was a banker and an amateur mycologist. He changed Western civilization's understanding of its own origins.

R. Gordon Wasson was a vice president at J.P. Morgan who spent his spare time studying mushrooms. He traveled to Mexico to participate in a Mazatec mushroom ceremony and wrote about it for Life magazine in 1957, reaching three and a half million readers.

He was not a trained anthropologist, ethnobotanist, or classicist. He was a banker who had read everything and was willing to go everywhere.

The Road to Eleusis (1978) is the product of Wasson's peculiar position: an amateur with the resources and access of a professional, able to bring together people — Hofmann the chemist, Ruck the classicist — who would not otherwise have collaborated. The book is possible only because of Wasson's particular combination of amateur enthusiasm and professional network.

The criticism of Wasson has always been that his enthusiasm outran his evidence — that he was too ready to find confirmation of his theories. This criticism is partly fair. The Road to Eleusis is stronger for Hofmann's pharmacological rigor and Ruck's philological exactness.

But the hypothesis would not exist without Wasson. The question would not have been asked. Amateurs with big questions and the means to pursue them are a feature of intellectual history, not a bug.

The Road to Eleusis176 words

391 CE: The Year the Light Went Out

The Eleusinian Mysteries were not fading when they were suppressed. They were still active. An institution serving thousands of initiates per year for a thousand years was abolished by decree.

In 391 CE, the Emperor Theodosius issued an edict banning non-Christian religious practice throughout the Roman Empire. The Eleusinian Mysteries — operating continuously for approximately one thousand years — were prohibited along with all other pagan practice.

In 395 CE, Alaric's Visigoths sacked the sanctuary at Eleusis and destroyed the Telesterion.

The institution was not dying when it was killed. The Mysteries were still drawing thousands of initiates annually in the fourth century. The prohibition was not a response to a failing institution — it was the deliberate elimination of a competitor.

The Christian church's argument against the Mysteries was primarily theological: they claimed to offer direct experience of the divine, which was incompatible with the church's claim to mediate that experience through its institutional forms. The Mysteries were dangerous not because they were corrupt but because they worked.

This is the pattern Ruck identifies as recurring: the suppression of direct experiential access to the sacred by institutions that manage access to the sacred. The Mysteries in 392. LSD in 1968. The pattern is not accidental.

The Road to Eleusis215 words

The Bones and the Ergot: The 2020 Discovery

In 2019-2020, archaeologists found ergot alkaloids in dental calculus at an Eleusinian cult site in Catalonia. The hypothesis that had been argued from text for forty years found its first physical evidence.

The Road to Eleusis was published in 1978. For forty years, it argued from text: the classical testimonies, the Homeric Hymn to Demeter, the pharmacological analysis, the architectural argument about the Telesterion. Compelling and unconfirmed.

In 2019-2020, Juan-Tresserras's bioarchaeological analysis of material from Mas Castellar de Pontós — an ancient Catalan site associated with the Demeter cult — produced significant findings. In dental calculus from a woman buried at the site in the third to second century BCE, apparent ergot alkaloids were identified. In a sealed ritual vessel, ergot spores and residues were found in association with beer-making equipment.

The Catalonia site is not Eleusis. It is an Eleusinian-affiliated sanctuary in the western Mediterranean. But it demonstrates that the cult of Demeter used grain-based preparations that incorporated ergot.

The 2026 Scientific Reports paper by Antonopoulos and Dadiotis then demonstrated experimentally that the preparation method available in antiquity — using lye from wood ash — converts toxic ergot alkaloids into water-soluble psychoactive forms. The chemical pathway was feasible. The archaeological evidence of its use exists at an Eleusinian site.

The hypothesis has gone from 'this might be possible' to 'this was demonstrated to be chemically feasible and archaeologically evidenced at a cult site.' The remaining question is whether the evidence will be found at Eleusis itself.

The Road to Eleusis216 words

Plato's Prerequisite

Plato was an Eleusinian initiate. The theory of Forms may have an experiential source.

Plato was an Eleusinian initiate. Historical fact, not speculation. He was initiated at Eleusis and received whatever experience the Telesterion provided.

The Road to Eleusis does not argue that Plato's philosophy was 'caused by' the kykeon. It argues something more modest: that the phenomenological reference point for the distinction Plato draws — between the apparent world (cave shadows) and the real world (sunlit reality outside) — may have been the Eleusinian experience rather than purely rational argument.

The theory of Forms claims that this visible world is a shadow or imitation of a more real, permanent, meaningful world that can be apprehended by a higher faculty than sense perception. This is a strange metaphysical claim to arrive at by pure reason. It is a very natural claim to arrive at if you have experienced, in a specific context, something that made ordinary reality feel exactly like shadows by comparison.

The psychedelic mystical experience characteristically produces what subjects describe as a sense of encountering more reality than ordinary consciousness provides — that the usual filter is lifted, that what is normally suppressed floods in. This is precisely what Plato's Allegory of the Cave describes.

Whether the kykeon was the source of Plato's reference point is not established. That the phenomenology overlaps in ways worth taking seriously is.

Was It Leary's Fault?

Stevens is careful about assigning blame. Leary was not the only cause of the 1968 collapse. He was the most visible accelerant.

Jay Stevens does not write Timothy Leary as a villain in Storming Heaven. He writes him as a man of considerable intelligence who made a series of decisions that destroyed, in the short term, something more valuable than what he was building.

The chain of causation is more complex than 'Leary's fault.' The CIA's coercive research had already given prohibition its evidence. The counterculture's enthusiastic adoption of LSD had already created the political conditions for suppression. Anslinger's framework was already in place.

Leary did not create the conditions for the 1968 crackdown. He accelerated them.

What he did: he moved LSD from a clinical tool being carefully developed into a public symbol of rebellion against the social order. He made the connection between LSD and anti-war, anti-establishment politics explicit and theatrical. He gave the Nixon administration exactly the association they needed to make scheduling politically viable.

Huxley saw this coming. His letters to Osmond in the early 1960s include the warning that public advocacy would provoke a crackdown. He recognized the impulse as genuine. He was criticizing the strategy.

Stevens's judgment: the impulse was genuine and the strategy was catastrophic. What we cannot know is whether the crackdown would have come anyway, because the political conditions that made it possible were already present.

Storming Heaven190 words

What the CIA Was Looking For

The CIA spent a decade trying to weaponize LSD and produced nothing useful except a casualty. The program's only lasting contribution was Ken Kesey.

The CIA's interest in LSD was instrumental: could it extract information from unwilling subjects? Could it break down psychological resistance? Could it program behavior the subject wouldn't remember or resist?

The answer, after a decade of research including Operation Midnight Climax — in which unwitting subjects were dosed in San Francisco safe houses while agents watched through one-way mirrors — was no to all of the above.

What the program produced: in at least one documented case, a death. Frank Olson, the Army researcher secretly dosed by Sidney Gottlieb in 1953, fell from a New York hotel window.

The CIA program's ironic legacy is Ken Kesey. Kesey participated as a paid volunteer in a CIA-sponsored LSD study at the VA hospital in Menlo Park. He obtained LSD through the research network, formed the Merry Pranksters, organized the Acid Tests, and helped drive the counterculture's adoption of LSD — thereby providing the political conditions that made prohibition politically viable.

The CIA was looking for a weapon. What it found, through the pathway it inadvertently opened, was a movement that helped destroy the clinical research program it was simultaneously trying to weaponize.

Huxley's Warning: The Letter That Wasn't Heeded

Huxley spent his final years trying to slow down what was coming. He failed. The failure was not for lack of trying.

By 1960, Aldous Huxley understood that Timothy Leary was going to destroy something valuable. He said so in letters to Osmond.

Huxley's argument: the experiences these substances provide are genuine and potentially transformative, but the social conditions for their beneficial use are fragile. They require careful preparation, experienced guidance, proper setting, and institutional distance from politics. Any association with public rebellion would give the government the excuse it needed.

Leary heard Huxley's concern and did not share it. He believed the experience was powerful enough to transform people regardless of context, and that democratizing access through public advocacy was more important than protecting the clinical research program.

Both men were right about different things. Huxley was right that the advocacy would provoke the crackdown. Leary was right that the experiences were powerful. Neither was entirely wrong about the other's concern.

What neither anticipated was the speed: the crackdown came within eight years. The clinical program that Osmond had spent fifteen years building was ended before it reached regulatory maturity.

The Resumption: Picking Up Where 1968 Left Off

Stevens documented the interruption. He could not have anticipated its end. The end is happening now.

Storming Heaven ends in despair. The clinical program that Hoffer, Osmond, Grof, and Pahnke had built was ended by a scheduling decision that had nothing to do with the evidence.

Stevens published in 1987. He did not know the interruption would end.

The ending is happening now. COMPASS Pathways has completed two Phase 3 trials for psilocybin in treatment-resistant depression. The NDA submission is targeted for Q4 2026. Johns Hopkins, NYU, Imperial College, and dozens of other institutions are running clinical trials. Australia approved psilocybin for clinical use in 2023. Oregon has a licensed psilocybin services program.

The specific clinical program Stevens mourned — Hoffer and Osmond's alcoholism protocol — has been reproduced with psilocybin. A 2022 NYU trial found that psilocybin-assisted therapy produced significantly better outcomes than placebo for alcohol use disorder.

Stevens wrote a history of an interruption. It has since become a history of an interruption that ended. That is, ultimately, a better story than the one he wrote.

Open in Writing

Storming Heaven198 words

The Two Worlds: Clinic and Culture Cannot Be Separated

Stevens shows why the clinical and countercultural traditions cannot be separated, no matter how hard each tries. They share a molecule.

The central argument of Storming Heaven is about the impossibility of maintaining separation between clinical and countercultural psychedelic use. Osmond and Huxley tried. They built a careful, controlled clinical tradition that distinguished its use from recreational experimentation in every detail of protocol and intention.

The counterculture arrived anyway. Not because the clinical tradition failed — it was succeeding — but because the molecule was the same. The same compound that produced controlled therapeutic experiences in Weyburn and the Maryland Psychiatric Research Center produced the Acid Tests.

The compound couldn't be restricted to those who approached it correctly, because 'correctly' is not encoded in the chemistry.

This is the problem that the current psychedelic renaissance is also navigating. Every clinical trial takes place in a culture that already uses psilocybin recreationally. Every licensed service center operates in a state where psilocybin is simultaneously a therapeutic tool and a recreational substance.

Stevens documents the collapse of the attempt to separate them in the 1960s. The current movement is attempting to manage the relationship rather than enforce the separation — to build regulatory frameworks accommodating both therapeutic and adult-use contexts rather than insisting on one at the expense of the other.

The Emperor Wears No Clothes198 words

The $100,000 Challenge: Radical Transparency as Activism

Herer offered $100,000 to anyone who could disprove his central claims and renewed the offer with every edition. The challenge was never met.

The $100,000 challenge was both a rhetorical device and a genuine offer. Herer included it in every edition: if you can disprove my central claims about cannabis prohibition, hemp's industrial potential, and the suppressed medical literature, I will pay.

The challenge was never met. Nobody collected $100,000.

This does not mean every claim in the book is unassailable. Some of Herer's inferences — the specific DuPont orchestration thesis — exceed what the primary documents can support. But the challenge was carefully scoped to the central historical claims, which are substantially documented.

The challenge was also a way of forcing engagement. Herer understood that his audience would not believe him on authority — he had no institutional authority. What he had was documents. The $100,000 challenge was a dare: if you think these documents say something different from what I say they say, prove it.

No one did. The challenge sat unanswered across twelve editions and twenty-five years, which is itself a form of evidence. Not conclusive evidence — but it suggests that institutional opponents of cannabis legalization, who had every incentive to demolish Herer's argument if they could, were unable to do so from the available documentary record.

Open in Writing

The Emperor Wears No Clothes186 words

Hemp for Victory: The Film That Was Hidden

The US government denied the film existed. Then someone found it in the Library of Congress. The sequence is the argument.

Hemp for Victory is a thirteen-minute film produced by the USDA in 1942. It urged American farmers to grow cannabis hemp for the war effort after the Japanese occupation of the Philippines cut off the supply of Manila hemp.

By the 1980s, the USDA denied the film existed. Library of Congress records did not list it.

Maria Farrow and Carl Packard searched the Library of Congress holdings anyway. They found the film in 1989. Herer announced the discovery. The Library of Congress subsequently acknowledged the film's existence.

The sequence is the argument, compressed to its essential structure. The government produced a film urging farmers to grow cannabis hemp as a patriotic duty in 1942. The same government subsequently denied that the film had ever been made. When the film was found, the government acknowledged it.

Herer used this sequence repeatedly, not because it proved the DuPont conspiracy thesis but because it demonstrated something simpler and more damning: the government had a documented relationship with industrial hemp that directly contradicted its official position on cannabis prohibition. This contradiction was on film.

The film is now on YouTube.

Open in Writing

The Emperor Wears No Clothes184 words

The Timing of Nylon

Nylon was patented by DuPont in February 1938. The Marihuana Tax Act was signed into law in October 1937. Herer said this was not a coincidence.

The Marihuana Tax Act was signed into law on October 1, 1937. DuPont patented nylon on February 16, 1938. Popular Mechanics published its 'New Billion-Dollar Crop' article describing hemp's industrial potential the same month.

Herer's argument: these are not independent events. DuPont needed hemp eliminated from the market to protect nylon's commercial position.

The correlation is real. Whether the correlation is causal is the question historians disagree about.

The case for causation: DuPont's financial institution was Mellon Bank. Andrew Mellon was Secretary of Treasury. Harry Anslinger was Mellon's relative and his appointee as FBN commissioner. DuPont had been briefing Treasury officials on the decorticator technology that threatened nylon. The legislation was drafted by Herman Oliphant, who received DuPont's briefings.

The case against simple causation: the racial panic around cannabis, immigration anxiety, and the moral reform movement were independently sufficient to produce prohibition legislation. DuPont may have benefited without orchestrating.

The honest assessment: DuPont almost certainly benefited from hemp prohibition. Whether it engineered the prohibition or exploited existing political conditions is not fully established. Herer presents the former as fact. The evidence supports the latter.

Open in Writing

The Emperor Wears No Clothes219 words

Anderson's Lesson: Why the Title Is Right

In Andersen's tale, the emperor's nakedness is visible to everyone. The social pressure not to say so is what keeps the fiction functioning.

Hans Christian Andersen's 1837 fairy tale is about the social mechanics of false consensus. Two swindlers sell the emperor clothes invisible to those who are incompetent or stupid. The emperor, unwilling to appear incompetent, admires the clothes he cannot see. His court follows. Only a child says what everyone can see: the emperor is wearing nothing.

Herer's title borrows this structure precisely. The emperor — cannabis prohibition — is wearing no clothes. The scientific evidence for the scheduling was fabricated or absent. The congressional hearings that produced it lasted two hours. The medical evidence supported the opposite conclusion from the one enacted.

The child who says what everyone can see is effective precisely because children have not yet learned the social pressure not to say obvious things. Herer cast himself in this role: the person who will say the thing that everyone with power has tacitly agreed not to say.

The analogy holds well. The emperor's nakedness — the absence of evidence for cannabis's Schedule I status — was visible to anyone who looked at the primary documents. Herer looked. He said what he saw. He printed it and sold it in head shops for thirty years.

The emperor is now partially clothed again, by rescheduling proceedings and medical cannabis markets. The clothes are still not what was claimed.

Open in Writing

The Emperor Wears No Clothes199 words

Jack Herer: The Man Behind the Strain

Herer was born in New York, served in Korea, and spent the rest of his life in documentation and activism. He died in 2010 having been proven substantially right.

Jack Herer was born in New York City on June 18, 1939. He served in the Army as a military police officer in Korea. He encountered the California Marijuana Initiative in 1972 and discovered hemp's industrial potential. He spent the next thirty-eight years documenting the case that cannabis prohibition was an injustice, and he spent the last years of those thirty-eight years being substantially vindicated.

He was not a comfortable person to read or to know. He was loud, repetitive, sometimes imprecise, and cared about being right more than being polished.

It is also the foundational document of the modern cannabis legalization movement. The argument he assembled from government documents — that hemp prohibition was politically manufactured, that the medical evidence was suppressed, that the scheduling was scientifically unjustified — has been confirmed by the policy changes of the last decade.

He died in April 2010 having seen the beginning of what he had worked toward. He did not see the 2018 Farm Bill legalize industrial hemp. He did not see 24 states legalize recreational cannabis. He did not see the DOJ propose rescheduling.

He died with the strain that bears his name on dispensary menus across North America.

Open in Writing

The Cosmic Serpent189 words

The Question That Remains Open

In 80,000 plant species, indigenous peoples found the two whose combination creates oral DMT activity. The standard explanation — trial and error — is mathematically implausible.

The combinatorial problem is the sharpest single challenge in the psychedelic literature to the assumption that Western science has a monopoly on reliable knowledge.

In an Amazon containing approximately 80,000 plant species, indigenous peoples across multiple independent cultures identified the same two plants: Banisteriopsis caapi and Psychotria viridis. Their combination creates oral DMT activity. Neither alone produces the sustained visionary state. The interaction requires knowing both plants and discovering that combining an oral MAO inhibitor with an orally inactive tryptamine produces hours of visionary experience.

The standard Western explanation is trial and error. Across 80,000 species, searching for the combination of two specific ones whose interaction only becomes apparent when both are consumed together. The combinatorial mathematics of this search space are forbidding.

All indigenous peoples asked about the discovery give the same answer: the plants told us. Narby spent a decade investigating what this answer might mean. He did not resolve it. He established that Western science's dismissal — 'hallucination, not information' — is itself a philosophical position rather than an empirical finding.

The question is real. The standard dismissal is inadequate. The correct answer is not known.

Open in Writing

The Cosmic Serpent176 words

The Double Helix and the Caduceus

The medical symbol of the Western world is two serpents coiled around a staff. It is older than medicine. Narby says it represents DNA.

The caduceus — two serpents coiled around a staff — is the symbol of Western medicine. It is ancient: Hermes carries it in Homer. Some form of the twin-serpent image appears in Sumerian iconography from the third millennium BCE.

Jeremy Narby's argument: the double helix of DNA and the twin serpents of the caduceus are the same image, arriving through different pathways. The shamanic visions in which serpents appear are, in his hypothesis, perceptions of the molecular level of life — specifically of DNA, which emits biophotons in the visible range and which, at the scale at which these biophotons might be perceived, would appear as luminous helical structures.

Kekule's Ouroboros is the supporting anecdote: a Western chemist solved the ring structure of benzene after a serpent dream. The convergence of shamanic vision imagery and Western chemical discovery in the same serpent image is the data point Narby emphasizes most.

The hypothesis is speculative but not empty. It is interesting in the specific sense that it generates testable predictions. That is more than most speculation offers.

Open in Writing

The Cosmic Serpent185 words

The Ashaninca Answer

When Narby asked how his hosts had learned the medicinal properties of plants, they answered without hesitation: by drinking a hallucinogenic brew.

The anecdote Narby opens with is the book's engine.

An Ashaninca man tells him that his people learned the medicinal properties of plants by drinking ayahuasca. Narby, trained in social science, interprets this as metaphor — a culturally embedded explanation for systematic empirical observation.

But the man is not speaking metaphorically. He is making a literal claim: the plants teach us about the plants. The ayahuasca experience provides direct information about the pharmacological properties of other plants.

Narby spends a decade trying to dismiss this answer and eventually concludes that he cannot. Not because he accepts it uncritically — he does not — but because no alternative explanation is adequate to the phenomenon being explained.

The specific phenomenon: indigenous Amazonian pharmacological knowledge is systematically accurate. The compounds isolated from plants Schultes documented have produced medical treatments. The knowledge works.

If the knowledge works, and if the people who hold it say it came from the plants, the scientific response should be to take this seriously as data — not to accept it uncritically, but to design investigation around it rather than dismissing it before investigation.

Open in Writing

The Cosmic Serpent199 words

The Sacred Is Not for Sale

Narby reports a principle found in every shamanic tradition he studied: the sacred is not for sale. The use of spiritual knowledge for personal accumulation is, by definition, black magic.

'In shamanic traditions, it is invariably specified that spiritual knowledge is not marketable. The sacred is not for sale; the use of this knowledge for the accumulation of personal power is the definition of black magic.'

Narby is reporting a consistent finding, not editorializing. The rule is definitional to shamanism: what distinguishes the healer from the sorcerer is not the knowledge but the orientation toward it. Knowledge used for the community is healing. Knowledge used for personal power is sorcery.

The global ayahuasca economy has not been built on this principle. Retreat centers sell access to ayahuasca ceremonies. Traditional designs appear on products without benefit-sharing. Shamanic healing frameworks are marketed to Western wellness consumers.

This is not Narby's main argument — he makes it as a description of what the traditions themselves say. But the principle he reports is the most direct possible challenge to the psychedelic retreat industry's business model.

If the sacred is not for sale, then the $500-per-night ayahuasca retreat is, by the tradition's own definition, not engaged in healing. It is engaged in something the tradition calls black magic. Whether this framing should shape policy is debated. That Narby was reporting it accurately is not.

Open in Writing

The Cosmic Serpent191 words

Knowledge Without Mechanism: What Narby Gets Right

The most defensible claim in The Cosmic Serpent is the simplest: indigenous pharmacological knowledge is reliably accurate. How it was acquired is the open question.

The critics of The Cosmic Serpent are right that Narby's DNA-serpent-biophoton hypothesis is speculative and that he moves too readily from correlation to causation. They are wrong if they take this criticism to undermine the book's central argument.

The central argument is not about DNA. It is about epistemology: Western science has a standard of evidence that it applies inconsistently. Evidence that indigenous pharmacological knowledge is reliably accurate would, in any other domain, trigger serious investigation of how that knowledge was acquired. In this domain, it triggers dismissal of the explanation the knowledge holders provide — on the grounds that the explanation involves experiences that are epistemologically inadmissible.

The inadmissibility is a prior, not a finding. Western science has not found that ayahuasca visions cannot convey accurate pharmacological information. It has assumed they cannot, dismissed the testimonies that claim they do, without investigation.

The most defensible version of the Cosmic Serpent argument is not the DNA hypothesis but the epistemological challenge: 'We don't know how they knew' is a different statement from 'they didn't know.' The conflation of these two statements is not science. It is the refusal of a question.

Plants of the Gods198 words

The Aspirin Pill: Schultes's Most Prescient Observation

In 1967, Schultes said the greatest enemy of ethnopharmacological research was the aspirin pill. He was right. The pill is cheap; the knowledge is not.

'Perhaps the greatest enemy of ethnopharmacological research is the arrival and cheap availability of the aspirin pill.'

Schultes said this at the NIMH symposium in 1967, and it has become one of the most quoted observations in ethnobotany. Its truth has not diminished.

The mechanism is simple: when aspirin becomes available in a community that previously used plant-based pain relief, the plant-based practices begin to atrophy. The motivation to maintain and transmit the knowledge diminishes when a cheaper, more reliable alternative is available. The apprenticeship is long, the knowledge is complex, and the aspirin pill is easier.

This process has been documented across the world. The young people who might have become traditional healers choose other paths because Western medicine is available and the plants require decades of study.

What is lost with each atrophied knowledge tradition is not replaceable by the archive. Schultes's herbarium specimens are dried plant matter. They preserve the plant's chemistry but not the knowledge of dose, preparation, context, contraindication, and ceremonial integration that makes the plant useful. The knowledge requires a living person who learned it from another living person in a specific ecological and cultural context.

The aspirin pill continues to arrive.

Open in Writing

Plants of the Gods211 words

Why the Suit Mattered

Schultes wore a suit and tie in the field for fifty years. This was not eccentricity. It was a statement about how he understood his relationship with the communities he worked with.

The image of Richard Evans Schultes in a suit and tie in the Colombian Amazon has become legendary in ethnobotany — partly because it is genuinely remarkable, partly because Wade Davis described it in One River with enough specificity that anyone who read the book will never forget it.

The suit was not about fashion. It was about how Schultes understood the ethics of his fieldwork.

The standard anthropological approach of his era was either colonial (the scientist extracts knowledge and leaves) or romantic (the scientist goes native, adopts local dress and customs). Schultes did neither. He went to communities as a scientist — with notebooks, botanical presses, and the apparatus of professional inquiry — but he also took those communities seriously as holders of systematic knowledge.

The suit communicated: I am here to do professional work. Your knowledge is professional knowledge. I am not a tourist, and I am not going to pretend to be you. I am going to be myself, and I expect you to be yourselves, and we are going to learn from each other as professional equals.

The communities Schultes worked with were not confused about what he was. He was not confused about what they were. The suit was the sartorial expression of that clarity.

Open in Writing

Plants of the Gods174 words

How Schultes Found the Mushrooms

Schultes identified the sacred mushrooms of Mexico in 1938. He sent specimens to Hofmann's laboratory. Hofmann isolated psilocybin. The collaboration made Plants of the Gods possible.

When Gordon Wasson published his Life magazine article about the Mazatec mushroom ceremony in 1957, he was not the first Westerner to have identified the sacred mushrooms. That was Schultes, who had traveled to Oaxaca in 1938 — nearly twenty years earlier — and had identified the mushrooms used in Mazatec ceremony, collected specimens, and sent them for analysis.

The 1938 identification was not widely publicized, partly because Schultes was at the time a graduate student without the institutional platform that would later give his findings wider reach.

When Wasson's 1957 article created widespread interest, Schultes had the relevant botanical documentation already in his archives. He facilitated the exchange that led to Hofmann receiving specimens and isolating psilocybin and psilocin in 1958.

The collaboration between Schultes and Hofmann that produced Plants of the Gods twenty years later was the culmination of a two-decade relationship that had started with mushroom specimens from Oaxaca. The field knowledge and the laboratory analysis had been in dialogue since 1938 — the book was the record of that dialogue.

Open in Writing

Plants of the Gods178 words

The Urgency Is Still Real

Schultes called the investigation urgent in 1967. Fifty-seven years later, the urgency has not decreased.

'In the search for new hallucinogens, we have much to do and little time in which to do it.'

Schultes said this in 1967. He was describing a race between documentation and destruction — a race he knew he was losing.

In 2026, the urgency he described has not diminished. The Amazon has lost approximately 20 percent of its forest cover since Schultes made this statement. An estimated language — the primary carrier of ethnobotanical knowledge — is lost every two weeks globally.

What has changed is the response. Mark Plotkin's Amazon Conservation Team, the ICEERS Foundation, the Society of Ethnobiology, and dozens of other organizations are working to document, protect, and transmit the knowledge that Schultes identified as endangered. The Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework (2022) includes specific provisions for indigenous-managed territories.

This is progress. It is not sufficient. The race Schultes was watching in 1967 is still being lost at the macro scale, while individual documentation and protection efforts slow it in specific places.

Plants of the Gods was published as an emergency document. It remains one.

Open in Writing

Plants of the Gods218 words

The Riddle Schultes Couldn't Answer

Schultes spent twelve years in the Amazon and documented the ayahuasca preparation in systematic detail. He never answered the question of how it was discovered. He didn't pretend to.

Schultes documented the ayahuasca preparation more systematically than any previous Western researcher. He identified the botanical species, the preparation methods, the regional variations, the ritual contexts, and the pharmacological properties.

He did not explain how it was discovered.

In twelve years of fieldwork, Schultes heard the same answer Narby would hear twenty years later: we were taught by the plants. He recorded this in his field notes without elaboration. He was a botanist, not a philosopher of knowledge. The question of how indigenous peoples had identified the two specific plants in a forest of 80,000 species whose combination created an effect that neither plant alone produced was, to Schultes, an interesting question beyond his ability to answer.

He was honest about this in a way that subsequent commentators often are not. The standard 'trial and error over millennia' explanation is not one Schultes endorsed — he knew too much about the pharmacology and the search space to find it convincing. But he did not substitute a better explanation. He documented what was there and moved on.

Narby's Cosmic Serpent is, in part, the attempt to construct the explanation that Schultes declined to attempt. Whether it succeeds is debated. That the attempt was necessary — that the question Schultes declined to answer was real and important — is not.

The Scientific Annotation Layer

Then vs. Now

What the books claimed vs. what the science shows now — 112 comparisons across 11 books, each with the source entries attached to it.

Then (1992) — Food of the Gods

The Stoned Ape: Was McKenna Right?

Psilocybin mushrooms catalyzed human brain expansion, language, and consciousness. The doubling of the hominin brain over two million years was driven in part by psilocybin's effects on neuroplasticity and visual acuity.
It's Complicated
The neuroplasticity claim is partially supported: psilocybin does promote dendritic spine growth (Shao et al. 2021) and new synaptic connections. The specific evolutionary timeline lacks fossil or genetic confirmation. The mechanism McKenna proposed — improved hunting via visual acuity at low doses — is plausible but untested. The broad intuition (that the relationship between humans and psychoactive plants is ancient and significant) is well-supported by the archaeological record. The specific causal chain is not.

Sources

  • McKenna, Food of the Gods (1992)
  • Nichols, Pharmacological Reviews 68(2) (2016)
  • Shao et al. 2021
Then (1954) — The Doors of Perception

The Reducing Valve: Was Huxley Right?

The brain acts as a "reducing valve," filtering out most of what consciousness could perceive to prevent sensory overwhelm. Mescaline disables this filter, allowing access to "Mind at Large" — not creating hallucinations but removing suppression of what was already there.
Confirmed by Science
The default mode network model in contemporary neuroscience is structurally similar: the DMN maintains predictive models that suppress perceptual inputs not confirming expectations. Psychedelics reduce DMN connectivity (documented across multiple fMRI studies). The predictive coding framework formalizes what Huxley described intuitively. The asymmetry Huxley failed to account for — that opened perception is sometimes terrifying, not just beautiful — remains without a complete explanation in either model.

Sources

  • Huxley, The Doors of Perception (1954)
  • Nichols, Pharmacological Reviews (2016)
  • Carhart-Harris et al., various
Then (1990s) — True Hallucinations

The Pineal Gland as DMT Source: Was Strassman Right?

The pineal gland produces DMT endogenously, particularly at birth, death, and during deep meditation or near-death experiences. This endogenous DMT mediates mystical and anomalous experiences.
It's Complicated
Confirmed: DMT is present in human blood, urine, and cerebrospinal fluid — an endogenous compound. The pineal as primary production site: not confirmed. The pineal contains the enzyme machinery required for DMT synthesis, but measurement data showing it produces DMT in pharmacologically significant quantities does not yet exist. The broader hypothesis (endogenous DMT mediates naturally occurring mystical states) remains open and scientifically interesting.

Sources

  • Nichols, Pharmacological Reviews (2016)
  • Roney-Dougal in Paranthropology Vol.2 No.2 (2011)
Then (1970) — Storming Heaven

Psychedelic Prohibition: What the Evidence Actually Showed

LSD and other psychedelics were placed in Schedule I in 1970 as substances with "no accepted medical use" and "high potential for abuse." The Nixon administration and congressional testimony described them as highly dangerous with no therapeutic value.
Refuted by Evidence
The Cambridge HPS dissertation (2007) documented that 40,000+ patients received LSD therapy in the 1950s-70s with promising outcomes. The Schedule I classification was based on inadequate evidence and driven by political rather than pharmacological reasoning. Current Phase 2/3 clinical trials at Johns Hopkins, NYU, Imperial College, and MAPS show significant therapeutic efficacy for depression, PTSD, addiction, and anxiety in terminal illness. David Nichols (2016): no established physiological lethal dose for classical psychedelics.

Sources

  • Medical History of Psychedelic Drugs, Cambridge HPS (2007)
  • Nichols, Pharmacological Reviews (2016)
  • Marlan, Beyond Cannabis (2019)
Then (1978) — The Road to Eleusis

The Kykeon Hypothesis: Eleusis and the Ergot

The kykeon — the ritual drink consumed by initiates at the Eleusinian Mysteries — contained an ergot-derived psychedelic. The Mysteries' power to transform the most philosophically sophisticated people in the ancient world came from a pharmacological experience.
Still Open
The hypothesis remains unconfirmed but has not been refuted. Hofmann's chemistry (that a psychoactive ergot preparation was achievable with ancient technology) stands. The botanical question — whether Claviceps purpurea was present in Eleusinian barley in sufficient form — remains debated. The Ruck philological argument (that the accounts describe pharmacological experience, not theatrical ritual) continues to be debated among classicists. The 2,000-year oath of silence makes definitive evidence structurally unavailable.

Sources

  • Wasson, Hofmann & Ruck, The Road to Eleusis (1978)
  • Medical History of Psychedelic Drugs, Cambridge HPS (2007)
Then (1970s–1980s) — Chasing the Scream

Rat Park: Was Alexander Right?

Social isolation, not pharmacological dependency, is the primary driver of addictive behavior. Rats in enriched social environments with other rats largely choose plain water over drug-laced water, even after being forced to consume drugs.
Confirmed by Science
Rat Park has been replicated in multiple formats. The broader principle — that social connection, meaning, and purpose are protective factors against addictive behavior — has substantial epidemiological support in human populations. Portugal's 2001 decriminalization, which invested drug enforcement savings in social services and treatment, produced sustained declines in HIV transmission, drug-related deaths, and incarceration. The ayahuasca and psilocybin therapeutic literature shows that integration (ongoing social/therapeutic support post-session) determines outcomes more than the pharmacological event itself.

Sources

  • Hari, Chasing the Scream (2015)
  • Labate & Cavnar, Ayahuasca Healing and Science (2021)
Then (1954) — The Doors of Perception

Art as 'Ersatz Suchness': Huxley's Claim

Art is 'only for beginners' — a preparation for direct experience, not a substitute for it. The best art points toward the kind of direct perception mescaline temporarily enables, but cannot itself deliver that perception.
contested
Aesthetic neuroscience has complicated Huxley's hierarchy. Studies of peak aesthetic experiences show they activate many of the same brain regions as psychedelic-induced states — particularly the default mode network and salience network in overlapping ways. The distinction between mediated aesthetic experience and direct perception may be less categorical than Huxley claimed. That said, qualitative studies of psychedelic experience consistently report a quality of perceptual immediacy that subjects describe as categorically different from aesthetic rapture. The debate remains open.

  • Chatterjee & Vartanian, Science (2014)
  • Barrett et al., Front. Psychol. (2017)

Then (1954) — The Doors of Perception

Mescaline and Schizophrenia: The Psychotomimetic Theory

The mescaline experience illuminates schizophrenia from the inside. The schizophrenic, Huxley argued, is permanently in a state analogous to what the mescaline session temporarily produces — unable to filter the overwhelming flood of unmediated experience.
partially-confirmed
The schizophrenia-psychedelic analogy remains active in research but is more nuanced than Huxley described. Classic psychedelics and schizophrenia both involve 5-HT2A receptor activity and both show increased thalamocortical activity, but the phenomenologies differ significantly: psychedelic states are typically accompanied by insight and preserved reality-testing, while acute psychosis often is not. The Osmond-Hoffer model of LSD as a 'psychotomimetic' for training clinicians has been partly revived — Johns Hopkins now trains therapists partly through psychedelic experience — but the mechanistic claims are disputed.

Then (1954) — The Doors of Perception

Psychedelic Education Reform: Huxley's Proposal

Education that teaches only verbal reasoning produces people who mistake symbols for things. A complete education would include training in direct perception — and mescaline could assist this training in appropriate contexts.
emerging
As of 2025, no jurisdiction has formally integrated psychedelic education into curriculum. However, 'contemplative education' — mindfulness, somatic practices, non-verbal learning modalities — has gained significant institutional traction in K-12 and university settings. Johns Hopkins and NYU now train clinicians through guided psychedelic experiences. Oregon's Measure 109 (2023) created a licensed service framework for psilocybin sessions. The educational argument Huxley made remains ahead of institutional readiness but is no longer fringe.

Then (1954) — The Doors of Perception

The Gratuitous Grace: Huxley's Theology

The mescaline experience is a 'gratuitous grace' — not necessary to salvation but potentially helpful, to be accepted thankfully if available. It is compatible with genuine religious life and may prepare the way for deeper practice.
confirmed
Current psilocybin research routinely measures 'mystical experience' using validated scales (MEQ30) and finds it both common and therapeutic. A 2024 meta-analysis found that mystical experience quality predicts therapeutic outcomes better than drug dose. Several US religious communities (Native American Church, UDV, Santo Daime) now have legal religious exemptions for sacramental psychedelic use under RFRA. The 'gratuitous grace' framing — not salvation but a gift to be received properly — maps closely to how current clinical practice treats the experience.

Then (1956) — Moksha: Letters of Huxley & Osmond

The Psychedelic Word: Osmond's Coinage in 2025

Osmond coined 'psychedelic' to replace 'psychotomimetic' and 'hallucinogen' — arguing that 'mind-manifesting' was a more accurate description of what these substances do. He and Huxley believed the word would shape how the substances were researched.
It's Complicated
The word 'psychedelic' became dominant in both research and culture — but its meaning has drifted far from Osmond's original clinical intent. 'Entheogen' (coined by Ruck et al. in 1979) is now preferred in ethnobotanical contexts. 'Classical serotonergic psychedelics' is the preferred neuroscience term. 'Hallucinogen' has partially returned in regulatory documents. 'Psychedelic' is simultaneously the most culturally powerful and most definitionally unstable of the available terms. Osmond's hope that the naming would control the framing has been only partially realized.

  • Osmond, Ann. N.Y. Acad. Sci. (1957)
  • Nichols, Pharmacol. Rev. (2016)
  • Ruck et al., J. Psychedelic Drugs (1979)
Then (1954-1960) — Moksha: Letters of Huxley & Osmond

LSD as Alcoholism Treatment: Hoffer-Osmond Results

Hoffer and Osmond treated over 1,000 alcoholic patients with LSD at Weyburn. Approximately half achieved lasting sobriety — a result they attributed to the peak mystical experience the drug could produce. They argued LSD worked by providing the same kind of insight that underlies spontaneous recovery from alcoholism.
contested
A 2012 meta-analysis of six randomized trials from the 1960s-70s (Krebs & Johansen, J. Psychopharmacol.) found LSD associated with a significant reduction in alcohol misuse, with effects lasting six to twelve months. Psilocybin for alcohol use disorder showed promising results in a 2022 RCT at NYU (Bogenschutz et al., JAMA Psychiatry) — the first such trial since prohibition. As of 2025, MAPS-affiliated researchers are running Phase 2 trials of psilocybin for AUD. The Hoffer-Osmond result has been substantially reproduced, fifty years later.

Then (1963) — Moksha: Letters of Huxley & Osmond

LSD Assisted Dying: Huxley's Death

Huxley requested LSD for his death from laryngeal cancer, and Laura administered it as he lost consciousness. His death was described by attending nurses as unusually serene. He had long argued that psychedelics could ease the transition of death.
confirmed
Psilocybin for end-of-life anxiety is now the most replicated finding in psychedelic medicine. A 2016 double-blind study at Johns Hopkins (Griffiths et al.) found that a single psilocybin session reduced end-of-life anxiety and depression in cancer patients with effects persisting six months. A 2016 NYU study produced similar results. A 2023 meta-analysis confirmed the effect size. As of 2025, COMPASS Pathways is running Phase 3 trials for psilocybin in treatment-resistant depression, and LSD-assisted therapy for anxiety is in Phase 2 at several European sites. Huxley's intuition has become a robust clinical program.
